But those [heats] contained in fine-particled substances sometimes do not bite at all, but only heat; and there are times when it is biting, yet does not thereby also burn.

One must keep in mind the notion of fine-particled and coarse-particled things, namely that we call fine-particled those which are quickly dissolved into fine parts, and coarse-particled those which cannot undergo this.

Now that which dissolves them is the heat in the body of the animal, in whatever manner they happen to be applied on each occasion; but their being broken up into fine or coarse parts they have from their own nature, so that, among cooling drugs too, those which are coarse-particled cannot bite, since they do not get so far as to penetrate the outer surface of the skin.

beads.greek: ὅσα δὲ λεπτομερῆ καὶ διαδύεται ῥᾳδίως καὶ πρὸς τὸ [628] βάθος ἐξικνεῖται καὶ δάκνει τὰ μαλακὰ τοῦ ζώου μόρια, μᾶλλον δ’ ἔτι δάκνει τὰ λεπτομερῆ τε ἅμα καὶ ταῖς κράσεσιν ἀνώμαλα. δέδεικται δ’ ἐν τοῖς πρόσθεν ὡς σχεδὸν ἅπαντά ἐστιν ἀνώμαλα.
beads.english: But those that are fine-particled both penetrate easily and reach to the [628] depth and bite the soft parts of the animal; and still more biting are those that are at once fine-particled and uneven in their mixtures.

beads.greek: ἢ γὰρ ἀδύνατον, ἢ πάνυ χαλεπὸν ἐξευρεῖν οὐσίαν ἡντιναοῦν ἀκριβῶς ὁμοιομερῆ.
beads.english: And it has been shown in what precedes that nearly all are uneven.

beads.greek: τὸν γοῦν οἶνον ἐλέγομεν ἓν μὲν ἔχειν ἐν αὑτῷ περίττωμα παχυμερὲς, ἐξ οὗ τῷ χρόνῳ διακρινομένου τε καὶ καταφερομένου συνίστασθαι τὴν τρύγα.
beads.english: For it is either impossible or very difficult to find any substance whatsoever that is precisely homoeomerous.

beads.greek: ἕτερον δ’, ὅπερ ἄνθος ὀνομάζεται, κατὰ μὲν τὸν τῆς ζέσεως χρόνον πολάζον, ὕστερον δ’ εἰς τὴν τρύγα καταφερόμενον. ἄλλο δὲ τρίτον ὑδατῶδες, ἀναμεμιγμένον ἅπαντι τῷ οἴνῳ, οὗ καὶ τὴν ζέσιν εἶναι πρῶτον καὶ μάλιστα.

beads.greek: τέταρτον δ’ ἐπὶ τούτοις ἐστὶν αὐτὸς ὁ ὄντως οἶνος.
beads.english: And a fourth, in addition to these, is the real wine itself.

beads.greek: δέδεικται δ’ ὡς καὶ κατὰ τοὔλαιον καὶ τὸ γάλα καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους ἅπαντας χυλοὺς ὁμοία φύσις ἐστὶ περιττωμάτων, ἔτι δὲ μᾶλλον ἒν ὅλοις τοῖς μεταλλευομένοις ἅπασιν.
beads.english: And it has been shown that in oil too and in milk and in all the other juices there is a similar nature of residues, and still more in all mined substances taken as wholes.

beads.greek: ὧν ἀναμνησθέντας χρὴ νῦν ἐπισκέψασθαι περὶ τῶν φαρμάκων ἁπάντων, καὶ πρῶτον μὲν φυλάξασθαι παθεῖν ὅπερ οἱ πλεῖστοι τῶν τὰ τοιαῦτα ζητησάντων ﻿ [629] ἔπαθον.
beads.english: Having recalled these things, we must now investigate concerning all drugs, and first of all guard against suffering what most of those who have inquired into such matters [629] have suffered.

beads.greek: ὡς γὰρ ὁμοιομερῶν ἁπάντων ὄντων, οὕτω ποιοῦνται τὸν λόγον, οὐ συγχωροῦντες οὔτε τὸν οἶνον οὔτε τοὔλαιον οὔτε τῶν ἄλλων οὐδὲν ἐκ διαφερόντων ταῖς δυνάμεσι συγκεῖσθαι μορίων, ἔτι δὲ τούτων μᾶλλον ἐπὶ ὄξους θαυμάζουσιν εἰ τολμῶμεν αὐτὸ λέγειν, ἀπολωλεκέναι μὲν τὴν ἔμφυτον τοῦ οἴνου θερμότητα, τὴν δ’ ἐκ σήψεως ἔχειν, ὅπερ δὴ καὶ Ἀριστοτέλει καὶ Θεοφράστῳ δοκεῖ.
beads.english: For they construct their argument as though all of them were homoeomerous, not conceding that either wine or oil or any of the others is composed of parts differing in their powers; and still more than in these cases, with regard to vinegar they are amazed if we dare to say that it has lost the innate heat of the wine but possesses the heat that comes from putrefaction—which is indeed also the view of Aristotle and Theophrastus.

beads.greek: τὰ μὲν γὰρ οἰνώδη μόρια τοῦ οἴνου κατὰ τὴν εἰς ὄξος μεταβολὴν ἀποψύχεται, τὸ δ’ ὑδατῶδες περίττωμα σηπόμενον ἐπίκτητόν τινα ἴσχει θερμότητα, ὥσπερ καὶ τἄλλα πάντα τὰ σαπέντα.
beads.english: For the vinous parts of the wine are chilled in the change into vinegar, while the watery residue, as it putrefies, comes to possess a certain acquired heat, just as do all other things that have putrefied.

beads.greek: καὶ γίγνεται σύνθετόν τι τὸ ὄξος ἐξ ἐναντιωτάτων ταῖς δυνάμεσι μορίων, τῶν μὲν ἀπεψυγμένων, τῶν δὲ θερμῶν, ὥσπερ αἱ τῶν καυθέντων ξύλων τέφραι πᾶσαι.
beads.english: And vinegar becomes something composite, made up of parts most opposite in their powers, some of them chilled, others hot, just like all the ashes of burnt wood.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ ἐν ἐκείναις τὸ μὲν οἷον ἐμπύρευμα κατὰ μικρὰ μόρια παρέσπαρται, καὶ τοῦτο μὲν ἱκανῶς ἐστι θερμὸν, τὸ δ’ ἄλλο πᾶν γεῶδές τε καὶ ψυχρόν.

And vinegar becomes something composite, made up of parts most opposite in their powers, some of them chilled, others hot, just like all the ashes of burnt wood.
For in those too what is, as it were, an ember-like residue (empyreuma) is scattered about in small particles, and this is quite hot, while all the rest is earthy and cold.

beads.greek: καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἐπειδὰν ὕδατι βραχεῖσα τέφρα διὰ τινῶν σωμάτων ἀραιῶν συμμέτρως ἠθεῖται, συναποφέρεται μὲν ἐν τῷδε τὰ θερμὰ καὶ [630] δριμέα μόρια, τὸ δ’ ὑπόλοιπον οὐκέτι θερμόν ἐστιν, ἐναποθέμενον τῷ ὕδατι τὰ πυρώδη μόρια.
beads.english: And for this reason, whenever ash that has been steeped in water is strained in due measure through certain rare bodies, the hot and [630] pungent parts are carried off together with it in this process, while what is left over is no longer hot, since it has deposited its fiery parts in the water.

beads.greek: καλοῦσι δὲ τὸ τοιοῦτον ὕδωρ οἱ ἄνθρωποι κονίαν, ἀνάλογον τῇ θαλάττῃ καὶ ἅλμῃ, διαθέσεως καὶ γενέσεως ἕνεκα καὶ δυνάμεως.
beads.english: People call such water lye, which is analogous to sea-water and brine in respect of its condition, its generation, and its power.

beads.greek: ἐκεῖνα μὲν γὰρ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ ἁλῶν σύγκειται, τὸ δὲ περιπλῦνον ὕδωρ τὴν τέφραν σύνθετον ἐξ αὐτοῦ καὶ ὧν ἐπηνέγκατο μορίων γενόμενον οὕτως ἀπειργάσατο τὴν ὀνομαζομένην κονίαν, ἣν εἰ μὴ φθάνοντες ἐγινώσκομεν, ὡς ἐξ ὕδατός τε καὶ τῶν αἰθαλωδῶν μορίων τῆς τέφρας ἐγένετο, τάχ’ ἂν ὑπελαμβάνομεν ἁπλοῦν καὶ ἀσύνθετον ὑπάρχειν σῶμα.
beads.english: For those are composed of water and salts, while the water that washes through the ash, having become composite out of itself and the parts it has carried along, in this way produces what is named lye; and if we did not already know beforehand that it came into being from water and the sooty parts of the ash, we would perhaps suppose it to be a simple and uncompounded body.

καλοῦσι δὲ τὸ τοιοῦτον ὕδωρ οἱ ἄνθρωποι κονίαν, ἀνάλογον τῇ θαλάττῃ καὶ ἅλμῃ, διαθέσεως καὶ γενέσεως ἕνεκα καὶ δυνάμεως.

ἐκεῖνα μὲν γὰρ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ ἁλῶν σύγκειται, τὸ δὲ περιπλῦνον ὕδωρ τὴν τέφραν σύνθετον ἐξ αὐτοῦ καὶ ὧν ἐπηνέγκατο μορίων γενόμενον οὕτως ἀπειργάσατο τὴν ὀνομαζομένην κονίαν, ἣν εἰ μὴ φθάνοντες ἐγινώσκομεν, ὡς ἐξ ὕδατός τε καὶ τῶν αἰθαλωδῶν μορίων τῆς τέφρας ἐγένετο, τάχ’ ἂν ὑπελαμβάνομεν ἁπλοῦν καὶ ἀσύνθετον ὑπάρχειν σῶμα.
english_sentences: And for this reason, whenever ash that has been steeped in water is strained in due measure through certain rare bodies, the hot and [630] pungent parts are carried off together with it in this process, while what is left over is no longer hot, since it has deposited its fiery parts in the water.
People call such water lye, which is analogous to sea-water and brine in respect of its condition, its generation, and its power.

For those are composed of water and salts, while the water that washes through the ash, having become composite out of itself and the parts it has carried along, in this way produces what is named lye; and if we did not already know beforehand that it came into being from water and the sooty parts of the ash, we would perhaps suppose it to be a simple and uncompounded body.

beads.greek: τοιοῦτον γάρ τι κᾀπὶ τοῦ ὄξους πεπόνθαμεν, οὐ δυνάμενοι δι’ αἰσθήσεως ἰδεῖν αὐτοῦ τὴν γένεσιν, ἀπιστοῦμεν τῷ λόγῳ· ἀλλ’ εἰ μηδὲν ἄλλο, τὴν γοῦν τῆς ὄμφακος διαφορὰν πρὸς αὐτὸ κατανοήσαντες δίκαιοι πιστεύειν ἐσόμεθα ὡς οὐκ ὀξὺς μόνον, ἀλλὰ δριμύς τις ἕτερος ἀναμέμικται χυμὸς αὐτῷ, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τελέως ὁ τῆς ὄμφακος ἐμψύχει χυλὸς, ὥστε καὶ πρὸς καῦσον ἄκρως ἁρμόττει, κατὰ τοῦ στόματος τῆς γαστρὸς ἢ τῶν ὑποχονδρίων ὅλων ἐπιτιθέμενος, καὶ πρὸς ἅπαν ὅ τι περ ἂν ἐμψύξαι βουληθῶμεν, [631] οὐχ ὁμοίως δ’ ὄξος.
beads.english: For we have experienced something of this sort also in the case of vinegar: being unable to see its generation through sense-perception, we disbelieve the argument. But, if nothing else, having at least observed the difference of the unripe grape from it, we shall be right to believe that not only a sour flavour but also some other, pungent flavour has been mixed into it; and for this reason the juice of the unripe grape cools completely, so that it is also supremely suited for causus, when applied over the mouth of the stomach or the whole of the hypochondria, and for everything whatsoever that we may wish to cool, [631] whereas vinegar is not so in like manner.

beads.greek: οὐ γὰρ ἀκριβῶς ἓν οὐδ’ ὀξὺ μόνον ἐστὶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ δριμύ.
beads.english: For it is not strictly one thing, nor sour only, but also pungent.

beads.greek: τὸ μὲν οὖν ὀξὺ μόνον ὅ τι περ ἂν ᾖ ψυχρὸν πάντως ἐστὶν εἴτ’ οὖν ἄπιος, εἴτε μῆλον, εἴτε ῥοῦς, εἴτε ὁ ἀπὸ τῶν βάτων καρπὸς, εἴτε ὁ ἀπὸ τῆς μορέας, εἴθ’ ὁ ἀπὸ τῆς ῥοιᾶς, εἴθ’ ὅστις οὖν ἄλλος ἢ καρπὸς, ἢ χυλὸς, ἢ φυτὸν, ὡς ὀξυλάπαθον καὶ ὀξαλὶς, ἣν δὴ καὶ ὀξύδα προσαγορεύουσιν.
beads.english: So then, whatever is sour only is in every case cold, whether it be pear, or apple, or sumach, or the fruit from brambles, or that from the mulberry, or that from the pomegranate, or whatever other fruit, or juice, or plant, such as oxylapathon and oxalis, which indeed they also call oxys.

beads.greek: ἂν γάρ σοι γευομένῳ σφοδρὰ μὲν καὶ σαφὴς ἡ ὀξύτης ἐν αὐτῷ καταφαίνηται, μηδὲν δ’ ἐμφαίνηται δριμύτητος, πάντως τοῦτον εὑρήσεις ἐμψύχοντα τὸν χυμὸν, καὶ χρῶ θαῤῥῶν, εἴτε πρὸς καῦσον ἐθέλοις χρῆσθαι καθ’ ὑποχονδρίων ἐπιτιθεὶς, εἴτε πρὸς ἐρυσίπελας, εἴτε πρὸς ἄλλο τι πάθος θερμόν.
beads.english: For if, when you taste it, the sourness in it appears to you strong and clear, but nothing of pungency shows itself, you will in every case find this flavour to be cooling; and use it with confidence, whether you wish to use it against causus, applying it on the hypochondria, or against erysipelas, or against some other hot affection.

beads.greek: ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ τὰ ψυχρὰ πάντα νοσήματα βλαπτόμενα πρὸς αὐτοῦ σαφῶς εὑρήσεις.
beads.english: And in the same way you will clearly find all cold diseases harmed by it.

beads.greek: ὅταν δ’ ἐπίμηκτος ἡ ποιότης φαίνηταί σοι, μετὰ μὲν δριμύτητος καὶ ὑποτοπεῖσθαι χρὴ θερμότητα, μετὰ δὲ στύψεως ἕτερόν τι γένος ψυχρότητος.
beads.english: But when the quality appears to you mixed, then along with pungency one must also suspect heat, while along with astringency one must suspect another kind of coldness.

beads.greek: ἡ μὲν γὰρ ὀξεῖα ψυχρότης λεπτομερὴς, ἡ δὲ στύφουσα παχυμερής.
beads.english: For sour coldness is fine-particled, whereas astringent coldness is coarse-particled.

beads.greek: [632] Ἀλλὰ τούτων μὲν ὀλίγον ὕστερον ἐροῦμεν τὰς πίστεις.
beads.english: [632] But the proofs of these matters we shall state a little later.

beads.greek: ὅ δὲ χρὴ πρότερον συμβουλεῦσαι τοῖς τὰ τοιαῦτα χωρὶς ἀλαζονείας σοφιστικῆς αὐτῆς ἕνεκεν τῆς ἀληθείας ἐπισκοπουμένοις, ἤδη μοι καιρὸς εἰπεῖν, ὡς οὐ χρὴ μόνῳ τῷ λόγῳ γεγυμνάσθαι δι’ ὧν ἀεὶ παρακελεύομαι μεθόδων λογικῶν, ἃς ἐν τοῖς περὶ τῶν ἀποδείξεων ὑπομνήμασιν εἶπον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν αἴσθησιν τὴν γευστικὴν ἐπὶ τῶν χυμῶν γυμνάζειν ἐπιμελῶς, ἀρχομένους ἀπὸ τῶν ἐναργεστάτην ἐχόντων ἡντιναοῦν ποιότητα μίαν.
beads.english: What it is necessary first to advise those who investigate such things, without sophistical imposture, for the sake of truth itself, it is now time for me to say: that one must not only be trained in reasoning, by means of the logical methods which I constantly recommend, and which I set out in my commentaries on demonstrations, but must also carefully exercise the sense of taste upon the humours (flavours), beginning from those that possess some single quality whatsoever in the most evident manner.

greek_sentences: [632] Ἀλλὰ τούτων μὲν ὀλίγον ὕστερον ἐροῦμεν τὰς πίστεις.

ὅ δὲ χρὴ πρότερον συμβουλεῦσαι τοῖς τὰ τοιαῦτα χωρὶς ἀλαζονείας σοφιστικῆς αὐτῆς ἕνεκεν τῆς ἀληθείας ἐπισκοπουμένοις, ἤδη μοι καιρὸς εἰπεῖν, ὡς οὐ χρὴ μόνῳ τῷ λόγῳ γεγυμνάσθαι δι’ ὧν ἀεὶ παρακελεύομαι μεθόδων λογικῶν, ἃς ἐν τοῖς περὶ τῶν ἀποδείξεων ὑπομνήμασιν εἶπον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν αἴσθησιν τὴν γευστικὴν ἐπὶ τῶν χυμῶν γυμνάζειν ἐπιμελῶς, ἀρχομένους ἀπὸ τῶν ἐναργεστάτην ἐχόντων ἡντιναοῦν ποιότητα μίαν.
english_sentences: [632] But the proofs of these matters we shall state a little later.

What it is necessary first to advise those who investigate such things, without sophistical imposture, for the sake of truth itself, it is now time for me to say: that one must not only be trained in reasoning, by means of the logical methods which I constantly recommend, and which I set out in my commentaries on demonstrations, but must also carefully exercise the sense of taste upon the humours (flavours), beginning from those that possess some single quality whatsoever in the most evident manner.

beads.greek: εἰ μὲν τὴν δριμύτητα κατανοῆσαι σαφῶς ἐθέλοις, ἐπὶ σκορόδου καὶ κρομμύου καὶ τῶν ὁμοίων αὐτοῖς, ἀπογευόμενός τε συνεχῶς καὶ διαμασώμενον ἐπὶ πλεῖστον καὶ τὴν μνήμην πειρώμενον ἀκριβῶς παρατίθεσθαι τοῦ γιγνομένου πάθους τὴν αἴσθησιν· εἰ δὲ τὴν στύψιν, ἐπὶ κικίδος τε καὶ ῥοῦ καὶ τῶν ὁμοίων· εἰ δὲ τὴν πικρότητα, νίτρου καὶ χολῆς γευόμενον· εἰ δὲ τὴν γλυκύτητα, σιραίου καὶ μέλιτος, ἔτι δὲ πρὸς τούτοις εἴτ’ οὖν ἄποιον ἐθέλοις εἴτε μέσον ἐν ποιότητι τῇ πρὸς τὴν γεῦσιν ὑπολαμβάνειν, τὸ [633] ὕδωρ ἀξιῶ σε καὶ τούτου γευσάμενον, ἀκριβῶς ἔχειν ἐν τῇ μνήμῃ, καὶ μάλιστά γε τοῦ μηδεμίαν ὧν νῦν εἴρηκα ἐμφαίνοντος ποιότητα, μήτε γλυκύτητα μήτε δριμύτητα μήτ’ ὀξύτητα μήτε πικρότητα, καὶ πρὸς τούτοις ἔτι μήθ’ ἱκανῶς θερμοῦ μήθ’ ὑπερβαλλόντως ψυχροῦ.
beads.english: If you wish to understand pungency clearly, [do so] in the case of garlic and onion and the things similar to them, tasting continually and chewing for a very long time and trying to store accurately in your memory the perception of the affection that arises; if astringency, in the case of gall-nut and sumach and the like; if bitterness, by tasting nitre and bile; if sweetness, boiled-down must and honey; and further, in addition to these, whether you wish to take water as being without quality or as intermediate in quality with respect to taste, I ask you, having tasted this [633] water too, to hold it accurately in memory, and most of all that water which displays none of the qualities I have now mentioned, neither sweetness nor pungency nor sourness nor bitterness, and in addition to these, moreover, which is neither considerably hot nor excessively cold.

beads.greek: ἐντεῦθεν γὰρ ὁρμώμενος ἑτοιμότερον ἐπί τε τὴν τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων ἀμυδρῶν χυμῶν ἀφίξῃ διάγνωσιν ἐπί τε τὴν τῶν ὡς ἐγὼ μέν φημι γλυκέων, ὡς δ’ ἄλλοι τινὲς, ὑδατωδῶν, οἷος ὅ τε τῶν καλάμων ἐστὶ τῶν χλωρῶν καὶ ἀγρώστεως καὶ προσέτι πυρῶν καὶ κριθῶν καὶ ζειῶν καὶ ἄλλων πολλῶν, ὧν καὶ Θεόφραστος μέμνηται, ζητῶν εἴτ’ εἴδη πλείονα θετέον ἐστὶν τῶν γλυκέων χυμῶν, εἴτε τῷ μᾶλλόν τε καὶ ἧττον αὐτοὺς ὑποληπτέον διαφέρειν ἀλλήλων.
beads.english: For setting out from here you will arrive more readily both at the discrimination of all the other faint flavours and at that of those which, as I for my part say, are sweet, but as certain others say, watery, such as is the flavour of green reeds and of dog's-tooth grass and, in addition, of wheat and barley and emmer and many others, which Theophrastus too mentions, inquiring whether several species of sweet flavours are to be posited, or whether they are to be supposed to differ from one another by the more and the less.

beads.greek: ἀλλὰ περὶ μὲν τούτων αὖθις διαιρήσομαι.
beads.english: But concerning these matters I shall make the distinctions again later.

ἀλλὰ περὶ μὲν τούτων αὖθις διαιρήσομαι.
english_sentences: If you wish to understand pungency clearly, [do so] in the case of garlic and onion and the things similar to them, tasting continually and chewing for a very long time and trying to store accurately in your memory the perception of the affection that arises; if astringency, in the case of gall-nut and sumach and the like; if bitterness, by tasting nitre and bile; if sweetness, boiled-down must and honey; and further, in addition to these, whether you wish to take water as being without quality or as intermediate in quality with respect to taste, I ask you, having tasted this [633] water too, to hold it accurately in memory, and most of all that water which displays none of the qualities I have now mentioned, neither sweetness nor pungency nor sourness nor bitterness, and in addition to these, moreover, which is neither considerably hot nor excessively cold.

For setting out from here you will arrive more readily both at the discrimination of all the other faint flavours and at that of those which, as I for my part say, are sweet, but as certain others say, watery, such as is the flavour of green reeds and of dog's-tooth grass and, in addition, of wheat and barley and emmer and many others, which Theophrastus too mentions, inquiring whether several species of sweet flavours are to be posited, or whether they are to be supposed to differ from one another by the more and the less.
But concerning these matters I shall make the distinctions again later.

beads.greek: Ὁποίαν δ’ ἄν σοι τὸ ἀποιότατον ὕδωρ αἴσθησιν παράσχῃ, τοιαύτην ὅταν ἔν τινι τῶν ξηρῶν εὑρίσκῃς, ἔξω δηλονότι πάσης τὸ τοιοῦτον θερμότητός τε καὶ ψυχρότητος ἐπιφανοῦς ἐστι, μέσην ὡς οἷόν τε μάλιστα κατάστασιν ﻿ [634] ἔχον, ἢ καὶ μικρόν τι ῥέπον ἐπὶ τὸ ψυχρόν.
beads.english: Whatever sensation the most qualityless water affords you, whenever you find such a sensation in one of the dry things, such a thing is clearly outside all manifest heat and cold, having a condition [634] as nearly as possible in the middle, or even inclining a little toward the cold.

beads.greek: ἀλλ’ εἴπερ οὕτως ἔχον ἐν τῇ κατὰ θερμότητα καὶ ψυχρότητα διαφορᾷ ξηρὸν εἴη τὴν σύστασιν, ἀνάγκη γεῶδες ὑπάρχειν αὐτὸ καὶ ξηραίνειν ἀδήκτως.
beads.english: But if, being so disposed in respect of the difference according to heat and cold, it should be dry in its consistency, it must necessarily be earthy and dry without biting.

beads.greek: ὀνομάζεται δὲ πρὸς τῶν ἰατρῶν ἅπαντα τὰ τοιαῦτα τῶν φαρμάκων ἐμπλαστικὰ, καθάπερ τὰ πλεῖστα τῶν ἀκριβῶς πεπλυμένων, ἄμυλος, πομφόλυξ καὶ ψιμμύθιον καὶ τίτανος καὶ καδμεία καὶ γῆ ἡ Κρητικὴ καὶ Κιμωλία καὶ χόνδρος καὶ Σάμιος ἀστὴρ καὶ ἡ τῶν γναφέων γῆ, τῶν ἐμπλαστικῶν ἐστι φαρμάκων.
beads.english: All such drugs are called by the physicians "clogging", just as most of those that have been thoroughly washed; starch, pompholyx and white lead and lime and cadmia and Cretan earth and Cimolian earth and chondros and Samian star and fullers' earth are among the clogging drugs.

beads.greek: τινὰ δ’ ἐξ αὐτῶν οὐ γεώδη μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑδατώδη τὴν φύσιν ἐστὶν, ἔνια δὲ καὶ ἀέρα οὐκ ὀλίγον ἐν αὐτοῖς περιέχει, γλίσχρα μέντοι ταῦτα πάντα καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἐμπλαστικά.
beads.english: Some of them are not only earthy but also watery in nature, and some also contain in themselves not a little air; all these, however, are viscous, and for this reason clogging.

beads.greek: Διττὴ γὰρ ἡ τῶν ἐμπλαστικῶν ἐστι φύσις, ἡ μὲν ἑτέρα γεώδης ἀκριβῶς καὶ ξηρὰ, ἡ δ’ ἑτέρα γλίσχρα μὲν πάντως, μικτὴ δ’ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς καὶ τὰ πολλὰ καὶ ἀέρος, ὥσπερ καὶ τοὔλαιον τὸ γλυκύ.
beads.english: For the nature of the clogging drugs is twofold: the one precisely earthy and dry, the other in every case viscous, but mixed from water and earth and for the most part also air, as sweet oil also is.

beads.greek: λέλεκται δ’ ἔμπροσθεν ὁποῖον λέγω τὸ γλυκύ.
beads.english: It has been said earlier what kind of thing I mean by "sweet".

greek_sentences: Ὁποίαν δ’ ἄν σοι τὸ ἀποιότατον ὕδωρ αἴσθησιν παράσχῃ, τοιαύτην ὅταν ἔν τινι τῶν ξηρῶν εὑρίσκῃς, ἔξω δηλονότι πάσης τὸ τοιοῦτον θερμότητός τε καὶ ψυχρότητος ἐπιφανοῦς ἐστι, μέσην ὡς οἷόν τε μάλιστα κατάστασιν ﻿ [634] ἔχον, ἢ καὶ μικρόν τι ῥέπον ἐπὶ τὸ ψυχρόν.
ἀλλ’ εἴπερ οὕτως ἔχον ἐν τῇ κατὰ θερμότητα καὶ ψυχρότητα διαφορᾷ ξηρὸν εἴη τὴν σύστασιν, ἀνάγκη γεῶδες ὑπάρχειν αὐτὸ καὶ ξηραίνειν ἀδήκτως.

ὀνομάζεται δὲ πρὸς τῶν ἰατρῶν ἅπαντα τὰ τοιαῦτα τῶν φαρμάκων ἐμπλαστικὰ, καθάπερ τὰ πλεῖστα τῶν ἀκριβῶς πεπλυμένων, ἄμυλος, πομφόλυξ καὶ ψιμμύθιον καὶ τίτανος καὶ καδμεία καὶ γῆ ἡ Κρητικὴ καὶ Κιμωλία καὶ χόνδρος καὶ Σάμιος ἀστὴρ καὶ ἡ τῶν γναφέων γῆ, τῶν ἐμπλαστικῶν ἐστι φαρμάκων.
τινὰ δ’ ἐξ αὐτῶν οὐ γεώδη μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑδατώδη τὴν φύσιν ἐστὶν, ἔνια δὲ καὶ ἀέρα οὐκ ὀλίγον ἐν αὐτοῖς περιέχει, γλίσχρα μέντοι ταῦτα πάντα καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἐμπλαστικά.
Διττὴ γὰρ ἡ τῶν ἐμπλαστικῶν ἐστι φύσις, ἡ μὲν ἑτέρα γεώδης ἀκριβῶς καὶ ξηρὰ, ἡ δ’ ἑτέρα γλίσχρα μὲν πάντως, μικτὴ δ’ ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ γῆς καὶ τὰ πολλὰ καὶ ἀέρος, ὥσπερ καὶ τοὔλαιον τὸ γλυκύ.
λέλεκται δ’ ἔμπροσθεν ὁποῖον λέγω τὸ γλυκύ.
english_sentences: Whatever sensation the most qualityless water affords you, whenever you find such a sensation in one of the dry things, such a thing is clearly outside all manifest heat and cold, having a condition [634] as nearly as possible in the middle, or even inclining a little toward the cold.
But if, being so disposed in respect of the difference according to heat and cold, it should be dry in its consistency, it must necessarily be earthy and dry without biting.

All such drugs are called by the physicians "clogging", just as most of those that have been thoroughly washed; starch, pompholyx and white lead and lime and cadmia and Cretan earth and Cimolian earth and chondros and Samian star and fullers' earth are among the clogging drugs.
Some of them are not only earthy but also watery in nature, and some also contain in themselves not a little air; all these, however, are viscous, and for this reason clogging.

For the nature of the clogging drugs is twofold: the one precisely earthy and dry, the other in every case viscous, but mixed from water and earth and for the most part also air, as sweet oil also is.
It has been said earlier what kind of thing I mean by "sweet".

beads.greek: τουτὶ μὲν οὖν ἐξ ἀερώδους τε ἅμα καὶ γεώδους καὶ ὑδατώδους οὐσίας μέμικται· τὸ δὲ τοῦ ὠοῦ [635] λευκὸν ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν μέν πως, γεωδέστερον δέ ἐστιν ἐλαίου, καὶ μὲν δὴ καὶ τὸ τυρῶδες τοῦ γάλακτος ἐμπλαστικόν ἐστιν καὶ ἡ τοῦ ὑὸς πιμελή.
beads.english: This, then, is mixed from airy and earthy and watery substance together; the white of the egg [635] is composed in some way from the same things, but is earthier than oil; and indeed the cheesy part of milk is clogging too, as is the soft fat of the pig.

beads.greek: ταύρου μὲν γὰρ καὶ τράγου πιμελὴ δριμύτητα πολλὴν ἔχει καὶ πυρώδη· βοὸς δὲ καὶ αἰγὸς ἧττον μὲν, ἤδη δέ πως καὶ τούτων τὸ στέαρ δριμύ.
beads.english: For the soft fat of a bull and of a he-goat has much pungency, and fiery pungency at that; that of an ox and a she-goat less so, yet the hard fat of these too is already somewhat pungent.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ δὴ καὶ στέαρ ὀνομάζεται τῶν τοιούτων ζώων ἡ πιμελὴ, διὰ τὸ πάχος. ἔτι γὰρ οὐ θερμοτέρα μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ γεωδεστέρα τῆς τῶν ὑῶν.
beads.english: For indeed the soft fat of such animals is called hard fat (stear), on account of its thickness; for in addition it is not only hotter but also earthier than that of pigs.

beads.greek: χηνὸς δὲ καὶ ἀλεκτρυόνος ἐστὶ μὲν καὶ θερμοτέρα καὶ ξηροτέρα τὴν τῶν ὑῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ λεπτομερής τε καὶ ἥκιστα γεώδης.
beads.english: That of a goose and of a cock is both hotter and drier than that of pigs, but it is also fine-particled and least earthy.

beads.greek: οὕτω δὲ καὶ πάντων τῶν πτηνῶν, ὅτι καὶ ἡ οὐσία τοῦ σώματος αὐτῶν οὐκ ὀλίγον ἔχει τὸ ἀερῶδες.
beads.english: So too is that of all winged creatures, because the substance of their body too has no small share of the airy.

beads.greek: ἀλλὰ περὶ μὲν τούτων ἕτερος λόγος.
beads.english: But about these there is another discussion.

beads.greek: ὅσαι δ’ οὖν πιμελαὶ μήπω δριμύτητά τινα ἔχουσιν, ἐμπλαστικαὶ τῶν πόρων εἰσὶν, καὶ μᾶλλον αἱ ξηρότεραι καὶ γεωδέστεραι.
beads.english: At any rate, all soft fats that do not yet have any pungency are clogging of the pores, and the drier and earthier ones more so.

beads.greek: τοιοῦτος δ’ ἐστὶν καὶ ὁ πεπλυμένος κηρός. ἀποτίθεται γὰρ καὶ αὐτὸς τὴν ἐκ τοῦ μέλιτος δριμύτητα.
beads.english: Such too is washed wax; for it too lays aside the pungency that comes from the honey.

beads.greek: πρόδηλον δ’ ὡς οὐ περὶ τοῦ πικροῦ τῇ φύσει κηροῦ λέγεται ταῦτα, καθάπερ ὁ Ποντικός ἐστιν.
beads.english: It is evident that these things are not said about wax that is bitter by nature, as the Pontic is.

καὶ γὰρ δὴ καὶ στέαρ ὀνομάζεται τῶν τοιούτων ζώων ἡ πιμελὴ, διὰ τὸ πάχος.
ἔτι γὰρ οὐ θερμοτέρα μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ γεωδεστέρα τῆς τῶν ὑῶν.

οὕτω δὲ καὶ πάντων τῶν πτηνῶν, ὅτι καὶ ἡ οὐσία τοῦ σώματος αὐτῶν οὐκ ὀλίγον ἔχει τὸ ἀερῶδες.
ἀλλὰ περὶ μὲν τούτων ἕτερος λόγος.
ὅσαι δ’ οὖν πιμελαὶ μήπω δριμύτητά τινα ἔχουσιν, ἐμπλαστικαὶ τῶν πόρων εἰσὶν, καὶ μᾶλλον αἱ ξηρότεραι καὶ γεωδέστεραι.
τοιοῦτος δ’ ἐστὶν καὶ ὁ πεπλυμένος κηρός.
ἀποτίθεται γὰρ καὶ αὐτὸς τὴν ἐκ τοῦ μέλιτος δριμύτητα.
πρόδηλον δ’ ὡς οὐ περὶ τοῦ πικροῦ τῇ φύσει κηροῦ λέγεται ταῦτα, καθάπερ ὁ Ποντικός ἐστιν.
english_sentences: This, then, is mixed from airy and earthy and watery substance together; the white of the egg [635] is composed in some way from the same things, but is earthier than oil; and indeed the cheesy part of milk is clogging too, as is the soft fat of the pig.
For the soft fat of a bull and of a he-goat has much pungency, and fiery pungency at that; that of an ox and a she-goat less so, yet the hard fat of these too is already somewhat pungent.
For indeed the soft fat of such animals is called hard fat (stear), on account of its thickness; for in addition it is not only hotter but also earthier than that of pigs.
That of a goose and of a cock is both hotter and drier than that of pigs, but it is also fine-particled and least earthy.
So too is that of all winged creatures, because the substance of their body too has no small share of the airy.
But about these there is another discussion.
At any rate, all soft fats that do not yet have any pungency are clogging of the pores, and the drier and earthier ones more so.
Such too is washed wax; for it too lays aside the pungency that comes from the honey.
It is evident that these things are not said about wax that is bitter by nature, as the Pontic is.

beads.greek: ἐῥ ἀψινθίου [636] γὰρ ἐκεῖνος ἔχει τὴν πικρότητα, καὶ εἰ πλύναις αὐτὸν μυριάκις, οὐκ ἂν ἐκνίψαις τελέως τὴν πικρότητα.
beads.english: For that one has its bitterness from wormwood, and even if you were to wash it ten thousand times, you would not wash the bitterness out completely.

beads.greek: φυλάττεσθαι δὲ καὶ τὸν ἐκ δριμέος καὶ θυμώδους μέλιτος κηρὸν, ὅταν ἄδηκτον ἀκριβῶς ἐθέλοις σκευάσαι φάρμακον.
beads.english: One must also beware of the wax derived from pungent and thyme-flavoured honey, whenever you wish to prepare a drug that is entirely non-biting.

beads.greek: ἐπιτήδειος οὖν ὁ ἐξ ὑδατωδεστέρου καὶ ἥκιστα δριμέος μέλιτος εἰς τὸ πλύνεσθαι.
beads.english: Suitable for washing, therefore, is the wax from a more watery and least pungent honey.

beads.greek: Τὰ μὲν οὖν ἐμπλαστικὰ φάρμακα τοιαῦτα.
beads.english: Such, then, are the clogging drugs.

beads.greek: περὶ δὲ τῶν στυφόντων τε καὶ ὀξέων αὖθις ἐπάνειμι.
beads.english: Concerning the astringent and the sour ones I return once more.

beads.greek: τὰ μὲν στύφοντα γεώδη μέν ἐστι καὶ παχυμερῆ ταῖς τῶν ὄγκων συστάσεσι, ψυχρὰ δὲ ταῖς ποιότητι· τὰ δ’ ὀξέα λεπτομερῆ μέν ἐστι τοῖς σώμασιν, ψυχρὰ δ’ ὡσαύτως τοῖς στύφουσι.
beads.english: The astringent ones are earthy and coarse-particled in the consistency of their masses, and cold in their quality; the sour ones are fine-particled in their bodies, but cold in the same way as the astringent ones.

beads.greek: πίστις δ’ ὑπὲρ ἀμφοῖν διττὴ, κατὰ μὲν τὴν αἴσθησιν ἐξ ἀπαγωγῆς, κατὰ δὲ τὸν λόγον ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας αὐτῶν.
beads.english: The proof concerning both is twofold: according to sense-perception, by way of inference (ἐξ ἀπαγωγῆς), and according to reason, from their substance.

beads.greek: εἰρήσεται δὲ προτέρα τῶν πίστεων ἡ σαφεστέρα μὲν τοῖς πολλοῖς, ἀσθενεστέρα δ’ ὡς πρὸς ἀπόδειξιν ἐπιστημονικήν.
beads.english: Of the proofs there will be stated first the one that is clearer to most people, but weaker with regard to scientific demonstration.

greek_sentences: ἐῥ ἀψινθίου [636] γὰρ ἐκεῖνος ἔχει τὴν πικρότητα, καὶ εἰ πλύναις αὐτὸν μυριάκις, οὐκ ἂν ἐκνίψαις τελέως τὴν πικρότητα.
φυλάττεσθαι δὲ καὶ τὸν ἐκ δριμέος καὶ θυμώδους μέλιτος κηρὸν, ὅταν ἄδηκτον ἀκριβῶς ἐθέλοις σκευάσαι φάρμακον.
ἐπιτήδειος οὖν ὁ ἐξ ὑδατωδεστέρου καὶ ἥκιστα δριμέος μέλιτος εἰς τὸ πλύνεσθαι.
Τὰ μὲν οὖν ἐμπλαστικὰ φάρμακα τοιαῦτα.
περὶ δὲ τῶν στυφόντων τε καὶ ὀξέων αὖθις ἐπάνειμι.
τὰ μὲν στύφοντα γεώδη μέν ἐστι καὶ παχυμερῆ ταῖς τῶν ὄγκων συστάσεσι, ψυχρὰ δὲ ταῖς ποιότητι· τὰ δ’ ὀξέα λεπτομερῆ μέν ἐστι τοῖς σώμασιν, ψυχρὰ δ’ ὡσαύτως τοῖς στύφουσι.
πίστις δ’ ὑπὲρ ἀμφοῖν διττὴ, κατὰ μὲν τὴν αἴσθησιν ἐξ ἀπαγωγῆς, κατὰ δὲ τὸν λόγον ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας αὐτῶν.
εἰρήσεται δὲ προτέρα τῶν πίστεων ἡ σαφεστέρα μὲν τοῖς πολλοῖς, ἀσθενεστέρα δ’ ὡς πρὸς ἀπόδειξιν ἐπιστημονικήν.
english_sentences: For that one has its bitterness from wormwood, and even if you were to wash it ten thousand times, you would not wash the bitterness out completely.
One must also beware of the wax derived from pungent and thyme-flavoured honey, whenever you wish to prepare a drug that is entirely non-biting.
Suitable for washing, therefore, is the wax from a more watery and least pungent honey.
Such, then, are the clogging drugs.
Concerning the astringent and the sour ones I return once more.

The astringent ones are earthy and coarse-particled in the consistency of their masses, and cold in their quality; the sour ones are fine-particled in their bodies, but cold in the same way as the astringent ones.
The proof concerning both is twofold: according to sense-perception, by way of inference (ἐξ ἀπαγωγῆς), and according to reason, from their substance.
Of the proofs there will be stated first the one that is clearer to most people, but weaker with regard to scientific demonstration.

beads.greek: οἱ ἀπὸ τῶν δένδρων καρποὶ πάντες, ὅσοι γλυκεῖς ἡμῖν φαίνονται πεπανθέντες, ἄρτι γεννώμενοι στρυφνοί τέ εἰσι καὶ ξηροὶ ταῖς συστάσεσι καὶ κατὰ τὴν τοῦ [637] γεννῶντος δένδρου φύσιν ἕκαστος, ὥς που καὶ Θεόφραστος ἔλεγεν, ἐλαῖαι, σταφυλαὶ, μῆλα, ῥοιαὶ, μόρα, φοίνικες, ἄπιοι.
beads.english: All the fruits from trees, as many as appear sweet to us when they have ripened, are, when just coming into being, both acerbic and dry in their consistency, each according to the nature of the [637] tree that generates it, as Theophrastus too said somewhere—olives, grapes, apples, pomegranates, mulberries, dates, pears.

beads.greek: προϊόντες δὲ τῷ χρόνῳ γίγνονται μὲν ὑγρότεροι, προσλαμβάνουσι δὲ ὀξύτητα τῇ στρυφνότητι, καὶ ταύτην ἀποτιθέμενοι κατὰ βραχὺ γλυκεῖς αὖθις γίνονται τελειούμενοι.
beads.english: But as they advance in time they become moister, and they take on sourness in addition to the acerbity, and, laying this aside little by little, they become sweet in turn as they are brought to completion.

beads.greek: τινὲς δ’ οὐδ’ ἐπὶ τοῖς δένδροις, ἀλλ’ ἀφαιρούμενοι μετὰ χρόνον ἀπολαμβάνουσι τὴν γλυκύτητα.
beads.english: Some, however, do not acquire the sweetness even on the trees, but only after they have been removed, with time.

beads.greek: ἄλλοι δέ τινες οὐδὲ διὰ μέσης τῆς ὀξύτητος, ἀλλ’ ἄντικρυς ἀπὸ τῆς στρυφνότητος ἐπὶ τὴν γλυκύτητα παραγίνονται, καθάπερ καὶ ὁ τῆς ἐλαίας.
beads.english: Others again do not pass through sourness as an intermediate stage, but arrive directly from acerbity at sweetness, as does also that of the olive.

beads.greek: καὶ μὴν ὅτι γε τῷ θερμῷ πέπτονται πάντες δῆλον, ὅτι τε διττόν ἐστι τοῦτο, τὸ μὲν ἴδιον ἔμφυτον ἑκάστου, τὸ δ’ ἔξωθεν μὲν ἀπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου, σύμφυτον δὲ καὶ οἰκεῖον αὐτοῖς, εἴπερ μεμνήμεθα τῶν ὑποκειμένων ἡμῖν ἀεὶ στοιχείων, ἴσμεν δήπου σαφῶς.
beads.english: And indeed, that all are concocted by the hot is clear, and that this is of two kinds—the one the proper innate heat of each, the other from without, from the sun, yet connate and proper to them—we surely know plainly, if we remember the elements that always underlie our account.

beads.greek: ἀλλ’ εἴπερ στρυφνότεροι μέν εἰσι κατ’ ἀρχὰς, πεπαινόμενοι δὲ γίνονται γλυκεῖς, ἐκ θερμασίας ἡ γλυκύτης αὐτοῖς ἐκ ψύξεως δὲ ἡ ὀξύτης τε καὶ στρυφνότης ὑπῆρξεν.
beads.english: But if they are more acerbic at the beginning, and become sweet as they ripen, then their sweetness arose for them from warmth, and their sourness and acerbity from cooling.

καὶ μὴν ὅτι γε τῷ θερμῷ πέπτονται πάντες δῆλον, ὅτι τε διττόν ἐστι τοῦτο, τὸ μὲν ἴδιον ἔμφυτον ἑκάστου, τὸ δ’ ἔξωθεν μὲν ἀπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου, σύμφυτον δὲ καὶ οἰκεῖον αὐτοῖς, εἴπερ μεμνήμεθα τῶν ὑποκειμένων ἡμῖν ἀεὶ στοιχείων, ἴσμεν δήπου σαφῶς.

But as they advance in time they become moister, and they take on sourness in addition to the acerbity, and, laying this aside little by little, they become sweet in turn as they are brought to completion.
Some, however, do not acquire the sweetness even on the trees, but only after they have been removed, with time.
Others again do not pass through sourness as an intermediate stage, but arrive directly from acerbity at sweetness, as does also that of the olive.

And indeed, that all are concocted by the hot is clear, and that this is of two kinds—the one the proper innate heat of each, the other from without, from the sun, yet connate and proper to them—we surely know plainly, if we remember the elements that always underlie our account.
But if they are more acerbic at the beginning, and become sweet as they ripen, then their sweetness arose for them from warmth, and their sourness and acerbity from cooling.

beads.greek: ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ [638] κατ’ ἀρχὰς μὲν ἔτι ξυλώδεις, ὥς καὶ Θεόφραστος ἔλεγε, ξηροί τέ εἰσιν ἅμα καὶ στρυφνοὶ, τὸ πλῆθος δ’ αὐτοὺς τῆς ἐπιῤῥεούσης ὑγρότητος ὀξεῖς ἐργάζεται, πρόδηλον ὡς γεωδέστερος μέν ἐστιν ὁ στρυφνὸς χυμὸς, ὑγρότερος δ’ ὁ ὀξὺς, ὥστε καὶ Πλάτων ὁρίζων ὀρθῶς ἔλεγεν· ὅσα τοιαῦτα τοῖς χυλοῖς ἐμφέρεται γεώδη μόρια, κατατηκόμενα ταῦτα καὶ συνάγοντα καὶ ἀποξηραίνοντα τὰ νοτερὰ τῶν τῆς γλώττης αἰσθητικῶν μορίων, τραχύτερα μὲν ὄντα στρυφνὰ, ἧττον δὲ τραχύνοντα αὐστηρὰ φαίνεται. καὶ ἡμεῖς δὲ πρὸς τούτοις, ὅτι καὶ ψυχρός ἐστιν τὴν κρᾶσιν ὁ τοιοῦτος χυμὸς ὀρθῶς ἐροῦμεν.
beads.english: And since, at [638] the beginning, while they are still woody, as Theophrastus too said, they are at once dry and acerbic, whereas the abundance of the moisture flowing into them renders them sour, it is evident that the acerbic flavour is earthier, the sour one moister; so that Plato too spoke correctly when he defined them: 'all such earthy particles as are carried in the juices, which, being dissolved (κατατηκόμενα) and contracting and drying up the moist portions of the sensitive parts of the tongue, appear acerbic when they are rougher, and harsh when they roughen less.' And we, in addition to this, shall correctly say that such a flavour is also cold in its mixture.

beads.greek: ἂν γὰρ γεώδης ᾖ μόνον, ἐμπλαστικὸς, οὐ στρυφνὸς ἔσται, καί πως ὁ λόγος ἐπὶ τὴν οὐσίαν αὐτὴν ἤδη μεταβὰς τῶν χυμῶν ἐπιστημονικῆς ἀποδείξεως ἅπτεται.
beads.english: For if it were earthy only, it would be clogging, not acerbic; and in a way the argument, having now passed over to the very substance of the flavours, lays hold of scientific demonstration.

ἂν γὰρ γεώδης ᾖ μόνον, ἐμπλαστικὸς, οὐ στρυφνὸς ἔσται, καί πως ὁ λόγος ἐπὶ τὴν οὐσίαν αὐτὴν ἤδη μεταβὰς τῶν χυμῶν ἐπιστημονικῆς ἀποδείξεως ἅπτεται.
english_sentences: And since, at [638] the beginning, while they are still woody, as Theophrastus too said, they are at once dry and acerbic, whereas the abundance of the moisture flowing into them renders them sour, it is evident that the acerbic flavour is earthier, the sour one moister; so that Plato too spoke correctly when he defined them: 'all such earthy particles as are carried in the juices, which, being dissolved (κατατηκόμενα) and contracting and drying up the moist portions of the sensitive parts of the tongue, appear acerbic when they are rougher, and harsh when they roughen less.' And we, in addition to this, shall correctly say that such a flavour is also cold in its mixture.
For if it were earthy only, it would be clogging, not acerbic; and in a way the argument, having now passed over to the very substance of the flavours, lays hold of scientific demonstration.

beads.greek: εἰ γὰρ τῷ στρυφνῷ χυλῷ συνάγειν καὶ ξηραίνειν καὶ τραχύνειν τὴν γλῶτταν ὑπάρχει σαφῶς, ἐδείχθη δ’ ἐν τοῖς ἔμπροσθεν λόγοις ὑπὸ ψυχροῦ μόνου συνάγεσθαι καὶ σφίγγεσθαι καὶ πιλεῖσθαι τὰ σώματα, πρόδηλον ὡς πάντως ψυχρός ἐστιν ὁ στρυφνὸς χυμός· ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ ἀνωμάλως ﻿ [639] ξηραίνει, τοῦτο γὰρ ἦν τὸ τραχῦνον, εἴη ἂν πάντως καὶ γεώδης.
beads.english: For if it clearly belongs to the acerbic juice to contract and dry and roughen the tongue, and it was shown in the preceding discussions that bodies are contracted and constricted and compacted by cold alone, it is evident that the acerbic flavour is in every case cold; and since it also dries unevenly [639] — for this was what does the roughening — it would in every case also be earthy.

beads.greek: ὁμαλῶς γὰρ ἅπαντα ὁ ὑδατώδης διεξέρχεται.
beads.english: For the watery [flavour] passes through everything evenly.

beads.greek: ὑπάρχει γὰρ ἀχώριστον αὐτῷ, κᾂν διασπασθῇ, τὸ πάλιν ἑνοῦσθαι, τῷ δὲ γεώδει σώματι τῷ κατὰ τοὺς χυμοὺς ἐμφερομένῳ καὶ τὸ διασπᾶσθαι μὲν ἤδη πάρεστιν, καὶ τὸ μηκέτι δὲ συνιέναι ῥᾳδίως ὑπάρχει.
beads.english: For it is inseparable from it, even if it is torn apart, to be united again; whereas for the earthy body that is carried along in the juices both being torn apart is already present, and no longer coming together easily belongs to it as well.

beads.greek: καὶ μέντοι καὶ τὸ τῆς αἰσθήσεως ἴδιον ἑκατέρου πάθους ἀναμνησθέντι σοι τοῖς αὐτοῖς μαρτυρήσει.
beads.english: And moreover, the peculiar character of the sensation of each of the two affections, if you recall it, will bear witness to the same things.

beads.greek: ταχεῖα μὲν γὰρ ἡ τῶν ὀξέων χυμῶν διέξοδος ἐν τοῖς αἰσθητικοῖς σώμασι φαίνεται γιγνομένη, βραδεῖα δ’ ἡ τῶν στρυφνῶν.
beads.english: For the passage of sour flavours through the sentient bodies appears to take place quickly, but that of acerbic ones slowly.

beads.greek: καὶ τὰ μὲν ὀξέα διὰ βάθους ἐνεργεῖν φαίνεται μᾶλλον, ἐπιπολῆς δὲ τὰ στρυφνά.
beads.english: And sour things appear to act rather in depth, acerbic things on the surface.

beads.greek: ταῦτ’ οὖν ἅπαντα παχυμερῆ μὲν εἶναι ἐνδείκνυνται τὰ στρυφνὰ σώματα, λεπτομερῆ δὲ ὑπάρχειν τὰ ὀξέα.
beads.english: All these things, then, indicate that acerbic bodies are coarse-particled, while sour ones are fine-particled.

greek_sentences: εἰ γὰρ τῷ στρυφνῷ χυλῷ συνάγειν καὶ ξηραίνειν καὶ τραχύνειν τὴν γλῶτταν ὑπάρχει σαφῶς, ἐδείχθη δ’ ἐν τοῖς ἔμπροσθεν λόγοις ὑπὸ ψυχροῦ μόνου συνάγεσθαι καὶ σφίγγεσθαι καὶ πιλεῖσθαι τὰ σώματα, πρόδηλον ὡς πάντως ψυχρός ἐστιν ὁ στρυφνὸς χυμός· ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ ἀνωμάλως ﻿ [639] ξηραίνει, τοῦτο γὰρ ἦν τὸ τραχῦνον, εἴη ἂν πάντως καὶ γεώδης.
ὁμαλῶς γὰρ ἅπαντα ὁ ὑδατώδης διεξέρχεται.

english_sentences: For if it clearly belongs to the acerbic juice to contract and dry and roughen the tongue, and it was shown in the preceding discussions that bodies are contracted and constricted and compacted by cold alone, it is evident that the acerbic flavour is in every case cold; and since it also dries unevenly [639] — for this was what does the roughening — it would in every case also be earthy.
For the watery [flavour] passes through everything evenly.

For it is inseparable from it, even if it is torn apart, to be united again; whereas for the earthy body that is carried along in the juices both being torn apart is already present, and no longer coming together easily belongs to it as well.
And moreover, the peculiar character of the sensation of each of the two affections, if you recall it, will bear witness to the same things.
For the passage of sour flavours through the sentient bodies appears to take place quickly, but that of acerbic ones slowly.
And sour things appear to act rather in depth, acerbic things on the surface.
All these things, then, indicate that acerbic bodies are coarse-particled, while sour ones are fine-particled.

beads.greek: ταυτὶ μὲν οὖν ἱκανῶς ἀλλήλοις ὡμολόγηται, τά τ’ ἀπὸ τῆς οὐσίας αὐτῆς τῶν πραγμάτων εἰρημένα καὶ τὰ διὰ τῆς τῶν εὑρημένων κατὰ τὴν αἴσθησιν ἐπαγωγῆς· οὐδὲν δ’ ἂν εἴη χεῖρον ἔτι καὶ ταῦτα προσθεῖναι, μεμνημένους πάλιν κᾀνταῦθα τῆς τῶν ὀνομάτων χρήσεως, ὡς στύφειν μὲν ἄμφω λέγεται, τό τ’ αὐστηρὸν καὶ τὸ στρυφνὸν, ἐν δὲ τῷ μᾶλλον [640] καὶ ἧττον διαφέρει.
beads.english: These points, then, are sufficiently in agreement with one another — both what has been said on the basis of the very substance of the things and what has been said by way of induction from what is discovered by perception. But it would be no worse to add these points too, recalling here again the usage of the names: that both are said to be astringent, the harsh and the acerbic, but they differ in the more [640] and the less.

beads.greek: καὶ μὴν καὶ ὅτι πολλαὶ τοῖς φαρμάκοις ὑπάρχουσι ποιότητες οὐ διάφοροι μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ μαχόμεναι πρὸς ἀλλήλας, ἐνίοτε δὲ καὶ παντάπασιν ὑπεναντίαι, δέδεικται μὲν ἔμπροσθεν αὐτάρκως, ἄρξασθαι δ’ ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ καὶ νῦν ἀναγκαῖον.
beads.english: And indeed, that drugs possess many qualities, not only different but also in conflict with one another, and sometimes even wholly opposed, has been sufficiently shown before; but it is necessary now too to begin from this point.

beads.greek: εἰ μὲν γάρ σοι φαίνοιτο γευομένῳ καὶ στρυφνὸν ἅμα καὶ δάκνον ταὐτὸ, τουτὶ μὲν ἀπολιπεῖν σε κελεύσω τὸ φάρμακον, ἔρχεσθαι δ’ ἐπὶ τὸ στρυφνὸν ἄνευ τοῦ δάκνειν.
beads.english: For if, when you taste it, the same thing appears to you to be at once both acerbic and biting, I shall bid you leave this drug aside and go on to the one that is acerbic without being biting.

beads.greek: εἰ δὲ μηδ’ ὀξὺ φαίνοιτο, μηδὲ γλυκὺ, μηδὲ πικρὸν, ἀλλ’ ὡς οἷόν τε μάλιστα μίαν ἔχον ἄμικτον ποιότητα τὴν τῆς στύψεως, οὕτως ἤδη βασανίζειν αὐτὸ τῇ πείρᾳ καθ’ ὃν πολλάκις ἔμπροσθεν ὑπεθέμην σοι τρόπον.
beads.english: And if it appears neither sour nor sweet nor bitter, but, as far as is at all possible, having a single unmixed quality, that of astringency, then at that point to test it by experience in the manner I have often laid down for you before.

beads.greek: ἐὰν γὰρ ἅμα τό τε στύφειν ἔχῃ καὶ τὸ δάκνειν ἤ τινα ἄλλην ἐναργῆ ποιότητα καὶ δύναμιν ἐπιμεμιγμένην τῇ στύψει, περιττὸν καὶ μάταιον εἰς πεῖραν ἄγειν τὸ τοιοῦτον φάρμακον, ἐπειδὰν δοκιμάζῃς ἐνέργειαν στύψεως.
beads.english: For if it has at once both the astringent and the biting, or some other evident quality and power mingled with the astringency, it is superfluous and vain to bring such a drug to the test when you are examining the activity of astringency.

beads.greek: ἄδηλον γὰρ εἴτε διὰ τὴν στύψιν, εἴτε διά τινα τῶν ἀναμεμιγμένων αὐτῇ ποιοτήτων, εἴτε καὶ δι’ ἀμφοτέρας ἐνήργησεν ὡδί πως περὶ τὸ πλησιάζον αὐτῷ σῶμα.
beads.english: For it is unclear whether it was because of the astringency, or because of one of the qualities mixed in with it, or indeed because of both, that it acted in this or that way upon the body that came into contact with it.

greek_sentences: ταυτὶ μὲν οὖν ἱκανῶς ἀλλήλοις ὡμολόγηται, τά τ’ ἀπὸ τῆς οὐσίας αὐτῆς τῶν πραγμάτων εἰρημένα καὶ τὰ διὰ τῆς τῶν εὑρημένων κατὰ τὴν αἴσθησιν ἐπαγωγῆς· οὐδὲν δ’ ἂν εἴη χεῖρον ἔτι καὶ ταῦτα προσθεῖναι, μεμνημένους πάλιν κᾀνταῦθα τῆς τῶν ὀνομάτων χρήσεως, ὡς στύφειν μὲν ἄμφω λέγεται, τό τ’ αὐστηρὸν καὶ τὸ στρυφνὸν, ἐν δὲ τῷ μᾶλλον [640] καὶ ἧττον διαφέρει.

εἰ μὲν γάρ σοι φαίνοιτο γευομένῳ καὶ στρυφνὸν ἅμα καὶ δάκνον ταὐτὸ, τουτὶ μὲν ἀπολιπεῖν σε κελεύσω τὸ φάρμακον, ἔρχεσθαι δ’ ἐπὶ τὸ στρυφνὸν ἄνευ τοῦ δάκνειν.

εἰ δὲ μηδ’ ὀξὺ φαίνοιτο, μηδὲ γλυκὺ, μηδὲ πικρὸν, ἀλλ’ ὡς οἷόν τε μάλιστα μίαν ἔχον ἄμικτον ποιότητα τὴν τῆς στύψεως, οὕτως ἤδη βασανίζειν αὐτὸ τῇ πείρᾳ καθ’ ὃν πολλάκις ἔμπροσθεν ὑπεθέμην σοι τρόπον.

ἄδηλον γὰρ εἴτε διὰ τὴν στύψιν, εἴτε διά τινα τῶν ἀναμεμιγμένων αὐτῇ ποιοτήτων, εἴτε καὶ δι’ ἀμφοτέρας ἐνήργησεν ὡδί πως περὶ τὸ πλησιάζον αὐτῷ σῶμα.
english_sentences: These points, then, are sufficiently in agreement with one another — both what has been said on the basis of the very substance of the things and what has been said by way of induction from what is discovered by perception.

But it would be no worse to add these points too, recalling here again the usage of the names: that both are said to be astringent, the harsh and the acerbic, but they differ in the more [640] and the less.

And indeed, that drugs possess many qualities, not only different but also in conflict with one another, and sometimes even wholly opposed, has been sufficiently shown before; but it is necessary now too to begin from this point.
For if, when you taste it, the same thing appears to you to be at once both acerbic and biting, I shall bid you leave this drug aside and go on to the one that is acerbic without being biting.

And if it appears neither sour nor sweet nor bitter, but, as far as is at all possible, having a single unmixed quality, that of astringency, then at that point to test it by experience in the manner I have often laid down for you before.

For if it has at once both the astringent and the biting, or some other evident quality and power mingled with the astringency, it is superfluous and vain to bring such a drug to the test when you are examining the activity of astringency.

For it is unclear whether it was because of the astringency, or because of one of the qualities mixed in with it, or indeed because of both, that it acted in this or that way upon the body that came into contact with it.

beads.greek: χαλκῖτις οὖν καὶ μίσυ [641] καὶ χάλκανθος καὶ λεπὶς χαλκοῦ καὶ σῶρυ, στύφοντά τε ἅμα καὶ δάκνοντα, δρᾷ μὲν κατ’ ἀμφοτέρας τὰς ποιότητας εἰς ἕκαστον τῶν ὁμιλούντων σωμάτων, οὐ μὴν διδάξαι γε ἡμᾶς δύναται σαφῶς εἴτε διὰ τὴν στύψιν ἔχει τὸ καίειν, εἴτε διὰ τὴν δριμύτητα.
beads.english: Chalkitis, then, and misy [641] and chalkanthos and scale of copper and sory, being at once astringent and biting, act according to both qualities upon each of the bodies with which they come into contact, yet they cannot teach us clearly whether they have their burning on account of the astringency or on account of the pungency.

beads.greek: καταλιπεῖν οὖν ἄμεινον αὐτὰ καὶ γεύεσθαι πολλῶν ἐφεξῆς ἄλλων ἐπισκοπούμενον εἰλικρινῆ στύψιν ἰδίᾳ καὶ καθ’ ἑαυτὴν ὡς οἷόν τ’ ἐστὶ μάλιστα, κᾀπειδὰν τοιαύτην εὕρῃς, οὕτως ἤδη κρίνειν τὸ φάρμακον αἷς πολλάκις ἔμπροσθεν ἤκουσας μεθόδοις, οἷον εἴ σοι γευομένῳ φαίνοιτο βαλαύστιον, ἢ κικὶς, ἢ κύτινος, ἢ ὑποκυστὶς, ἢ στρύχνος, ἢ γλαύκιον, ἢ ἀκακία, ἢ ῥοῦ χυλὸς, ἤ τι τοιοῦτον ἕτερον ἀκριβῶς μὲν εἶναι στρυφνὸν, ἔκδηλον δ’ ἑτέραν ποιότητα μηδεμίαν ἔχον, ἐξετάζειν ἐπὶ τῶν τοιούτων ἤδη καὶ βασανίζειν ἀκριβῶς ἐνέργειαν στύψεως.
beads.english: It is better, therefore, to leave these aside and to taste many others in succession, looking for a pure astringency, separately and by itself as far as is at all possible, and when you have found such a one, then at that point to judge the drug by the methods you have often heard before: for instance, if on tasting balaustion, or oak-gall, or kytinos, or hypokistis, or strychnos, or glaukion, or acacia, or juice of sumach, or some other such thing, it should appear to you to be precisely acerbic, while having no other manifest quality, then on such things to examine and test precisely the activity of astringency.

beads.greek: ἡ δὲ ἐξέτασις, ὡς εἴρηται πολλάκις, ἐπί τε τῶν ἐν ἀρίστῃ κατασκευῇ σωμάτων ἀκριβῶς ὑγιαινόντων, ἐπί τε τῶν ἁπλῶν γινέσθω σοι παθῶν, ἤτοιν θερμῶν, ἢ ψυχρῶν, ἢ ξηρῶν, ἢ ὑγρῶν.
beads.english: And let the examination, as has often been said, be made by you both on bodies in the best constitution that are precisely healthy, and on the simple affections, whether hot, or cold, or dry, or moist.

καταλιπεῖν οὖν ἄμεινον αὐτὰ καὶ γεύεσθαι πολλῶν ἐφεξῆς ἄλλων ἐπισκοπούμενον εἰλικρινῆ στύψιν ἰδίᾳ καὶ καθ’ ἑαυτὴν ὡς οἷόν τ’ ἐστὶ μάλιστα, κᾀπειδὰν τοιαύτην εὕρῃς, οὕτως ἤδη κρίνειν τὸ φάρμακον αἷς πολλάκις ἔμπροσθεν ἤκουσας μεθόδοις, οἷον εἴ σοι γευομένῳ φαίνοιτο βαλαύστιον, ἢ κικὶς, ἢ κύτινος, ἢ ὑποκυστὶς, ἢ στρύχνος, ἢ γλαύκιον, ἢ ἀκακία, ἢ ῥοῦ χυλὸς, ἤ τι τοιοῦτον ἕτερον ἀκριβῶς μὲν εἶναι στρυφνὸν, ἔκδηλον δ’ ἑτέραν ποιότητα μηδεμίαν ἔχον, ἐξετάζειν ἐπὶ τῶν τοιούτων ἤδη καὶ βασανίζειν ἀκριβῶς ἐνέργειαν στύψεως.
ἡ δὲ ἐξέτασις, ὡς εἴρηται πολλάκις, ἐπί τε τῶν ἐν ἀρίστῃ κατασκευῇ σωμάτων ἀκριβῶς ὑγιαινόντων, ἐπί τε τῶν ἁπλῶν γινέσθω σοι παθῶν, ἤτοιν θερμῶν, ἢ ψυχρῶν, ἢ ξηρῶν, ἢ ὑγρῶν.
english_sentences: Chalkitis, then, and misy [641] and chalkanthos and scale of copper and sory, being at once astringent and biting, act according to both qualities upon each of the bodies with which they come into contact, yet they cannot teach us clearly whether they have their burning on account of the astringency or on account of the pungency.

It is better, therefore, to leave these aside and to taste many others in succession, looking for a pure astringency, separately and by itself as far as is at all possible, and when you have found such a one, then at that point to judge the drug by the methods you have often heard before: for instance, if on tasting balaustion, or oak-gall, or kytinos, or hypokistis, or strychnos, or glaukion, or acacia, or juice of sumach, or some other such thing, it should appear to you to be precisely acerbic, while having no other manifest quality, then on such things to examine and test precisely the activity of astringency.

And let the examination, as has often been said, be made by you both on bodies in the best constitution that are precisely healthy, and on the simple affections, whether hot, or cold, or dry, or moist.

beads.greek: εἰ μὲν γὰρ αὐτό τε τὸ ὑγιαῖνον [642] σῶμα φαίνοιτο σαφῶς ἐμψῦχον, ἐπί τε τῶν θερμῶν ἁρμόττει παθῶν, ἐναργῆ δὲ καὶ αὐτῷ τῷ κάμνοντι τὴν ψυχρὰν προσβάλλει ποιότητα, τολμᾷν ἤδη τι περὶ τῆς στύψεως ὡς ψυχούσης ἀποφαίνεσθαι.
beads.english: For if the healthy [642] body itself should appear to be clearly cooled, and it is suited to hot affections, and it imparts a manifest cold quality to the patient himself, then one may at that point venture to declare something about astringency as cooling.

beads.greek: εἰ δ’ ἔμπαλιν ἔχον εὑρίσκοιτο καὶ τῶν ὑγιαινόντων σωμάτων ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ θερμαινομένων καὶ τῶν θερμῶν νοσημάτων παροξυνομένων καὶ τῶν ψυχρῶν ὠφελουμένων οὐ ψύχειν, ἀλλὰ θερμαίνειν ἡγεῖσθαι χρὴ τὸ τοιοῦτον φάρμακον.
beads.english: But if it should be found to be the opposite, with healthy bodies being heated by it, hot diseases being exacerbated and cold ones benefited, one must consider such a drug not to cool but to heat.

beads.greek: οὕτω δὲ καὶ περὶ τῶν δριμέων αὐτῶν καθ’ ἑαυτὰ ποιεῖσθαι τὴν βάσανον, ἐπί τε κρόμμυον ἰόντα καὶ σκόροδον καὶ πέπερι καὶ πύρεθρον καὶ ζιγγίβερι καὶ στρούθιον, ἑλένιόν τε καὶ τίτανον.
beads.english: In the same way one should also make the test of pungent things themselves by themselves, turning to onion and garlic and pepper and pellitory and ginger and soapwort, elecampane and lime.

beads.greek: ὥσπερ γὰρ ὁ μίξας στρύχνου χυλῷ πέπερι δοκιμάζειν οὐδέτερον αὐτῶν ἱκανός ἐστιν, οὕτως οὐδ’ ὁ τὰ πρὸς τῆς φύσεως μεμιγμένα.
beads.english: For just as one who has mixed pepper with juice of strychnos is not competent to test either of them, so neither is one who tests things that have been mixed by nature.

beads.greek: κατὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον ἀξιῶ σε καὶ τὴν ὀξεῖαν ποιότητα καὶ τὴν πικρὰν καὶ τὴν γλυκεῖαν ἐπισκέπτεσθαι σφοδρὰς καὶ μόνας ὡς οἷόν τ’ ἐστὶν εἰς τὴν δοκιμασίαν ἄγοντα καὶ τῇ πείρᾳ τὰς δυνάμεις αὐτῶν ἐξευρίσκοντα.
beads.english: And in the same manner I require you to investigate also the sour quality and the bitter and the sweet, bringing them to the test as intense and as isolated as is possible, and discovering their powers by experience.

greek_sentences: εἰ μὲν γὰρ αὐτό τε τὸ ὑγιαῖνον [642] σῶμα φαίνοιτο σαφῶς ἐμψῦχον, ἐπί τε τῶν θερμῶν ἁρμόττει παθῶν, ἐναργῆ δὲ καὶ αὐτῷ τῷ κάμνοντι τὴν ψυχρὰν προσβάλλει ποιότητα, τολμᾷν ἤδη τι περὶ τῆς στύψεως ὡς ψυχούσης ἀποφαίνεσθαι.

εἰ δ’ ἔμπαλιν ἔχον εὑρίσκοιτο καὶ τῶν ὑγιαινόντων σωμάτων ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ θερμαινομένων καὶ τῶν θερμῶν νοσημάτων παροξυνομένων καὶ τῶν ψυχρῶν ὠφελουμένων οὐ ψύχειν, ἀλλὰ θερμαίνειν ἡγεῖσθαι χρὴ τὸ τοιοῦτον φάρμακον.

ὥσπερ γὰρ ὁ μίξας στρύχνου χυλῷ πέπερι δοκιμάζειν οὐδέτερον αὐτῶν ἱκανός ἐστιν, οὕτως οὐδ’ ὁ τὰ πρὸς τῆς φύσεως μεμιγμένα.

κατὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον ἀξιῶ σε καὶ τὴν ὀξεῖαν ποιότητα καὶ τὴν πικρὰν καὶ τὴν γλυκεῖαν ἐπισκέπτεσθαι σφοδρὰς καὶ μόνας ὡς οἷόν τ’ ἐστὶν εἰς τὴν δοκιμασίαν ἄγοντα καὶ τῇ πείρᾳ τὰς δυνάμεις αὐτῶν ἐξευρίσκοντα.
english_sentences: For if the healthy [642] body itself should appear to be clearly cooled, and it is suited to hot affections, and it imparts a manifest cold quality to the patient himself, then one may at that point venture to declare something about astringency as cooling.
But if it should be found to be the opposite, with healthy bodies being heated by it, hot diseases being exacerbated and cold ones benefited, one must consider such a drug not to cool but to heat.
In the same way one should also make the test of pungent things themselves by themselves, turning to onion and garlic and pepper and pellitory and ginger and soapwort, elecampane and lime.
For just as one who has mixed pepper with juice of strychnos is not competent to test either of them, so neither is one who tests things that have been mixed by nature.

And in the same manner I require you to investigate also the sour quality and the bitter and the sweet, bringing them to the test as intense and as isolated as is possible, and discovering their powers by experience.

beads.greek: τὸ δὲ πᾶν ὅ τι περ ἂν ᾖ στρυφνὸν, ἢ αὐστηρὸν, ἢ πικρὸν, ἄγειν εἰς πεῖραν, ὡς ἤτοι στρυφνότητος, ἢ αὐστηρότητος, [643] ἢ πικρότητος ἐν αὐτῷ βάσανον ληψόμενον ἄτοπον δεινῶς.
beads.english: But to bring to trial everything whatsoever that is acerbic, or harsh, or bitter, as though one were going to obtain in it a test of acerbity, or harshness, [643] or bitterness, is dreadfully absurd.

beads.greek: εἰ γὰρ μιᾶς μόνης μετέχει ποιότητος, τὴν αὐτὴν τοῦ φαρμάκου πεῖραν ἕξεις καὶ τῆς ποιότητος· εἰ δὲ πλειόνων, ἐξ ἁπασῶν ἤδη δηλονότι μικτὴν ἐνέργειαν ἐνεργήσει τὸ φάρμακον, ὥσθ’ ἡ τῆς μιᾶς τῆς κρινομένης ἔτ’ ἄδηλος μένει.
beads.english: For if it partakes of one quality only, you will have the same trial of the drug and of the quality; but if of several, the drug will then clearly perform an activity mixed from all of them, so that the activity of the single quality under judgment still remains unclear.

beads.greek: εἴπερ οὖν ὡς προείρηται χρὴ κρίνειν, οὐκ ὀρθῶς ὑπέλαβον οἵ τε μηδ’ ὅλως ἀποφήνασθαί τι δυνατὸν εἶναι νομίσαντες ὑπὲρ τῆς τῶν χυμῶν δυνάμεως, οἵ θ’ ἑτέρως τὴν κρίσιν ποιησάμενοι.
beads.english: If, then, one must judge as has been stated before, both those who supposed that it is not possible at all to declare anything about the power of the flavours, and those who made the judgment in another way, supposed incorrectly.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ ἀποφήνασθαί τι δυνατὸν ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν ἐστιν καὶ τὴν κρίσιν οὐκ ἄλλως ἢ ὡς εἴρηται νῦν προσήκει ποιεῖσθαι.
beads.english: For it is both possible to declare something about them, and it is fitting to make the judgment in no other way than as has now been stated.

beads.greek: εἰ μὲν οὖν ὅλως μηδὲν δεῖσθαι τῆς κατὰ τοὺς χυμοὺς ἐπισκέψεως εἰρήκεισαν, ἐπειδὰν τὰς δυνάμεις τῶν φαρμάκων ἐξετάζωμεν, ἐγχωρεῖ γὰρ καὶ χωρὶς τούτων ἐξευρίσκειν τῇ πείρᾳ τὴν δύναμιν αὐτῶν, ἐπῄνοουν ἂν μᾶλλον ἢ ἐμεμφόμην αὐτούς.
beads.english: Now if they had said that there is no need at all of the examination concerning the flavours when we investigate the powers of drugs—for it is possible even without these to discover their power by experience—I would have praised rather than blamed them.

beads.greek: ἐπεὶ δ’ ὡς ὑπὲρ ἀναγκαίου μὲν, ἀγνώστου δὲ διέρχονται, διχῇ μέμψασθαι τοὺς ἄνδρας δίκαιον, ὅτι τε τὸ μὴ ἀναγκαῖον ὑπέλαβον ὡς ἀναγκαῖον, ὅτι τε προαπέγνωσαν αὐτοῦ τῆς εὑρέσεως.
beads.english: But since they treat of it as something necessary, yet unknowable, it is just to blame these men on two counts: both because they took what is not necessary to be necessary, and because they despaired in advance of its discovery.

greek_sentences: τὸ δὲ πᾶν ὅ τι περ ἂν ᾖ στρυφνὸν, ἢ αὐστηρὸν, ἢ πικρὸν, ἄγειν εἰς πεῖραν, ὡς ἤτοι στρυφνότητος, ἢ αὐστηρότητος, [643] ἢ πικρότητος ἐν αὐτῷ βάσανον ληψόμενον ἄτοπον δεινῶς.

εἰ γὰρ μιᾶς μόνης μετέχει ποιότητος, τὴν αὐτὴν τοῦ φαρμάκου πεῖραν ἕξεις καὶ τῆς ποιότητος· εἰ δὲ πλειόνων, ἐξ ἁπασῶν ἤδη δηλονότι μικτὴν ἐνέργειαν ἐνεργήσει τὸ φάρμακον, ὥσθ’ ἡ τῆς μιᾶς τῆς κρινομένης ἔτ’ ἄδηλος μένει.

καὶ γὰρ ἀποφήνασθαί τι δυνατὸν ὑπὲρ αὐτῶν ἐστιν καὶ τὴν κρίσιν οὐκ ἄλλως ἢ ὡς εἴρηται νῦν προσήκει ποιεῖσθαι.

For if it partakes of one quality only, you will have the same trial of the drug and of the quality; but if of several, the drug will then clearly perform an activity mixed from all of them, so that the activity of the single quality under judgment still remains unclear.

If, then, one must judge as has been stated before, both those who supposed that it is not possible at all to declare anything about the power of the flavours, and those who made the judgment in another way, supposed incorrectly.
For it is both possible to declare something about them, and it is fitting to make the judgment in no other way than as has now been stated.

Now if they had said that there is no need at all of the examination concerning the flavours when we investigate the powers of drugs—for it is possible even without these to discover their power by experience—I would have praised rather than blamed them.

But since they treat of it as something necessary, yet unknowable, it is just to blame these men on two counts: both because they took what is not necessary to be necessary, and because they despaired in advance of its discovery.

beads.greek: ἡ γάρ τοι κρίσις ἑκάστου τῶν φαρμάκων τῆς ﻿ [644] δυνάμεως ἄνευ τῆς τῶν χυμῶν διαγνώσεως αὐτάρκως εὑρίσκεται τῇ πείρᾳ μόνῃ βασανιζομένῃ καθ’ ὃν εἴρηκα μυριάκις ἤδη τρόπον.
beads.english: For indeed the judgment of the power of each of the [644] drugs is found sufficiently, without the discrimination of the flavours, by experience alone, when it is tested in the manner I have already stated countless times.

beads.greek: κᾀγὼ νῦν, οὐχ ὡς οὐκ ἐνὸν ἄλλως ἐξευρεῖν τὸ ζητούμενον, ἀλλὰ διά τε τὸ πρὸς τὰς ἀρχὰς ἀκόλουθον, ἵν’ ἐπιδείξαιμι πάντα τοῖς τῶν στοιχείων λογισμοῖς ἑπόμενα καὶ μηδὲν μηδαμόθι μαχόμενον, ἐξελέγξαιμί τε τοὺς ἅπαντα τὰ στύφοντα θερμαίνειν εἰπόντας, ἐπὶ τὸν περὶ τῶν χυμῶν ἀφικόμην λόγον.
beads.english: And I myself have now come to the discussion concerning the flavours, not on the grounds that it is impossible to discover what is sought otherwise, but both on account of consistency with the first principles, so that I might show that everything follows upon the reasonings about the elements and that nothing anywhere conflicts with them, and so that I might refute those who said that all astringent things heat.

beads.greek: εὑρεθείη δ’ ἄν τις αὐτοῦ καὶ χρεία πρὸς τὴν ἐνεστῶσαν ἡμῖν πραγματείαν.
beads.english: Some use of it, too, might be found for the treatise now before us.

beads.greek: ἀλλὰ ταῦτα μὲν ὕστερον ἐπιδεῖξαι πειράσομαι· νυνὶ δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ προκείμενον ἐπάνειμι, παρακελεύομαί τε τῆς ἀληθείας ὀρεγομένοις, αὐτοῖς γευομένοις ἁπάντων τῶν στυφόντων, ὥσπερ ἡμεῖς ἐποιήσαμεν, ὅταν εὕρωσιν ἀκριβῶς κατά τι σῶμα τὴν στύψιν, ἄμικτον ὡς οἷόν τε μάλιστα τῶν ἄλλων ποιοτήτων, τηνικαῦτα διὰ τῆς πείρας ἐξετάζειν εἴτε θερμὸν, εἴτε ψυχρὸν, εἴτε ξηρὸν, εἴτε ὑγρὸν ὑπάρχει τὸ τοιοῦτον σῶμα.
beads.english: But these things I shall try to show later; for now I return to the matter at hand, and I urge those who desire the truth, tasting for themselves all astringent things, just as we did, whenever they find astringency precisely in some body, unmixed as far as possible with the other qualities, then to examine through experience whether such a body is hot, or cold, or dry, or moist.

beads.greek: τουτὶ μὲν οὖν ἕκαστος, ἄν περ σωφρονῇ, ποιήσει καταμόνας αὐτός.
beads.english: This, then, each person, if he is sensible, will do by himself on his own.

greek_sentences: ἡ γάρ τοι κρίσις ἑκάστου τῶν φαρμάκων τῆς ﻿ [644] δυνάμεως ἄνευ τῆς τῶν χυμῶν διαγνώσεως αὐτάρκως εὑρίσκεται τῇ πείρᾳ μόνῃ βασανιζομένῃ καθ’ ὃν εἴρηκα μυριάκις ἤδη τρόπον.

κᾀγὼ νῦν, οὐχ ὡς οὐκ ἐνὸν ἄλλως ἐξευρεῖν τὸ ζητούμενον, ἀλλὰ διά τε τὸ πρὸς τὰς ἀρχὰς ἀκόλουθον, ἵν’ ἐπιδείξαιμι πάντα τοῖς τῶν στοιχείων λογισμοῖς ἑπόμενα καὶ μηδὲν μηδαμόθι μαχόμενον, ἐξελέγξαιμί τε τοὺς ἅπαντα τὰ στύφοντα θερμαίνειν εἰπόντας, ἐπὶ τὸν περὶ τῶν χυμῶν ἀφικόμην λόγον.
εὑρεθείη δ’ ἄν τις αὐτοῦ καὶ χρεία πρὸς τὴν ἐνεστῶσαν ἡμῖν πραγματείαν.

ἀλλὰ ταῦτα μὲν ὕστερον ἐπιδεῖξαι πειράσομαι· νυνὶ δὲ ἐπὶ τὸ προκείμενον ἐπάνειμι, παρακελεύομαί τε τῆς ἀληθείας ὀρεγομένοις, αὐτοῖς γευομένοις ἁπάντων τῶν στυφόντων, ὥσπερ ἡμεῖς ἐποιήσαμεν, ὅταν εὕρωσιν ἀκριβῶς κατά τι σῶμα τὴν στύψιν, ἄμικτον ὡς οἷόν τε μάλιστα τῶν ἄλλων ποιοτήτων, τηνικαῦτα διὰ τῆς πείρας ἐξετάζειν εἴτε θερμὸν, εἴτε ψυχρὸν, εἴτε ξηρὸν, εἴτε ὑγρὸν ὑπάρχει τὸ τοιοῦτον σῶμα.
τουτὶ μὲν οὖν ἕκαστος, ἄν περ σωφρονῇ, ποιήσει καταμόνας αὐτός.
english_sentences: For indeed the judgment of the power of each of the [644] drugs is found sufficiently, without the discrimination of the flavours, by experience alone, when it is tested in the manner I have already stated countless times.

And I myself have now come to the discussion concerning the flavours, not on the grounds that it is impossible to discover what is sought otherwise, but both on account of consistency with the first principles, so that I might show that everything follows upon the reasonings about the elements and that nothing anywhere conflicts with them, and so that I might refute those who said that all astringent things heat.
Some use of it, too, might be found for the treatise now before us.

But these things I shall try to show later; for now I return to the matter at hand, and I urge those who desire the truth, tasting for themselves all astringent things, just as we did, whenever they find astringency precisely in some body, unmixed as far as possible with the other qualities, then to examine through experience whether such a body is hot, or cold, or dry, or moist.
This, then, each person, if he is sensible, will do by himself on his own.

beads.greek: ἐμοὶ δ’ ἀναγκαῖον ἴσως [645] ἀποφαίνεσθαί τι περὶ τῆς ἐμαυτοῦ πείρας ἐν μὲν τῷ νῦν ἐνεστῶτι λόγῳ καθόλου, κατὰ μέρος δὲ διὰ τῶν ἑξῆς ὑπομνημάτων.
beads.english: But for me it is perhaps necessary [645] to make some declaration about my own experience, in general terms in the present discourse, and in particular through the treatises that follow.

beads.greek: εἴη δ’ ἂν ὁ μὲν καθόλου λόγος ὑπὲρ ἁπάντων τοιόσδε.
beads.english: The general account concerning all of them would be as follows.

beads.greek: Πᾶν στῦφον σῶμα, τό γε τῶν ἄλλων καθαρεῦον, ὥσπερ πρὸς τὴν αἴσθησιν ποιοτήτων, εὗρον ἀεὶ πειρώμενος ψυχρόν.
beads.english: Every astringent body, at least one that is pure of the other qualities, so far as regards perception, I have always found, upon testing, to be cold.

beads.greek: ἤδη δὲ καὶ τῶν ἐπιμίκτων ταῖς ποιότησιν ἔνια, τά τε μετρίως γλυκέα καὶ πικρὰ καὶ δριμέα, σαφῶς εὑρέθη ψύχοντα, κρατούσης γὰρ ἐν αὐτοῖς δηλονότι τῆς τοῦ στύφειν τε καὶ ψύχειν δυνάμεως, ὡς ἀμαυροῦσθαι τὰς ἄλλας.
beads.english: Indeed, even some of those that are mixed in their qualities, namely those that are moderately sweet and bitter and pungent, were clearly found to be cooling, since evidently the power of being astringent and of cooling prevails in them, so that the other powers are obscured.

beads.greek: κατὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν λόγον καὶ τὰ ὀξέα πάντα, τά θ’ ἁπλῶς ὀξέα, καθάπερ ὀξαλίδα καὶ ὀξυλάπαθον, ἔνιά τε τῶν ἐπιμίκτων ἑτέραις ποιότησιν, ἤτοι γλυκείαις ἢ δριμείαις ἢ πικραῖς, οὐδὲν ἧττον εὑρίσκεται ψύχοντα καὶ ῥοιαὶ καὶ μῆλα καὶ κοκύμηλα καὶ σταφυλαὶ καὶ σῦκα καὶ συκάμινα καὶ κεράσια καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ὄξος.
beads.english: By the same reasoning, all sour things too, both those that are simply sour, such as oxalis and oxylapathon, and some of those mixed with other qualities, whether sweet or pungent or bitter, are found no less to be cooling: pomegranates and apples and plums and grapes and figs and mulberries and cherries and vinegar itself.

beads.greek: ἀλλὰ τούτῳ μὲν, ὡς εἴρηται πρόσθεν, ἐπιμέμικταί τις δριμύτης, ταῖς δ’ ὀπώραις γλυκύτητές τε καὶ στρυφνότητες, καί τισιν αὐτῶν καὶ πικρότητες ἀμυδραί.
beads.english: But with this last, as was said before, a certain pungency is mixed in, while with the fruits sweetnesses and acerbities, and in some of them also faint bitternesses.

greek_sentences: ἐμοὶ δ’ ἀναγκαῖον ἴσως [645] ἀποφαίνεσθαί τι περὶ τῆς ἐμαυτοῦ πείρας ἐν μὲν τῷ νῦν ἐνεστῶτι λόγῳ καθόλου, κατὰ μέρος δὲ διὰ τῶν ἑξῆς ὑπομνημάτων.
εἴη δ’ ἂν ὁ μὲν καθόλου λόγος ὑπὲρ ἁπάντων τοιόσδε.
Πᾶν στῦφον σῶμα, τό γε τῶν ἄλλων καθαρεῦον, ὥσπερ πρὸς τὴν αἴσθησιν ποιοτήτων, εὗρον ἀεὶ πειρώμενος ψυχρόν.

ἤδη δὲ καὶ τῶν ἐπιμίκτων ταῖς ποιότησιν ἔνια, τά τε μετρίως γλυκέα καὶ πικρὰ καὶ δριμέα, σαφῶς εὑρέθη ψύχοντα, κρατούσης γὰρ ἐν αὐτοῖς δηλονότι τῆς τοῦ στύφειν τε καὶ ψύχειν δυνάμεως, ὡς ἀμαυροῦσθαι τὰς ἄλλας.

κατὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν λόγον καὶ τὰ ὀξέα πάντα, τά θ’ ἁπλῶς ὀξέα, καθάπερ ὀξαλίδα καὶ ὀξυλάπαθον, ἔνιά τε τῶν ἐπιμίκτων ἑτέραις ποιότησιν, ἤτοι γλυκείαις ἢ δριμείαις ἢ πικραῖς, οὐδὲν ἧττον εὑρίσκεται ψύχοντα καὶ ῥοιαὶ καὶ μῆλα καὶ κοκύμηλα καὶ σταφυλαὶ καὶ σῦκα καὶ συκάμινα καὶ κεράσια καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ὄξος.
ἀλλὰ τούτῳ μὲν, ὡς εἴρηται πρόσθεν, ἐπιμέμικταί τις δριμύτης, ταῖς δ’ ὀπώραις γλυκύτητές τε καὶ στρυφνότητες, καί τισιν αὐτῶν καὶ πικρότητες ἀμυδραί.
english_sentences: But for me it is perhaps necessary [645] to make some declaration about my own experience, in general terms in the present discourse, and in particular through the treatises that follow.
The general account concerning all of them would be as follows.
Every astringent body, at least one that is pure of the other qualities, so far as regards perception, I have always found, upon testing, to be cold.

Indeed, even some of those that are mixed in their qualities, namely those that are moderately sweet and bitter and pungent, were clearly found to be cooling, since evidently the power of being astringent and of cooling prevails in them, so that the other powers are obscured.

By the same reasoning, all sour things too, both those that are simply sour, such as oxalis and oxylapathon, and some of those mixed with other qualities, whether sweet or pungent or bitter, are found no less to be cooling: pomegranates and apples and plums and grapes and figs and mulberries and cherries and vinegar itself.
But with this last, as was said before, a certain pungency is mixed in, while with the fruits sweetnesses and acerbities, and in some of them also faint bitternesses.

beads.greek: καὶ μέντοι καὶ [646] ὅσα στύφει τε ἅμα καὶ ὀξέα ταῖς ποιότησίν ἐστιν, ἅπαντα καὶ ταῦτά μοι εὑρέθη πειρωμένῳ σαφῶς ψύχοντα· τὰ δὲ γλυκέα μόνον ἅπαντα κατὰ τὸ ποσὸν τῆς γλυκύτητος εὐθὺς καὶ τῆς θερμότητος μετέχειν, ὥστ’ οὐδὲν μὲν τῶν λίαν γλυκέων ψυχρόν· εἴη δ’ ἄν τι καὶ μετρίως γλυκὺ ψυχρὸν, ἐπειδὰν τὸ πλεῖστον αὐτοῦ τῆς τοῦ σώματος οὐσίας ὑδατῶδες ᾖ, οὐ μὴν οὕτω γε ψυχρὸν, ὡς τὸ στρυφνὸν ἱκανῶς ἢ τὸ ὀξὺ, ἀλλ’ ὡς καὶ πρόσθεν που λέλεκται περὶ τῶν χλιαρᾶς θερμασίας μετεχόντων. καὶ τὰ πικρά γε πάντα θερμὰ, καθάπερ ἥ τε χολὴ καὶ τὸ νίτρον καὶ οἱ πάνυ παλαιοὶ τῶν οἴνων καὶ τῶν σπερμάτων μυρία.
beads.english: And indeed, [646] all those things too that are astringent and at the same time sour in their qualities were, as I found on trial, all of them clearly cooling; whereas all those that are merely sweet [I found] to partake straightaway of heat too, in proportion to the amount of their sweetness, so that none of the very sweet things is cold; yet something moderately sweet might also be cold, whenever the greater part of the substance of its body is watery—not, however, cold to such a degree as that which is strongly acerbic or sour, but in the way that has been stated somewhere earlier concerning the things that partake of a lukewarm warmth.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ τὸ τοῦ πηγάνου καὶ μάλιστα τὸ τοῦ ἀγρίου καὶ τὸ τοῦ τορδύλου καὶ τὸ τοῦ σπονδύλου καὶ τὸ τοῦ μελανθίου καὶ οἱ θέρμοι καὶ μᾶλλον οἱ ἄγριοι καὶ οἱ ὄροβοι, καὶ τούτων οἱ ἄγριοι μᾶλλον, ὅ τε προσαγορευόμενος πελεκῖνος.
beads.english: And all bitter things are hot, as for instance bile and nitre and the very old wines and countless seeds.

beads.greek: εὑρίσκεται δὲ ἐν τοῖς πυροῖς. ἀμυγδαλαῖ τέ τινες, αἳ δὴ καὶ δι’ αὐτὸ τοῦτο προσαγορεύονται πικραὶ, καὶ συκίων ἄττα σπέρματα καὶ τὸ τοῦ μήλου τοῦ Μηδικοῦ, καὶ πρὸς τούτοις ἕτερα μυρία πικρὰ φαίνεται τοῖς γευομένοις.
beads.english: For the seed of rue, and especially that of the wild kind, and that of tordylium and that of spondylium and that of melanthium, and lupins, and more so the wild ones, and bitter vetch, and of these too the wild ones more so, and the so-called pelekinos (it is found among wheat), and certain almonds, which are indeed for this very reason called bitter, and certain seeds of gourds (συκίων), and that of the Median apple, and in addition to these countless other things appear bitter to those who taste them.

καὶ γὰρ τὸ τοῦ πηγάνου καὶ μάλιστα τὸ τοῦ ἀγρίου καὶ τὸ τοῦ τορδύλου καὶ τὸ τοῦ σπονδύλου καὶ τὸ τοῦ μελανθίου καὶ οἱ θέρμοι καὶ μᾶλλον οἱ ἄγριοι καὶ οἱ ὄροβοι, καὶ τούτων οἱ ἄγριοι μᾶλλον, ὅ τε προσαγορευόμενος πελεκῖνος.
εὑρίσκεται δὲ ἐν τοῖς πυροῖς.
