english_sentences: For not only milk, but also the sulphurous, the bituminous and the nitrous, and all such as are of this kind among the naturally occurring [428] waters, came into being from an admixture of the opposite powers, if indeed water is cold and moist according to its own nature, while bitumen and sulphur and misy and chalcitis and the other things of this kind are hot.
One must also remember that many of the hot things are coarse-particled, and many of the cold things fine-particled, and on these principles pronounce with security about the power of drugs.
For instance, it suffices to say that vinegar is fine-particled, and cooling and drying, leaving aside the more physical reasonings about it.
For from knowing these things one will know how one ought to mix it with the other drugs.

beads.greek: Ταῦτα μὲν οὖν μέμφομαι τοῖς ἀδολεσχήσασιν περὶ τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ μακρὰ, καὶ τούτων ἔτι μᾶλλον ὀλίγου δεῖν ἅπασι τοῖς ἰατροῖς, ὅτι μὴ διεστήσαντο κατὰ τὸ μᾶλλόν τε καὶ ἧττον ἁπάντων τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων ἤρκεσεν αὐτοῖς ταυτὶ μὲν, εἰ τύχοι, θερμαίνειν φάναι, ταυτὶ δὲ ψύχειν, καὶ ταυτὶ μὲν ξηραίνειν, ταυτὶ δὲ ὑγραίνειν, οὐ γὰρ τοῦτο χρήσι μον ἁπλῶς οὑτωσὶ γνωσθὲν, [429] ἀλλὰ μέχρι πόσου μὲν ψύλλιον ψύχει, μέχρι πόσου καὶ στρύχνος ἢ σκάνδυξ ἢ ψιμμύθιον, ἀνδράχνη τε καὶ θριδακίνη, καὶ μέχρι πόσου μὲν κασία θερμαίνει, μέχρι δὲ πόσου κινάμωμον, ἢ ἄμωμον ἢ ἀμάρακον.
beads.english: These things, then, I find fault with in those who have prattled at length about its [sc. vinegar's] power, and still more than in these, in almost all the physicians: that they did not distinguish all the simple drugs according to the more and the less, but it sufficed them to say that these, as it may be, heat and those cool, and these dry and those moisten. For this, known simply in this way, is not useful, [429] but rather to what degree fleawort cools, and to what degree nightshade or chervil or white lead, and purslane and lettuce; and to what degree cassia heats, and to what degree cinnamon, or amomum or marjoram.

beads.greek: οὕτω δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ξηραινόντων τε καὶ ὑγραινόντων ταῖς δυνάμεσι φαρμάκων, οὐ τὸ καθόλου μόνον ἐπίστασθαι χρὴ, ἀλλὰ τί μὲν πρῶτον ἀποκεχώρηκεν τοῦ συμμέτρου τε καὶ μέσου τῶν ἐναντίων ταῖς δυνάμεσιν, τί δ’ ἐφεξῆς ἐκείνῳ, καὶ τρίτην δὴ καὶ τετάρτην καὶ πέμπτην, εἰ δυνατὸν, ἀπόστασιν οὕτω διαστείλασθαι, σαφέσιν ὅροις ὁρισάμενον.
beads.english: So too with drugs that dry and moisten in their powers, one must know not only the general fact, but which has first departed from what is well-proportioned and intermediate between the contraries in their powers, and which comes next after that one; and thus to distinguish also a third and a fourth and a fifth remove, if possible, defining them by clear boundaries.

beads.greek: ἐν γὰρ τῇ τοιαύτῃ τῶν δυνάμεων ἐπιγνώσει τό τε τοῖς ἁπλοῖς αὐτοῖς χρῆσθαι τεχνικῶς καὶ τὸ συνθεῖναι δύνασθαι κατὰ μέθοδον ἡμῖν ὑπάρξει, καὶ πρὸς τούτοις καὶ αὐτοῖς ἤδη συγκειμένοις ὀρθῶς χρήσασθαι.
beads.english: For in such a recognition of the powers lies our ability both to use the simples themselves according to art and to be able to compound them methodically, and in addition to this also to use them correctly once they have been compounded.

For in such a recognition of the powers lies our ability both to use the simples themselves according to art and to be able to compound them methodically, and in addition to this also to use them correctly once they have been compounded.

beads.greek: ἔστι μὲν οὖν χαλεπώτατον τοῦτο καὶ πολλῆς ἀκριβείας τε καὶ τριβῆς δεόμενον, ἄρχεσθαι μὲν γὰρ ἀπὸ τῆς πείρας ἐν ἅπασι τοῖς τοιούτοις ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστιν, ὥσπερ ἤδη εἴρηται, ἀσφαλῶς δὲ συλλογίσασθαι φυλαττόμενον [430] ἐμπλέκειν ἑαυτὸν ἀπόροις ζητήμασιν.
beads.english: This, then, is a most difficult matter, and one requiring much precision and practice. For in all such matters it is necessary to begin from experience, as has already been said, and to reason securely, taking care not to [430] entangle oneself in insoluble questions.

beads.greek: ᾧ καὶ θαυμάσειεν ἄν τις τῶν τὰ τοιαῦτα ζητησάντων, ὁρῶν περιπίπτοντας αὐτοὺς ἑαυτῶν χερσὶν ἐν τοῖς πλείστοις οἷς ζητοῦσί τε καὶ γράφουσιν, ὥσπερ Ἡρόδοτον.
beads.english: For which reason one might well be astonished at those who have investigated such things, seeing them come to grief at their own hands in most of what they investigate and write, as Herodotus does.

beads.greek: Ἐξ ἁπάσης γὰρ τῆς παλαιοτάτης ἱστορίας ἀρχόμενοι τῶν συνθέτων φαρμάκων, ἐπὶ τὴν ἐξέτασιν ἔρχονται τῶν ἐν αὐτοῖς ἁπλῶν.
beads.english: For, beginning from the whole of the most ancient record of compound drugs, they proceed to the examination of the simples contained in them.

beads.greek: ἐπειδὴ τοῖσδέ τισι τῶν φαρμάκων θερμαίνουσιν, εἰ τύχοι, μέμικται τὸ ὄξος, οὕτως ἤδη καὶ αὐτὸ θερμὸν ἀποφαίνοντες.
beads.english: Since, say, vinegar has been mixed into these or those warming drugs, they thereupon declare it too to be hot.

beads.greek: οὔτε γὰρ εἰ καλῶς μέμικται δῆλον τῷ πρὶν ἐξευρεῖν αὐτοῦ μόνον τὴν δύναμιν, οὔτ’ εἰ καὶ συγχωρηθείη, γινώσκομεν ἤδη τὴν μέθοδον τῆς συνθέσεως τῶν φαρμάκων, ᾗ κρίνοντες ἐξευρήσομεν ᾧτινι μέμικται λόγῳ θερμαίνουσιν πολλοῖς φαρμάκοις ἓν ἐμψῦχον, ἢ δή διαψύχουσιν θερμαῖνον.
beads.english: But it is not clear whether it has been rightly mixed in, before one has discovered its power on its own. Nor, even if this were granted, do we yet know the method of the composition of drugs, by whose judgement we shall discover for what reason a single cooling drug has been mixed with many warming drugs, or indeed a warming one with chilling drugs.

english_sentences: This, then, is a most difficult matter, and one requiring much precision and practice.
For in all such matters it is necessary to begin from experience, as has already been said, and to reason securely, taking care not to [430] entangle oneself in insoluble questions.
For which reason one might well be astonished at those who have investigated such things, seeing them come to grief at their own hands in most of what they investigate and write, as Herodotus does.
For, beginning from the whole of the most ancient record of compound drugs, they proceed to the examination of the simples contained in them.
Since, say, vinegar has been mixed into these or those warming drugs, they thereupon declare it too to be hot.
But it is not clear whether it has been rightly mixed in, before one has discovered its power on its own.

Nor, even if this were granted, do we yet know the method of the composition of drugs, by whose judgement we shall discover for what reason a single cooling drug has been mixed with many warming drugs, or indeed a warming one with chilling drugs.

beads.greek: ὅτε δὲ καὶ διαθέσεων ἀδήλων μνημονεύωσιν πρὸς ἃς ἁρμόττειν δοκεῖ, κᾄπειτα δογματικαῖς ὑπολήψεσιν συνάπτωσιν παραλογισμοὺς ἑτέρους, ἐκ ζητουμένων ζητούμενα καὶ ἐξ ἀδήλων ἄδηλα [431] δι’ ἀλλήλων συλλογιζόμενοι, τότε δὴ καὶ μάλιστα καταμαθεῖν ἐστιν αὐτῶν τὴν ἀδολεσχίαν.
beads.english: And when they also mention non-evident conditions for which [the drug] seems to be suitable, and then attach further paralogisms to dogmatic assumptions, deducing things under inquiry from things under inquiry and non-evident things from non-evident [431] things by means of one another, then indeed one can most of all recognise their idle chatter.

beads.greek: Τῷ γὰρ λέγειν ὅτι καὶ τοῖς ἐμπειρικοῖς ἀφορμὴν ἀντιλογίας πα ρασκευάζουσιν, ἐξ ὧν ἑτοίμως πιστεύουσιν ἁπάσαις ταῖς συνθέτοις δυνάμεσιν, ὥσπερ οὐκ ἐγχωρεῖν ἡμαρτῆσθαί γε πολλὰς αὐτῶν καὶ μοχθηρῶς συγκεῖσθαι.
beads.english: For in speaking thus they also furnish the Empiricists with an occasion for counter-argument, since they readily trust all compound remedies, as though it were not possible that many of them have been made in error and badly compounded.

beads.greek: φήσουσι γὰρ οἶμαι καθάπερ καὶ λέγουσι, μάτην ἡμῖν ζητεῖσθαι τὰς πρώτας τε καὶ δραστικὰς δυνάμεις ἑκάστου τῶν φαρμάκων, φθανούσης τῆς ἐμπειρίας ἀναρίθμητόν τι ἔχειν φαρμάκων ἁπλῶν καὶ συνθέτων πλῆθος, ἃ καὶ παρ’ αὐτοῖς πεπίστευται τοῖς μάτην ζητοῦσι τὰς πρώτας δυνάμεις.
beads.english: For the Empiricists will say, I think, just as they in fact do say, that we inquire in vain into the primary and active powers of each of the drugs, since experience already possesses a countless multitude of simple and compound drugs, which are trusted even by those very people who inquire in vain into the primary powers.

beads.greek: εἰ γὰρ ἅπασαι μὲν αἱ κατὰ μέρος χρήσεις αὐτῶν γινώσκονταί τε καὶ συμφωνοῦνται πᾶσιν, αἱ δ’ αἰτίαι καθ’ ἃς ἐνεργεῖ μήπω συμπεφώνηνται, δῆλον ὡς οὐκ ἐκ τῆς τῶν πρώτων δυνάμεων γνώσεως οὔθ’ ἡ σύνθεσις οὔθ’ ἡ χρῆσις εὕρηται τῶν φαρμάκων, ἀλλ’ ἡ μὲν ἐμπειρία ταῦτα συνέθηκεν, ὁ λόγος δ’ ἄχρι τοῦ πιθανοῦ προέρχεται μόνον.
beads.english: For if all their particular uses are known and agreed upon by everyone, while the causes by which [each] acts have not yet been agreed upon, it is plain that neither the compounding nor the use of drugs has been discovered from knowledge of the primary powers; rather, experience put these together, and reason advances only as far as the plausible.

greek_sentences: ὅτε δὲ καὶ διαθέσεων ἀδήλων μνημονεύωσιν πρὸς ἃς ἁρμόττειν δοκεῖ, κᾄπειτα δογματικαῖς ὑπολήψεσιν συνάπτωσιν παραλογισμοὺς ἑτέρους, ἐκ ζητουμένων ζητούμενα καὶ ἐξ ἀδήλων ἄδηλα [431] δι’ ἀλλήλων συλλογιζόμενοι, τότε δὴ καὶ μάλιστα καταμαθεῖν ἐστιν αὐτῶν τὴν ἀδολεσχίαν.

Τῷ γὰρ λέγειν ὅτι καὶ τοῖς ἐμπειρικοῖς ἀφορμὴν ἀντιλογίας πα ρασκευάζουσιν, ἐξ ὧν ἑτοίμως πιστεύουσιν ἁπάσαις ταῖς συνθέτοις δυνάμεσιν, ὥσπερ οὐκ ἐγχωρεῖν ἡμαρτῆσθαί γε πολλὰς αὐτῶν καὶ μοχθηρῶς συγκεῖσθαι.

φήσουσι γὰρ οἶμαι καθάπερ καὶ λέγουσι, μάτην ἡμῖν ζητεῖσθαι τὰς πρώτας τε καὶ δραστικὰς δυνάμεις ἑκάστου τῶν φαρμάκων, φθανούσης τῆς ἐμπειρίας ἀναρίθμητόν τι ἔχειν φαρμάκων ἁπλῶν καὶ συνθέτων πλῆθος, ἃ καὶ παρ’ αὐτοῖς πεπίστευται τοῖς μάτην ζητοῦσι τὰς πρώτας δυνάμεις.

εἰ γὰρ ἅπασαι μὲν αἱ κατὰ μέρος χρήσεις αὐτῶν γινώσκονταί τε καὶ συμφωνοῦνται πᾶσιν, αἱ δ’ αἰτίαι καθ’ ἃς ἐνεργεῖ μήπω συμπεφώνηνται, δῆλον ὡς οὐκ ἐκ τῆς τῶν πρώτων δυνάμεων γνώσεως οὔθ’ ἡ σύνθεσις οὔθ’ ἡ χρῆσις εὕρηται τῶν φαρμάκων, ἀλλ’ ἡ μὲν ἐμπειρία ταῦτα συνέθηκεν, ὁ λόγος δ’ ἄχρι τοῦ πιθανοῦ προέρχεται μόνον.
english_sentences: And when they also mention non-evident conditions for which [the drug] seems to be suitable, and then attach further paralogisms to dogmatic assumptions, deducing things under inquiry from things under inquiry and non-evident things from non-evident [431] things by means of one another, then indeed one can most of all recognise their idle chatter.

For in speaking thus they also furnish the Empiricists with an occasion for counter-argument, since they readily trust all compound remedies, as though it were not possible that many of them have been made in error and badly compounded.

For the Empiricists will say, I think, just as they in fact do say, that we inquire in vain into the primary and active powers of each of the drugs, since experience already possesses a countless multitude of simple and compound drugs, which are trusted even by those very people who inquire in vain into the primary powers.

For if all their particular uses are known and agreed upon by everyone, while the causes by which [each] acts have not yet been agreed upon, it is plain that neither the compounding nor the use of drugs has been discovered from knowledge of the primary powers; rather, experience put these together, and reason advances only as far as the plausible.

beads.greek: ταῦτα μὲν οὖν καὶ τοιαῦθ’ ἕτερα πολλὰ καλῶς δόξουσι [432] λέγειν οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐμπειρίας ἰατροὶ πρὸς τοὺς ἅπασι τοῖς ὁπωσοῦν γεγραμμένοις φαρμάκοις πιστεύοντας, αἰτίας τε πιθανὰς ἐφαρμόττειν ταῖς ἐπαγγελίαις αὐτῶν προαιρουμένους.
beads.english: These things, then, and many other things of the kind, the physicians who proceed from experience will seem [432] to say rightly against those who trust all the drugs written down in any way whatsoever, and who choose to fit plausible causes to the claims made for them.

greek_sentences: ταῦτα μὲν οὖν καὶ τοιαῦθ’ ἕτερα πολλὰ καλῶς δόξουσι [432] λέγειν οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐμπειρίας ἰατροὶ πρὸς τοὺς ἅπασι τοῖς ὁπωσοῦν γεγραμμένοις φαρμάκοις πιστεύοντας, αἰτίας τε πιθανὰς ἐφαρμόττειν ταῖς ἐπαγγελίαις αὐτῶν προαιρουμένους.
english_sentences: These things, then, and many other things of the kind, the physicians who proceed from experience will seem [432] to say rightly against those who trust all the drugs written down in any way whatsoever, and who choose to fit plausible causes to the claims made for them.

beads.greek: ἐγὼ δὲ πρὸς τούτοις ἔτι κᾀκεῖνο εἴποιμ’ ἄν, ὡς Ἡρόδοτος μὲν ἁπάσας τὰς ἄλλας αἱρέσεις μοχθηρὰς ὑπολαμβάνων, πλὴν τῆς πνευματικῆς, Μητρόδωρος δὲ πλὴν τῆς Ἀσκληπιάδου, καὶ Ζήνων πλὴν τῆς Ἡροφίλου, καὶ Ἑρμογένης πλὴν τῆς Ἐρασιστράτου, καὶ ἄλλος τις ἄλλος ἁπάσας πλὴν τῆς ἑαυτοῦ, περὶ τῶν συνθέτων φαρμάκων μόνων ἀβασανίστως πιστεύουσιν ἅπασι τοῖς συγγράμμασιν, εἴθ’ ὁμοδόξων εἴτε καὶ τῶν ἐπιτυχόντων εἴη, καὶ πολλάκις γε αἰτίας ἀποδιδόναι πειρῶνται πιθανὰς κάκιστα συγκειμένων φαρμάκων· καὶ τὸ τούτου θαυμασιώτερον, ὅτι μηδεμίαν ἔχοντες ὧν ἐπαινοῦσι πεῖραν, ἀλλ’ ἑτέροις πεπιστευσκότες, ὥσπερ τις ἔναγχος ἐπαίνους μὲν διῄει πολλοὺς καὶ μεγάλους φαρμάκου ποδαγρικοῦ, μεταξὺ δ’ αὐτοῦ λέγοντος ἐπιστάντος τινὸς ποδαγρικοῦ μετρίως οὕτως ἔχοντος ὡς βαδίζειν δύνασθαι, καὶ ἡμῶν κελευσάντων ἐπ’ ἐκείνου πρώτου [433] πεῖραν αὐτοῦ παρασχεῖν, ὁ μὲν ἐπέθηκε τῷ ποδὶ τὸ φάρμακον, ὁ δ’ ἄνθρωπος ἄγρυπνός τε τῆς νυκτὸς ὅλης ἐγένετο καὶ κατὰ τὴν ὑστεραίαν οὐ μόνον οὐ βαδίζειν ὡς πρόσθεν, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ φέρεσθαι δυνατὸς ἦν.
beads.english: But I for my part would add to these this further point: that Herodotus, who holds all the other sects to be bad except the Pneumatic, and Metrodorus all except that of Asclepiades, and Zeno all except that of Herophilus, and Hermogenes all except that of Erasistratus, and each of the others all except his own, these men, in the matter of compound drugs alone, believe without scrutiny all the writings, whether of those who share their doctrine or of anyone who happens along, and often they even try to supply plausible causes for very badly composed drugs. And what is more remarkable than this: that, having no experience of the things they praise, but having trusted others...

beads.greek: οὕτως ἀβασανίστως τε καὶ προπετῶς οἱ μὲν ἑτέροις πιστεύουσιν, οἱ δ’ ἑκόντες ἄλλους ἐξαπατῶσιν.
beads.english: Thus someone recently was going through many great praises of a drug for gout. While he was still speaking, a certain gouty man came up, affected only moderately, so that he was able to walk, and we bade him make trial of it first on that man [433].

beads.greek: εἰ δὲ καὶ πᾶσαι καλῶς εἶχον αἱ συνθέσεις τῶν φαρμάκων ὧν μνημονεύουσιν, ἀλλὰ τήν γε χρεῖαν τῆς θεωρίας αὐτῶν ἀνατρέπουσιν ἐξ ὧν πράττουσιν.
beads.english: He applied the drug to the foot, and the man was sleepless the whole night, and on the following day he was able not only not to walk as before, but not even to be carried. So without scrutiny and so rashly do some trust others, while others deliberately deceive others.

beads.greek: φασὶ γὰρ ἕνεκα τῆς τῶν συνθέτων φαρμάκων κατασκευῆς τε καὶ χρήσεως ἐπισκέπτεσθαι τῶν ἁπλῶν τὰς δυνάμεις, καὶ τούτων μάρτυρας ἐπικαλοῦνται σχεδὸν ἅπαντας τοὺς παλαιοὺς, Ἐρασίστρατον, Ἡρόφιλον, Φιλότιμον, Διοκλέα, Πραξαγόραν καὶ αὐτὸν Ἱπποκράτην.
beads.english: But even if all the compositions of the drugs that they record were sound, they nevertheless overturn, by what they do, the usefulness of the theoretical study of them. For they say that it is for the sake of the preparation and use of compound drugs that they investigate the powers of the simples, and as witnesses to this they call upon nearly all the ancients: Erasistratus, Herophilus, Philotimus, Diocles, Praxagoras, and Hippocrates himself.

beads.greek: παραγενόμενοι δ’ ἐπὶ τὴν ἐξέτασιν αὐτῶν, ὡς γινώσκουσιν ἡμῖν ἤδη τὰς συνθέτους δυνάμεις ἁπάσας, οὕτω διαλέγονται.
beads.english: But when they come to the examination of them, they argue as though we already knew all the compound powers.

παραγενόμενοι δ’ ἐπὶ τὴν ἐξέτασιν αὐτῶν, ὡς γινώσκουσιν ἡμῖν ἤδη τὰς συνθέτους δυνάμεις ἁπάσας, οὕτω διαλέγονται.
english_sentences: But I for my part would add to these this further point: that Herodotus, who holds all the other sects to be bad except the Pneumatic, and Metrodorus all except that of Asclepiades, and Zeno all except that of Herophilus, and Hermogenes all except that of Erasistratus, and each of the others all except his own, these men, in the matter of compound drugs alone, believe without scrutiny all the writings, whether of those who share their doctrine or of anyone who happens along, and often they even try to supply plausible causes for very badly composed drugs.
And what is more remarkable than this: that, having no experience of the things they praise, but having trusted others...
Thus someone recently was going through many great praises of a drug for gout.
While he was still speaking, a certain gouty man came up, affected only moderately, so that he was able to walk, and we bade him make trial of it first on that man [433].
He applied the drug to the foot, and the man was sleepless the whole night, and on the following day he was able not only not to walk as before, but not even to be carried.
So without scrutiny and so rashly do some trust others, while others deliberately deceive others.
But even if all the compositions of the drugs that they record were sound, they nevertheless overturn, by what they do, the usefulness of the theoretical study of them.

For they say that it is for the sake of the preparation and use of compound drugs that they investigate the powers of the simples, and as witnesses to this they call upon nearly all the ancients: Erasistratus, Herophilus, Philotimus, Diocles, Praxagoras, and Hippocrates himself.
But when they come to the examination of them, they argue as though we already knew all the compound powers.

beads.greek: καὶ πῶς οὐ μάτην ζητεῖτε τὰς τῶν ἁπλῶν, εἴποι τὶς οἶμαι πρὸς [434] αὐτοὺς, εἰ τὰς τῶν συνθέτων ἤδη γινώσκετε;
beads.english: "And how are you not seeking in vain the [powers] of the simples," someone might say, I think, to [434] them, "if you already know those of the compound drugs?

beads.greek: εἰ γὰρ ὧν ἕνεκα τὴν ζήτησιν τῶν ἁπλῶν ἐνεστήσασθε, ταύτας ἤδη γινώσκετε, περιττὸν τὸ ζητεῖν ἐκείνας. εἰ καὶ τοῦτό τις αὐτοῖς συγχωρήσειεν, ἀλλὰ τό γε καὶ πρόσθεν ἤδη λελεγμένον οὐκ οἶδ’ ὅπως ἀνάσχοιτ’ ἄν τις, ὅταν ἐναντία τοῖς ἐναργῶς φαινομένοις, ἐκ λόγων μακρῶν ἐπιχειρῶσι κατασκευάζειν.
beads.english: For if you already know those for the sake of which you undertook the inquiry into the simples, it is superfluous to seek the former." Even if someone were to concede this point to them, yet as for what has already been said before, I do not know how anyone could tolerate it, when they attempt to establish, out of long arguments, things contrary to what is evidently apparent.

beads.greek: Ἤδη γάρ τινος εἰς τοσοῦτον ἐμπληξίας ἥκοντος ἐπειράθην, ὡς καταφρονεῖν ἀξιοῦντος τῶν αἰσθήσεων.
beads.english: For I have already had experience of someone who had come to such a pitch of senselessness that he thought fit to despise the senses.

beads.greek: ὃν εὐθὺς μὲν ἤρετό τις, εἰ τὸ λευκὸν αὐτῷ πέπερι δοκοίη θερμὸν ὑπάρχειν.
beads.english: Someone straightaway asked him whether white pepper seemed to him to be hot.

beads.greek: ὁ δ, ὡς τὸ εἰκὸς, ὡμολόγησεν, εἶτ’ αὖθις ἐρωτηθεὶς ὁπόθεν γινώσκεις τοῦτο; καὶ τοιοῦτον φαίνεσθαι φήσας, εἰκότως ὑπὸ τῶν παρόντων κατεγελάσθη μὴ συνιεὶς ὅπερ ἐφθέγγετο.
beads.english: He, as was to be expected, agreed; then, being asked in turn, "Whence do you know this?", and saying that it appears such, he was deservedly laughed at by those present, not understanding what he was uttering.

beads.greek: τοῦτο γὰρ αὐτὸ τὸ φαίνεσθαι πιστὴν αὐτῷ τὴν αἴσθησιν ἀπέφαινεν, ἧς ὀλίγον ἔμπροσθεν ὡς ἀπίστου κατεγίνωσκεν.
beads.english: For this very 'appearing' declared sensation trustworthy for him, which a little before he had condemned as untrustworthy.

beads.greek: ἐπεὶ πόθεν, ὦ πρὸς θεῶν, ὅτι θερμόν ἐστι τὸ πῦρ ἴσμεν, ἐκ τίνος συλλογισμοῦ μαθόντες;
beads.english: For whence, by the gods, do we know that fire is hot, having learned it from what syllogism?

greek_sentences: καὶ πῶς οὐ μάτην ζητεῖτε τὰς τῶν ἁπλῶν, εἴποι τὶς οἶμαι πρὸς [434] αὐτοὺς, εἰ τὰς τῶν συνθέτων ἤδη γινώσκετε;
εἰ γὰρ ὧν ἕνεκα τὴν ζήτησιν τῶν ἁπλῶν ἐνεστήσασθε, ταύτας ἤδη γινώσκετε, περιττὸν τὸ ζητεῖν ἐκείνας.

Ἤδη γάρ τινος εἰς τοσοῦτον ἐμπληξίας ἥκοντος ἐπειράθην, ὡς καταφρονεῖν ἀξιοῦντος τῶν αἰσθήσεων.
ὃν εὐθὺς μὲν ἤρετό τις, εἰ τὸ λευκὸν αὐτῷ πέπερι δοκοίη θερμὸν ὑπάρχειν.
ὁ δ, ὡς τὸ εἰκὸς, ὡμολόγησεν, εἶτ’ αὖθις ἐρωτηθεὶς ὁπόθεν γινώσκεις τοῦτο;
καὶ τοιοῦτον φαίνεσθαι φήσας, εἰκότως ὑπὸ τῶν παρόντων κατεγελάσθη μὴ συνιεὶς ὅπερ ἐφθέγγετο.

ἐπεὶ πόθεν, ὦ πρὸς θεῶν, ὅτι θερμόν ἐστι τὸ πῦρ ἴσμεν, ἐκ τίνος συλλογισμοῦ μαθόντες;
english_sentences: "And how are you not seeking in vain the [powers] of the simples," someone might say, I think, to [434] them, "if you already know those of the compound drugs?

For if you already know those for the sake of which you undertook the inquiry into the simples, it is superfluous to seek the former." Even if someone were to concede this point to them, yet as for what has already been said before, I do not know how anyone could tolerate it, when they attempt to establish, out of long arguments, things contrary to what is evidently apparent.
For I have already had experience of someone who had come to such a pitch of senselessness that he thought fit to despise the senses.
Someone straightaway asked him whether white pepper seemed to him to be hot.

He, as was to be expected, agreed; then, being asked in turn, "Whence do you know this?", and saying that it appears such, he was deservedly laughed at by those present, not understanding what he was uttering.
For this very 'appearing' declared sensation trustworthy for him, which a little before he had condemned as untrustworthy.
For whence, by the gods, do we know that fire is hot, having learned it from what syllogism?

beads.greek: [435] ἢ διὰ ποίας ἀποδείξεως πιστωσάμενοι;
beads.english: [435] Or by what kind of demonstration did we confirm it?

beads.greek: πόθεν δ’ ὅτι ψυχρὸς ὁ κρύσταλλος ἄλλοθεν ἢ ἐκ τῆς αἰσθήσεως ἐμάθομεν;
beads.english: And from what source other than sensation did we learn that ice is cold?

beads.greek: εἶτά τις ταύτην ἐάσας ἀναπίμπλησι τὰ βιβλία προβλημάτων φυσικῶν, ἢ οὐκ ἐξ ἐκείνων ἐστὶ καὶ τὸ διὰ τίνα αἰτίαν ἀναζυμοῖ τὴν γῆν τὸ ὄξος;
beads.english: Then someone, having set this aside, fills his books with problems of natural philosophy. Or is not this, too, one of them: for what cause vinegar makes the earth ferment?

beads.greek: ἔνεστι γὰρ, οἶμαι, λέγειν ἡμῖν ὡς ἀγνοοῦμεν, ὥσπερ καὶ ἄλλα πολλὰ τῶν τοιούτων προβλημάτων.
beads.english: For it is open to us, I think, to say that we do not know, as with many other problems of this kind.

beads.greek: ἢν δέ τις ἐκ προχείρου λαμβάνῃ, διότι θερμὸν ἢ διότι ψυχρὸν, ἑκάτερα γὰρ λέγουσιν, εἰς ἀμφισβητουμένους καὶ εἰς ἀσαφεῖς ἑαυτὸν ἐμβάλλει λόγους.
beads.english: But if someone readily assumes that it is because it is hot, or because it is cold (for they say both), he throws himself into disputed and obscure arguments. For my part, I would be content if I could discover with precision even the things lying next to what appears through the senses, defining and distinguishing among them what is so in itself from what is so by accident.

beads.greek: Ἐγὼ δὲ ἀγαπήσαιμ’ ἂν, εἰ καὶ τὰ παρακείμενα τοῖς διὰ τῶν αἰσθήσεων φαινομένοις ἐξευρεῖν ἀκριβῶς δυναίμην, ἀφορίζων ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ διακρίνων τὸ καθ’ ἑαυτὸ τοῦ κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς, οἷον αὐτίκα θέρους ὥρᾳ πιόντες ὀξύκρατον ἔνιοι, σαφῶς ἐμψύχονταί τε καὶ ἄδιψοι διατελοῦσιν, ἀλλ’ οὔπω δῆλον εἰ διὰ τὸ ὄξος, ὀλίγον γὰρ πολλῷ τῷ ὕδατι κεραννύντες αὐτὸ καὶ οὐδὲ θερμὸν, ἀλλὰ ψυχρὸν ὡς ἔνι μάλιστα προσφέρονται.
beads.english: For example, some people who drink oxycrate in the summer season are clearly cooled and remain free from thirst. But it is not yet clear whether this is because of the vinegar, for they mix a little of it with a great deal of water, and they take it not hot but as cold as possible.

greek_sentences: [435] ἢ διὰ ποίας ἀποδείξεως πιστωσάμενοι;
πόθεν δ’ ὅτι ψυχρὸς ὁ κρύσταλλος ἄλλοθεν ἢ ἐκ τῆς αἰσθήσεως ἐμάθομεν;
εἶτά τις ταύτην ἐάσας ἀναπίμπλησι τὰ βιβλία προβλημάτων φυσικῶν, ἢ οὐκ ἐξ ἐκείνων ἐστὶ καὶ τὸ διὰ τίνα αἰτίαν ἀναζυμοῖ τὴν γῆν τὸ ὄξος;
ἔνεστι γὰρ, οἶμαι, λέγειν ἡμῖν ὡς ἀγνοοῦμεν, ὥσπερ καὶ ἄλλα πολλὰ τῶν τοιούτων προβλημάτων.
ἢν δέ τις ἐκ προχείρου λαμβάνῃ, διότι θερμὸν ἢ διότι ψυχρὸν, ἑκάτερα γὰρ λέγουσιν, εἰς ἀμφισβητουμένους καὶ εἰς ἀσαφεῖς ἑαυτὸν ἐμβάλλει λόγους.

Ἐγὼ δὲ ἀγαπήσαιμ’ ἂν, εἰ καὶ τὰ παρακείμενα τοῖς διὰ τῶν αἰσθήσεων φαινομένοις ἐξευρεῖν ἀκριβῶς δυναίμην, ἀφορίζων ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ διακρίνων τὸ καθ’ ἑαυτὸ τοῦ κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς, οἷον αὐτίκα θέρους ὥρᾳ πιόντες ὀξύκρατον ἔνιοι, σαφῶς ἐμψύχονταί τε καὶ ἄδιψοι διατελοῦσιν, ἀλλ’ οὔπω δῆλον εἰ διὰ τὸ ὄξος, ὀλίγον γὰρ πολλῷ τῷ ὕδατι κεραννύντες αὐτὸ καὶ οὐδὲ θερμὸν, ἀλλὰ ψυχρὸν ὡς ἔνι μάλιστα προσφέρονται.
english_sentences: [435] Or by what kind of demonstration did we confirm it?
And from what source other than sensation did we learn that ice is cold?
Then someone, having set this aside, fills his books with problems of natural philosophy.
Or is not this, too, one of them: for what cause vinegar makes the earth ferment?
For it is open to us, I think, to say that we do not know, as with many other problems of this kind.
But if someone readily assumes that it is because it is hot, or because it is cold (for they say both), he throws himself into disputed and obscure arguments.

For my part, I would be content if I could discover with precision even the things lying next to what appears through the senses, defining and distinguishing among them what is so in itself from what is so by accident.
For example, some people who drink oxycrate in the summer season are clearly cooled and remain free from thirst.
But it is not yet clear whether this is because of the vinegar, for they mix a little of it with a great deal of water, and they take it not hot but as cold as possible.

beads.greek: τάχα οὖν τις φαίη, διότι βραδύτερόν ἐστι τὸ ὕδωρ καὶ πλεῖστον χρόνον ἐν τοῖς ὑποχονδρίοις διαμένει, [436] μήθ’ ὑποβιβαζόμενον μήτ’ ἀναδιδόμενον, διὰ τοῦτο αὐτῷ μίγνυσθαι τὸ ὄξος, οἷον ὄχημά τι τῆς πάντη φορᾶς γενησόμενον.
beads.english: Perhaps, then, someone might say that, because water is slower and remains for a very long time in the hypochondria, [436] being neither passed downward nor distributed, the vinegar is mixed with it for this reason, to become as it were a vehicle for its conveyance in every direction.

beads.greek: οὕτω δὲ κᾂν μετ’ οἴνου ποθῇ τὸ ὕδωρ, ἀδιψότερον ὑπάρχειν ἤπερ καθ’ αὑτὸ, ποδηγοῦντος αὐτὸ πρὸς τὴν ἀνάδοσιν τοῦ οἴνου.
beads.english: In the same way, if water is drunk with wine, it leaves one less thirsty than water by itself, since the wine guides it toward distribution.

beads.greek: τὴν μὲν οὖν ἔμψυξίν τε καὶ τὴν τοῦ δίψους ἴασιν ἐπὶ τῷ ὕδατι γίγνεσθαι, ψυχρῷ καὶ ὑγρῷ τὴν φύσιν ὑπάρχοντι.
beads.english: Thus the cooling and the cure of thirst come about from the water, which is cold and moist in its nature.

beads.greek: βοήθημα δ’ αὐτὸ καὶ οἷον πτέρωμα τῆς εἰς πάντα τὰ μόρια τοῦ ζώου φορᾶς, τὸν οἶνόν τε γίγνεσθαι καὶ ὄξος, οὐκ αὐτὰ ψύχοντά τε καὶ ὑγραίνοντα.
beads.english: The wine and the vinegar, on the other hand, become an aid to it and, as it were, wings for its conveyance into all the parts of the animal, without themselves cooling and moistening.

beads.greek: μόνα γὰρ ἂν οὕτω γε δίδοσθαι μᾶλλον ἢ μετὰ ὕδατος, ὅτι ῥᾳδίως ὑπὸ λεπτότητος ἀναδίδοται καὶ ἀποχωρεῖ τῶν ὑποχονδρίων.
beads.english: For otherwise they would be given alone rather than with water, since by their thinness they are readily distributed and pass away from the hypochondria.

beads.greek: ἐπεὶ δὲ ἅπαξ εἰς τοῦτον ἀφικόμεθα τὸν λόγον, οὐ χεῖρον ἀκριβῶς ἅπαντα διελθεῖν αὐτόν.
beads.english: But since we have once arrived at this argument, it is not amiss to go through the whole of it precisely.

beads.greek: ὅτι μὲν γὰρ ἐγχωρεῖ καὶ ποδηγεῖν τῷ ὕδατι τὸ ὄξος, οὐκ ἐμψύχειν αὐτὸ καὶ μὴ ποδηγεῖν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ψύχειν, ἄντικρυς δῆλον.
beads.english: That it is possible both for the vinegar to guide the water without itself cooling, and for it not merely to guide but also to cool, is plainly evident.

beads.greek: ὁπότερον δ’ ἀληθές ἐστιν ἐπισκέψεως δεῖται.
beads.english: But which of the two is true requires investigation.

greek_sentences: τάχα οὖν τις φαίη, διότι βραδύτερόν ἐστι τὸ ὕδωρ καὶ πλεῖστον χρόνον ἐν τοῖς ὑποχονδρίοις διαμένει, [436] μήθ’ ὑποβιβαζόμενον μήτ’ ἀναδιδόμενον, διὰ τοῦτο αὐτῷ μίγνυσθαι τὸ ὄξος, οἷον ὄχημά τι τῆς πάντη φορᾶς γενησόμενον.

english_sentences: Perhaps, then, someone might say that, because water is slower and remains for a very long time in the hypochondria, [436] being neither passed downward nor distributed, the vinegar is mixed with it for this reason, to become as it were a vehicle for its conveyance in every direction.
In the same way, if water is drunk with wine, it leaves one less thirsty than water by itself, since the wine guides it toward distribution.
Thus the cooling and the cure of thirst come about from the water, which is cold and moist in its nature.
The wine and the vinegar, on the other hand, become an aid to it and, as it were, wings for its conveyance into all the parts of the animal, without themselves cooling and moistening.
For otherwise they would be given alone rather than with water, since by their thinness they are readily distributed and pass away from the hypochondria.
But since we have once arrived at this argument, it is not amiss to go through the whole of it precisely.
That it is possible both for the vinegar to guide the water without itself cooling, and for it not merely to guide but also to cool, is plainly evident.
But which of the two is true requires investigation.

beads.greek: διορισθείη δ’ αὐτό γε τοιοῦτον, εἰ δοίη μέν [437] τινι καὶ οἶνον καὶ ὄξος, ἑκάτερον ἰδίᾳ καθ’ αὑτό.
beads.english: This very point could be settled in the following way, if one were to give [437] someone both wine and vinegar, each separately by itself.

beads.greek: φαίνεται γὰρ ἐπὶ μὲν τῷ οἴνῳ διψωδέστερος ἀεὶ γιγνόμενος ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ἐπὶ δὲ τῇ τοῦ ὄξους πόσει ποτὲ μὲν διψωδέστερός ἐστιν, ποτὲ δὲ ἀδιψότερος, ὅτι καὶ τὸ δίψος αὐτὸ διττῶς γίνεται, τὸ μὲν ὑγρότητος ἐνδείᾳ, τὸ δὲ πλεονεξίᾳ θερμότητος· ὥστ’ οὐδὲν θαυμαστὸν εἰ τὸ μὲν πρότερον οὐκ ἰᾶται, θάτερον δ’ ἰᾶται.
beads.english: For the person is evidently always made thirstier by wine, whereas after drinking vinegar he is sometimes thirstier and sometimes less thirsty. This is because thirst itself also arises in two ways, the one from a deficiency of moisture, the other from an excess of heat.

beads.greek: ὑγραίνειν μὲν γὰρ οὐ δύναται, ψύχει δὲ οὐκ ἀγεννῶς.
beads.english: So it is no wonder if vinegar does not cure the former but does cure the other, for it cannot moisten, but it cools not ignobly.

beads.greek: οὔκουν οὔτε τὴν ἐπὶ ξηρᾷ διαθέσει δίψαν οὔτε τὴν ἐπὶ θερμῇ καὶ ξηρᾷ δύναιτ’ ἄν ποτε ἰᾶσθαι πινόμενον ὄξος.
beads.english: Therefore vinegar when drunk could never cure either the thirst arising from a dry condition or that arising from a hot and dry one.

beads.greek: εἰ δὲ συνδράμῃ ποτὲ εἰς ταυτὸν ὑγρότης θερμότητι, τῆς τοιαύτης δίψης ἄριστον ἴαμα τὸ ὄξος ἔσται.
beads.english: But if moisture should ever concur with heat in the same body, vinegar will be the best remedy for such thirst.

beads.greek: σπανία δὴ τοιαύτη διάθεσις, ἐν ὑδρωπικαῖς ἐνίοτε παρεγχύσεσιν γι γνομένη, πλήθους ὑγροῦ ἁλμώδους ἠθροισμένου κατὰ τὴν γαστέρα καὶ ὅσοις ἁλμυρὸν φλέγμα κατ’ αὐτὴν ἐμπέπλασται.
beads.english: Such a condition is indeed rare. It occurs sometimes in dropsical effusions, when a quantity of briny fluid has collected in the stomach, and in those in whom salty phlegm has become plastered onto it.

greek_sentences: διορισθείη δ’ αὐτό γε τοιοῦτον, εἰ δοίη μέν [437] τινι καὶ οἶνον καὶ ὄξος, ἑκάτερον ἰδίᾳ καθ’ αὑτό.

φαίνεται γὰρ ἐπὶ μὲν τῷ οἴνῳ διψωδέστερος ἀεὶ γιγνόμενος ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ἐπὶ δὲ τῇ τοῦ ὄξους πόσει ποτὲ μὲν διψωδέστερός ἐστιν, ποτὲ δὲ ἀδιψότερος, ὅτι καὶ τὸ δίψος αὐτὸ διττῶς γίνεται, τὸ μὲν ὑγρότητος ἐνδείᾳ, τὸ δὲ πλεονεξίᾳ θερμότητος· ὥστ’ οὐδὲν θαυμαστὸν εἰ τὸ μὲν πρότερον οὐκ ἰᾶται, θάτερον δ’ ἰᾶται.

οὔκουν οὔτε τὴν ἐπὶ ξηρᾷ διαθέσει δίψαν οὔτε τὴν ἐπὶ θερμῇ καὶ ξηρᾷ δύναιτ’ ἄν ποτε ἰᾶσθαι πινόμενον ὄξος.
εἰ δὲ συνδράμῃ ποτὲ εἰς ταυτὸν ὑγρότης θερμότητι, τῆς τοιαύτης δίψης ἄριστον ἴαμα τὸ ὄξος ἔσται.
σπανία δὴ τοιαύτη διάθεσις, ἐν ὑδρωπικαῖς ἐνίοτε παρεγχύσεσιν γι γνομένη, πλήθους ὑγροῦ ἁλμώδους ἠθροισμένου κατὰ τὴν γαστέρα καὶ ὅσοις ἁλμυρὸν φλέγμα κατ’ αὐτὴν ἐμπέπλασται.
english_sentences: This very point could be settled in the following way, if one were to give [437] someone both wine and vinegar, each separately by itself.
For the person is evidently always made thirstier by wine, whereas after drinking vinegar he is sometimes thirstier and sometimes less thirsty.
This is because thirst itself also arises in two ways, the one from a deficiency of moisture, the other from an excess of heat.
So it is no wonder if vinegar does not cure the former but does cure the other, for it cannot moisten, but it cools not ignobly.
Therefore vinegar when drunk could never cure either the thirst arising from a dry condition or that arising from a hot and dry one.
But if moisture should ever concur with heat in the same body, vinegar will be the best remedy for such thirst.
Such a condition is indeed rare.
It occurs sometimes in dropsical effusions, when a quantity of briny fluid has collected in the stomach, and in those in whom salty phlegm has become plastered onto it.

beads.greek: τοῖς δ’ ἄλλως διψώδεσιν ἔν τε καύσοις πυρετοῖς καὶ τοῖς περικαέσιν ἅπασιν καὶ τοῖς ἐν θέρει καὶ θάλπει σφοδρῷ [438] σύνθετος ἡ διάθεσίς ἐστιν ἐκ θερμότητός τε καὶ ξηρότητος, ὥστ’ εἰκότως αὐτοῖς ἐστι σύνθετον καὶ τὸ ἴαμα, τὸ μὲν ὄξος οὐκ ἀγεννῶς γε ψῦχον καὶ πάντη ῥᾳδίως διϊὸν, τὸ ὕδωρ δὲ πρὸς τῷ ψύχειν ἔτι καὶ ὑγρότατον ἁπάντων ὑπάρχον· οὐδὲν γάρ ἐστιν ὑγρότερον ὕδατος.
beads.english: But for those who are thirsty in the other way, in burning fevers (kausoi), in all the intensely burning [fevers], and in those who are so in summer and in fierce heat, [438] the condition is compound, of heat and dryness, so that for them the remedy too is reasonably compound: vinegar, which cools not feebly and passes easily in every direction, and water, which besides cooling is also the moistest of all things, for nothing is moister than water.

beads.greek: Ὥσπερ οὖν οὐκ ἀσφαλής ἐστιν ὁ πόῤῥω τῆς αἰσθήσεως τοῦ δοκιμαζομένου φαρμάκου συλλογισμὸς, οὕτως οὐδ’ ἡ τοῦ μιχθέντος ἑτέρῳ χρῆσις.
beads.english: Therefore, just as reasoning that is remote from the perception of the drug under test is not secure, so neither is the use of it when it has been mixed with another.

beads.greek: αὐτὸ γὰρ χρὴ καθ’ αὑτὸ μόνον ἐξετάζεσθαι τὸ κρινόμενον ἐπὶ τε τῶν ὑγιαινόντων σωμάτων εὐκράτων τε καὶ δυσκράτων ἐπί τε τῶν νοσούντων.
beads.english: For the thing being judged must be examined by itself alone, both in healthy bodies, well-tempered and ill-tempered alike, and in the sick.

beads.greek: εὐκράτων μὲν οὖν, ὥσπερ καὶ πρόσθεν εἴρηται· δυσκράτων δὲ, ὥσπερ Ἱπποκράτης ἔλεγε, πικροχόλοις μὲν φύσεσιν χρηστότατον ὑπάρχει ὄξος, ἐναντιώτατον δ’ εἶναι μελαγχολικοῖς τὴν κρᾶσιν.
beads.english: In well-tempered bodies, then, as has also been said before; in ill-tempered ones, as Hippocrates said, vinegar is most beneficial to bitter-bilious natures, and is most contrary to those who are melancholic in their mixture.

beads.greek: ἐπὶ δ’ αὖ τῶν νοσούντων, εἰ ἁπλοῦν ἐξ ἁπλῆς ἐξετάζοιτο διαθέσεως.
beads.english: And again, in the sick, if a simple [drug] were examined in a simple condition.

greek_sentences: τοῖς δ’ ἄλλως διψώδεσιν ἔν τε καύσοις πυρετοῖς καὶ τοῖς περικαέσιν ἅπασιν καὶ τοῖς ἐν θέρει καὶ θάλπει σφοδρῷ [438] σύνθετος ἡ διάθεσίς ἐστιν ἐκ θερμότητός τε καὶ ξηρότητος, ὥστ’ εἰκότως αὐτοῖς ἐστι σύνθετον καὶ τὸ ἴαμα, τὸ μὲν ὄξος οὐκ ἀγεννῶς γε ψῦχον καὶ πάντη ῥᾳδίως διϊὸν, τὸ ὕδωρ δὲ πρὸς τῷ ψύχειν ἔτι καὶ ὑγρότατον ἁπάντων ὑπάρχον· οὐδὲν γάρ ἐστιν ὑγρότερον ὕδατος.
Ὥσπερ οὖν οὐκ ἀσφαλής ἐστιν ὁ πόῤῥω τῆς αἰσθήσεως τοῦ δοκιμαζομένου φαρμάκου συλλογισμὸς, οὕτως οὐδ’ ἡ τοῦ μιχθέντος ἑτέρῳ χρῆσις.
αὐτὸ γὰρ χρὴ καθ’ αὑτὸ μόνον ἐξετάζεσθαι τὸ κρινόμενον ἐπὶ τε τῶν ὑγιαινόντων σωμάτων εὐκράτων τε καὶ δυσκράτων ἐπί τε τῶν νοσούντων.
εὐκράτων μὲν οὖν, ὥσπερ καὶ πρόσθεν εἴρηται· δυσκράτων δὲ, ὥσπερ Ἱπποκράτης ἔλεγε, πικροχόλοις μὲν φύσεσιν χρηστότατον ὑπάρχει ὄξος, ἐναντιώτατον δ’ εἶναι μελαγχολικοῖς τὴν κρᾶσιν.
ἐπὶ δ’ αὖ τῶν νοσούντων, εἰ ἁπλοῦν ἐξ ἁπλῆς ἐξετάζοιτο διαθέσεως.
english_sentences: But for those who are thirsty in the other way, in burning fevers (kausoi), in all the intensely burning [fevers], and in those who are so in summer and in fierce heat, [438] the condition is compound, of heat and dryness, so that for them the remedy too is reasonably compound: vinegar, which cools not feebly and passes easily in every direction, and water, which besides cooling is also the moistest of all things, for nothing is moister than water.
Therefore, just as reasoning that is remote from the perception of the drug under test is not secure, so neither is the use of it when it has been mixed with another.
For the thing being judged must be examined by itself alone, both in healthy bodies, well-tempered and ill-tempered alike, and in the sick.

In well-tempered bodies, then, as has also been said before; in ill-tempered ones, as Hippocrates said, vinegar is most beneficial to bitter-bilious natures, and is most contrary to those who are melancholic in their mixture.
And again, in the sick, if a simple [drug] were examined in a simple condition.

beads.greek: εἰ δὲ καὶ μίγνυτό ποτε μετ’ ἄλλου, χρὴ τὸ μιγνύμενον αὐτῷ μέσον εἶναι τὴν κρᾶσιν, ὡς ἐφ’ ὕδατός τε καὶ κηρωτῆς ὁ πρόσθεν [439] λόγος ἀπέδειξεν.
beads.english: But if it should ever be mixed with something else, what is mixed with it must be intermediate in its mixture, as the earlier [439] argument demonstrated in the case of water and cerate.

beads.greek: εὐλόγως γὰρ, οἶμαι, τὸ τῷ μηδετέρῳ τῶν ἄκρων κατὰ τὴν κρᾶσιν, ἀλλ’ ὡς οἷόν τε μέσῳ συμπεπλεγμένον αὐτὸ, τῶν ἀποτελουμένων αἴτιον γίγνεσθαι.
beads.english: For it is reasonable, I think, that what has been combined with something that is neither of the extremes in its mixture, but as far as possible intermediate, should itself become the cause of the effects produced.

beads.greek: τῇ γοῦν ἁπλῇ κηρωτῇ μήτε θερμαινούσῃ μήτε ψυχούσῃ τὸ ψυχρὸν ὕδωρ μιχθὲν ἔψυξεν ὅτι ψυχρὸν ἦν τῇ κράσει.
beads.english: Thus cold water, mixed with simple cerate, which neither heats nor cools, cooled because it was cold in its mixture.

beads.greek: εἰ δέ γε τῶν θερμαινόντων ἔμιξάς τι τῇ τοιαύτῃ κηρωτῇ, θερμαῖνον ἄν σοι τὸ φάρμακον ἐγένετο, καθάπερ πολλάκις εὐφόρβιον, ἢ καστόριον ἐπεμίξαμεν ἐπὶ πολλῶν διαθέσεων.
beads.english: But if you had mixed one of the heating things with such a cerate, the drug would have become heating for you, just as we have often added euphorbium or castoreum in many conditions.

beads.greek: οὕτως οὖν, εἴπερ ὄξος ἀναμίξαις ἀκριβῶς ἁπλῇ κηρωτῇ, ψυχρότερον ἐργάσῃ πολλῷ τῆς κηρωτῆς τὸ φάρμακον, ὡς ἂν ψυχροῦ τοῦ μιχθέντος ὑπάρχοντος.
beads.english: In the same way, then, if you mix vinegar with a cerate that is strictly simple, you will make the drug much colder than the cerate, since what has been mixed in is cold.

beads.greek: καί σοι τοῦτο πρὸς ἐρυσιπέλατα καὶ φλεγμονὰς ἕρπητάς τε καὶ ἄνθρακας ἀγαθὸν ἔσται φάρμακον· εἰ δέ γε τὸ μικτὸν ὡς ἁπλοῦν ἐξετάζοις, καὶ γὰρ αὖ καὶ τοῦτο ποιοῦσιν, ἁμαρτήσεις τὰ μέγιστα.
beads.english: And this will be a good drug for you against erysipelata and inflammations, herpetes and anthraces. But if you examine the mixed drug as though it were simple, as indeed they also do, you will err most gravely.

greek_sentences: εἰ δὲ καὶ μίγνυτό ποτε μετ’ ἄλλου, χρὴ τὸ μιγνύμενον αὐτῷ μέσον εἶναι τὴν κρᾶσιν, ὡς ἐφ’ ὕδατός τε καὶ κηρωτῆς ὁ πρόσθεν [439] λόγος ἀπέδειξεν.
εὐλόγως γὰρ, οἶμαι, τὸ τῷ μηδετέρῳ τῶν ἄκρων κατὰ τὴν κρᾶσιν, ἀλλ’ ὡς οἷόν τε μέσῳ συμπεπλεγμένον αὐτὸ, τῶν ἀποτελουμένων αἴτιον γίγνεσθαι.
τῇ γοῦν ἁπλῇ κηρωτῇ μήτε θερμαινούσῃ μήτε ψυχούσῃ τὸ ψυχρὸν ὕδωρ μιχθὲν ἔψυξεν ὅτι ψυχρὸν ἦν τῇ κράσει.
εἰ δέ γε τῶν θερμαινόντων ἔμιξάς τι τῇ τοιαύτῃ κηρωτῇ, θερμαῖνον ἄν σοι τὸ φάρμακον ἐγένετο, καθάπερ πολλάκις εὐφόρβιον, ἢ καστόριον ἐπεμίξαμεν ἐπὶ πολλῶν διαθέσεων.
οὕτως οὖν, εἴπερ ὄξος ἀναμίξαις ἀκριβῶς ἁπλῇ κηρωτῇ, ψυχρότερον ἐργάσῃ πολλῷ τῆς κηρωτῆς τὸ φάρμακον, ὡς ἂν ψυχροῦ τοῦ μιχθέντος ὑπάρχοντος.
καί σοι τοῦτο πρὸς ἐρυσιπέλατα καὶ φλεγμονὰς ἕρπητάς τε καὶ ἄνθρακας ἀγαθὸν ἔσται φάρμακον· εἰ δέ γε τὸ μικτὸν ὡς ἁπλοῦν ἐξετάζοις, καὶ γὰρ αὖ καὶ τοῦτο ποιοῦσιν, ἁμαρτήσεις τὰ μέγιστα.
english_sentences: But if it should ever be mixed with something else, what is mixed with it must be intermediate in its mixture, as the earlier [439] argument demonstrated in the case of water and cerate.

For it is reasonable, I think, that what has been combined with something that is neither of the extremes in its mixture, but as far as possible intermediate, should itself become the cause of the effects produced.
Thus cold water, mixed with simple cerate, which neither heats nor cools, cooled because it was cold in its mixture.
But if you had mixed one of the heating things with such a cerate, the drug would have become heating for you, just as we have often added euphorbium or castoreum in many conditions.
In the same way, then, if you mix vinegar with a cerate that is strictly simple, you will make the drug much colder than the cerate, since what has been mixed in is cold.
And this will be a good drug for you against erysipelata and inflammations, herpetes and anthraces.
But if you examine the mixed drug as though it were simple, as indeed they also do, you will err most gravely.

beads.greek: κολλητικὸν γὰρ ἑλκῶν οὐκ ὄξος χρὴ λέγειν, ἀλλ’ ὀξύκρατον, ἕτερόν τι παρὰ πολὺ τὴν φύσιν [440] ὄξους ὑπάρχον.
beads.english: For one ought not to call vinegar agglutinating of wounds, but oxycrate, which is something by far different in nature [440] from vinegar.

beads.greek: ὥσπερ γὰρ οὐδὲ σαρκωτικὸν ἑλκῶν ἰὸς, ἀλλ’ ἡ κηρωτὴ προσλαβοῦσα βραχὺ μόριον ἰοῦ, κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον οὐδ’ ὄξος κολλητικὸν, ἀλλ’ ὕδωρ ὄξους ἐλάχιστον προσλαβὸν, αὐτὸ δὲ καθ’ ἑαυτὸ μόνον καὶ ψιλὸν ὄξος ἱκανῶς παροξύνει τὰ κολλήσεως δεόμενα τῶν ἑλκῶν, ὡς ἂν τῇ λεπτομερείᾳ διαβρωτικόν τε καὶ ὀδυνηρὸν ὑπάρχον.
beads.english: For just as verdigris is not flesh-forming of wounds, but rather the cerate that has taken up a small portion of verdigris, in the same way vinegar is not agglutinating either, but rather water that has taken up a very small amount of vinegar; vinegar itself, on its own, alone and unmixed, considerably exacerbates those wounds that require agglutination, since by its fine-particledness it is corrosive and painful.

beads.greek: οὔτ’ οὖν τὰ τοιαῦτα δεόντως λέγουσιν οὔθ’ ὅταν ἀγνώστοις ἄγνωστα συνάπτωσιν.
beads.english: Neither, then, do they speak properly about such things, nor when they join unknown things to unknown things.

beads.greek: Οὐδὲν γὰρ ἀποδείξαντες ἰδίᾳ περὶ τῶν κολληθησομένων, ἢ σαρκωθησομένων, ἢ ἐπουλωθησομένων ἑλκῶν ἐξ ἐπαγωγῆς συλλογίζονται, τὰ στύφοντα πάντα φάσκοντες ἑλκῶν εἶναι κολλητικά.
beads.english: For without having demonstrated anything specifically about wounds that are to be agglutinated, or filled with flesh, or cicatrised, they reason by induction, asserting that all astringent things are agglutinating of wounds.

beads.greek: χρὴ δ’ οὐκ ἐξ ἐπαγωγῆς, ἀλλὰ δι’ ἀποδείξεως ἐν τῷ καθόλου τὰ τοιαῦτα λαμβάνεσθαι, καθάπερ ἡμεῖς ἐν τοῖς τῆς θεραπευτικῆς μεθόδου ποιήσομεν ὑπομνήμασιν, ἀλλ’ ἁπλῶς γε οὕτως ῥηθὲν ὁτιοῦν τῶν τοιούτων οὐ μόνον ἀναπόδεικτον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ψεῦδός ἐστιν.
beads.english: But such things must be grasped in universal form not by induction but through demonstration, as we shall do in the commentaries on the Therapeutic Method; stated simply in this way, any one of such claims is not only undemonstrated but also false.

greek_sentences: κολλητικὸν γὰρ ἑλκῶν οὐκ ὄξος χρὴ λέγειν, ἀλλ’ ὀξύκρατον, ἕτερόν τι παρὰ πολὺ τὴν φύσιν [440] ὄξους ὑπάρχον.

ὥσπερ γὰρ οὐδὲ σαρκωτικὸν ἑλκῶν ἰὸς, ἀλλ’ ἡ κηρωτὴ προσλαβοῦσα βραχὺ μόριον ἰοῦ, κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον οὐδ’ ὄξος κολλητικὸν, ἀλλ’ ὕδωρ ὄξους ἐλάχιστον προσλαβὸν, αὐτὸ δὲ καθ’ ἑαυτὸ μόνον καὶ ψιλὸν ὄξος ἱκανῶς παροξύνει τὰ κολλήσεως δεόμενα τῶν ἑλκῶν, ὡς ἂν τῇ λεπτομερείᾳ διαβρωτικόν τε καὶ ὀδυνηρὸν ὑπάρχον.
οὔτ’ οὖν τὰ τοιαῦτα δεόντως λέγουσιν οὔθ’ ὅταν ἀγνώστοις ἄγνωστα συνάπτωσιν.
Οὐδὲν γὰρ ἀποδείξαντες ἰδίᾳ περὶ τῶν κολληθησομένων, ἢ σαρκωθησομένων, ἢ ἐπουλωθησομένων ἑλκῶν ἐξ ἐπαγωγῆς συλλογίζονται, τὰ στύφοντα πάντα φάσκοντες ἑλκῶν εἶναι κολλητικά.

english_sentences: For one ought not to call vinegar agglutinating of wounds, but oxycrate, which is something by far different in nature [440] from vinegar.

For just as verdigris is not flesh-forming of wounds, but rather the cerate that has taken up a small portion of verdigris, in the same way vinegar is not agglutinating either, but rather water that has taken up a very small amount of vinegar; vinegar itself, on its own, alone and unmixed, considerably exacerbates those wounds that require agglutination, since by its fine-particledness it is corrosive and painful.
Neither, then, do they speak properly about such things, nor when they join unknown things to unknown things.

For without having demonstrated anything specifically about wounds that are to be agglutinated, or filled with flesh, or cicatrised, they reason by induction, asserting that all astringent things are agglutinating of wounds.

But such things must be grasped in universal form not by induction but through demonstration, as we shall do in the commentaries on the Therapeutic Method; stated simply in this way, any one of such claims is not only undemonstrated but also false.

beads.greek: οὔτε γὰρ χαλκῖτις, οὔτε κηκὶς, οὔτε αὐτὰ τὰ λέμματα τῶν ῥοιῶν, [441] οὔτε ὀμφάκιον, οὔτε στυπτηρία, πολὺ δὲ μᾶλλον οὔτε χαλκὸς κεκαυμένος, οὔτε λεπὶς, οὔτε μίσυ κολλᾷν ἕλκη πέφυκεν, ἕτερά τε μυρία τῶν στυφόντων ἐστὶν ἀδύνατα κολλᾷν.
beads.english: For neither chalcitis, nor oak-gall, nor the very rinds of pomegranates, [441] nor omphacium, nor alum, and still much less burnt copper, nor scale, nor misy, is of a nature to agglutinate wounds, and countless others among the astringent things are unable to agglutinate.

beads.greek: εἰ δ’ ἄρα καὶ μὴ τοῦτό τις, ἀλλὰ τὰ κολλητικὰ πάντα στυπτικὰ λέγοι, δειχθήσεται κᾀνταῦθα πολλὰ κολλῶντα χωρὶς τοῦ στύφειν.
beads.english: But if, then, someone should say not this, but rather that all agglutinating things are astringent, it will be shown in this case too that many things agglutinate without being astringent.

beads.greek: οὐδέτερος οὖν ἀληθὴς λόγος ἁπλῶς καὶ ἀδιορίστως λεχθεὶς, οὔθ’ ὅταν ἅπαντα φάσκωσι τὰ στύφοντα κολλᾷν ἕλκος, οὔθ’ ὅταν πάντα τὰ κολλώμενα διὰ τῶν στυφόντων κολλᾶσθαι.
beads.english: Neither statement, then, is true when it is said simply and without distinction: neither when they assert that all astringent things agglutinate a wound, nor when they assert that all things that are agglutinated are agglutinated by means of astringent things.

beads.greek: πολὺ δὲ δὴ καὶ τούτων ἔτι μᾶλλον ἄτοπά τε καὶ ψεύδη λέγουσιν ἤδη καὶ περὶ τὴν αἴσθησιν, ὅταν καὶ τὰ δακνώδη καὶ τὰ δριμέα καὶ τὰ πικρὰ καὶ τὰ ἁλυκὰ καὶ πρὸς τούτοις ἔτι τὰ μαλακώτατα καὶ ἥδιστα ταῖς ποιότησι στύφειν λέγουσιν, ὥσπερ οὐ τῆς γεύσεως αἰσθητὸν τὸ στῦφον ὑπάρχον, ἀλλ’ ἐκ τῆς ἐκείνων νομοθεσίας λαμβανόμενον.
beads.english: And things still much more absurd and false than these they now say even concerning sensation itself, when they say that the biting, the pungent, the bitter and the salty things, and in addition to these even the things that are softest and most pleasant in their qualities, are astringent, as though the astringent were not something perceptible to taste, but something taken from their own legislation.

beads.greek: ἡ μὲν γὰρ ῥοιὰ καὶ τὸ μῆλον, εἰ τύχοι, καὶ τὸ μέσπιλον, ἀπίων τέ τινα γένη καὶ μύρτα καὶ οὖα καὶ οἶνος Ἀμυναῖος καὶ Μαρσὸς ἐναργῶς ἡμᾶς στύφει.
beads.english: For the pomegranate, and the apple, as it may be, and the medlar, and certain kinds of pears, and myrtle berries, and sorbs, and Aminaean and Marsian wine evidently have an astringent effect on us.

greek_sentences: οὔτε γὰρ χαλκῖτις, οὔτε κηκὶς, οὔτε αὐτὰ τὰ λέμματα τῶν ῥοιῶν, [441] οὔτε ὀμφάκιον, οὔτε στυπτηρία, πολὺ δὲ μᾶλλον οὔτε χαλκὸς κεκαυμένος, οὔτε λεπὶς, οὔτε μίσυ κολλᾷν ἕλκη πέφυκεν, ἕτερά τε μυρία τῶν στυφόντων ἐστὶν ἀδύνατα κολλᾷν.
εἰ δ’ ἄρα καὶ μὴ τοῦτό τις, ἀλλὰ τὰ κολλητικὰ πάντα στυπτικὰ λέγοι, δειχθήσεται κᾀνταῦθα πολλὰ κολλῶντα χωρὶς τοῦ στύφειν.
οὐδέτερος οὖν ἀληθὴς λόγος ἁπλῶς καὶ ἀδιορίστως λεχθεὶς, οὔθ’ ὅταν ἅπαντα φάσκωσι τὰ στύφοντα κολλᾷν ἕλκος, οὔθ’ ὅταν πάντα τὰ κολλώμενα διὰ τῶν στυφόντων κολλᾶσθαι.

πολὺ δὲ δὴ καὶ τούτων ἔτι μᾶλλον ἄτοπά τε καὶ ψεύδη λέγουσιν ἤδη καὶ περὶ τὴν αἴσθησιν, ὅταν καὶ τὰ δακνώδη καὶ τὰ δριμέα καὶ τὰ πικρὰ καὶ τὰ ἁλυκὰ καὶ πρὸς τούτοις ἔτι τὰ μαλακώτατα καὶ ἥδιστα ταῖς ποιότησι στύφειν λέγουσιν, ὥσπερ οὐ τῆς γεύσεως αἰσθητὸν τὸ στῦφον ὑπάρχον, ἀλλ’ ἐκ τῆς ἐκείνων νομοθεσίας λαμβανόμενον.

english_sentences: For neither chalcitis, nor oak-gall, nor the very rinds of pomegranates, [441] nor omphacium, nor alum, and still much less burnt copper, nor scale, nor misy, is of a nature to agglutinate wounds, and countless others among the astringent things are unable to agglutinate.
But if, then, someone should say not this, but rather that all agglutinating things are astringent, it will be shown in this case too that many things agglutinate without being astringent.

Neither statement, then, is true when it is said simply and without distinction: neither when they assert that all astringent things agglutinate a wound, nor when they assert that all things that are agglutinated are agglutinated by means of astringent things.

And things still much more absurd and false than these they now say even concerning sensation itself, when they say that the biting, the pungent, the bitter and the salty things, and in addition to these even the things that are softest and most pleasant in their qualities, are astringent, as though the astringent were not something perceptible to taste, but something taken from their own legislation.
For the pomegranate, and the apple, as it may be, and the medlar, and certain kinds of pears, and myrtle berries, and sorbs, and Aminaean and Marsian wine evidently have an astringent effect on us.

beads.greek: πυροὶ δὲ καὶ ζειαὶ καὶ κέγχροι Ἡρόδοτον μὲν [442] ἴσως ἔστυφον, τῶν δ’ ἄλλων ἀνθρώπων οὐδένα.
beads.english: But wheat, zeia and millet were perhaps astringent to Herodotus [442], though to no other human being.

beads.greek: μυρίων γὰρ ἐπυθόμην ἐγὼ καὶ περὶ τούτων καὶ πολὺ μᾶλλον ἔτι περὶ ἀμύλου, καὶ γὰρ καὶ τοῦτο στύφειν Ἡρόδοτός φησιν, ὥσπερ οὖν καὶ τὸ πέπερι, στῦφον μηδ’ αὐτὸ μηδένα τῶν ἄλλων ἀνθρώπων, ὅσοι καθαρῶς καὶ ἀδεκάστως ἐξετάζουσιν τὰς ποιότητας.
beads.english: For I inquired of countless people both about these and, much more still, about starch, since Herodotus says that this too is astringent, as indeed he says of pepper as well, which is itself astringent to none of the other people who examine the qualities purely and impartially.

beads.greek: ἀλλ’ Ἡρόδοτος μὲν συνέχεεν εἰς ταὐτὸν ἅπαντα, καὶ τὰ δριμύτατα ταῖς δυνάμεσιν καὶ τὰ ἄκρως διαβρωτικὰ καὶ τὰ μαλακώτατα καὶ τὰ προσηνέστατα.
beads.english: Herodotus, however, confounded everything into one and the same thing, both the things most pungent in their powers and the extremely corrosive ones, and the softest and the most gentle.

beads.greek: πάντα στύφειν ἔφησεν, ὡς ἐν τῷ καταψεύσασθαί τισι τῆς αἰσθήσεως τὸ τοῦ νικᾷν ὑπάρχοντος.
beads.english: He said that all are astringent, as though victory lay in bearing false witness against the senses in certain cases.

beads.greek: ἀλλ’ οὐκ αὐτὸ δή τοῦτο μέγιστον δεῖγμα τῆς τῶν λόγων αὐτοῦ μοχθηρίας ἐσόμενον.
beads.english: Yet this very thing will not be the greatest proof of the badness of his arguments.

beads.greek: Ὥσπερ δὲ ὑπερβάλλεσθαι βουλόμενος αὐτὸν τοῖς κατὰ τῶν αἰσθήσεων ψεύσμασιν ὁ Ἀσκληπιάδης Μητρόδωρος, ἄλλά τε καὶ ῥητίνην καὶ ἄσφαλτον οὐχ ὁμολογεῖ θερμαίνειν ἡμᾶς, ἅπαντά τε τὰ στύφοντα καὶ ψύχειν φησὶν, εἰ καὶ μηδενὸς ἄλλου χαλκίτεώς τε καὶ χαλκάνθης καὶ μίσυος ἱκανῶς μὲν στυφόντων, εἰς τοσοῦτον δ’ ἡκόντων δ’ ἡκόντων θερμότητος, ὥστε καίειν ἡμᾶς.
beads.english: For, as if wishing to outdo him in falsehoods against the senses, the Asclepiadean Metrodorus does not admit, among other things, that resin and asphalt heat us, and he says that all astringent things also cool, even though, if nothing else, chalcitis, chalcanthe and misy are sufficiently astringent and yet reach such a degree of heat as to burn us.

greek_sentences: πυροὶ δὲ καὶ ζειαὶ καὶ κέγχροι Ἡρόδοτον μὲν [442] ἴσως ἔστυφον, τῶν δ’ ἄλλων ἀνθρώπων οὐδένα.

μυρίων γὰρ ἐπυθόμην ἐγὼ καὶ περὶ τούτων καὶ πολὺ μᾶλλον ἔτι περὶ ἀμύλου, καὶ γὰρ καὶ τοῦτο στύφειν Ἡρόδοτός φησιν, ὥσπερ οὖν καὶ τὸ πέπερι, στῦφον μηδ’ αὐτὸ μηδένα τῶν ἄλλων ἀνθρώπων, ὅσοι καθαρῶς καὶ ἀδεκάστως ἐξετάζουσιν τὰς ποιότητας.
ἀλλ’ Ἡρόδοτος μὲν συνέχεεν εἰς ταὐτὸν ἅπαντα, καὶ τὰ δριμύτατα ταῖς δυνάμεσιν καὶ τὰ ἄκρως διαβρωτικὰ καὶ τὰ μαλακώτατα καὶ τὰ προσηνέστατα.
πάντα στύφειν ἔφησεν, ὡς ἐν τῷ καταψεύσασθαί τισι τῆς αἰσθήσεως τὸ τοῦ νικᾷν ὑπάρχοντος.
ἀλλ’ οὐκ αὐτὸ δή τοῦτο μέγιστον δεῖγμα τῆς τῶν λόγων αὐτοῦ μοχθηρίας ἐσόμενον.

Ὥσπερ δὲ ὑπερβάλλεσθαι βουλόμενος αὐτὸν τοῖς κατὰ τῶν αἰσθήσεων ψεύσμασιν ὁ Ἀσκληπιάδης Μητρόδωρος, ἄλλά τε καὶ ῥητίνην καὶ ἄσφαλτον οὐχ ὁμολογεῖ θερμαίνειν ἡμᾶς, ἅπαντά τε τὰ στύφοντα καὶ ψύχειν φησὶν, εἰ καὶ μηδενὸς ἄλλου χαλκίτεώς τε καὶ χαλκάνθης καὶ μίσυος ἱκανῶς μὲν στυφόντων, εἰς τοσοῦτον δ’ ἡκόντων δ’ ἡκόντων θερμότητος, ὥστε καίειν ἡμᾶς.
english_sentences: But wheat, zeia and millet were perhaps astringent to Herodotus [442], though to no other human being.

For I inquired of countless people both about these and, much more still, about starch, since Herodotus says that this too is astringent, as indeed he says of pepper as well, which is itself astringent to none of the other people who examine the qualities purely and impartially.
Herodotus, however, confounded everything into one and the same thing, both the things most pungent in their powers and the extremely corrosive ones, and the softest and the most gentle.
He said that all are astringent, as though victory lay in bearing false witness against the senses in certain cases.
Yet this very thing will not be the greatest proof of the badness of his arguments.

For, as if wishing to outdo him in falsehoods against the senses, the Asclepiadean Metrodorus does not admit, among other things, that resin and asphalt heat us, and he says that all astringent things also cool, even though, if nothing else, chalcitis, chalcanthe and misy are sufficiently astringent and yet reach such a degree of heat as to burn us.

beads.greek: οὔκουν ἔτι θαυμαστὸν οὐδὲν εἰ [443] ληροῦσί τε πολλὰ καὶ παραλογίζονται σφᾶς αὐτοὺς οἱ ἄνθρωποι, μηδὲ περὶ τῶν ἐναργῶς φαινομένων ὁμολογῆσαι τἀληθὲς τολμῶντες.
beads.english: It is therefore no longer at all surprising if [443] these men talk a great deal of nonsense and mislead themselves by false reasoning, since they do not dare to admit the truth even about things that are evidently apparent.

beads.greek: Εἶτά τινες ἐξ αὐτῶν, ὥσπερ Ἡρόδοτος καὶ Διοσκουρίδης, ἐκ τοῦ φάρμακα ἄττα διαῤῥοίας τε καὶ δυσεντερίας ὠφελεῖν συλλογίζονται στύφειν αὐτὰ, καίτοι μηδ’ ἐλαχίστης μετέχοντα στύψεως, ἀλλ’ αὐτὸ τοὐναντίον ἀραιότερα τε καὶ χαλαστικὰ ταῖς δυνάμεσιν ὑπάρχοντα τῶν στυφόντων, συναγαγόντων τε καὶ πιλούντων καὶ πυκνούντων καὶ σφιγγόντων τὰ σώματα.
beads.english: Then some of them, such as Herodotus and Dioscorides, infer from the fact that certain drugs benefit diarrhoeas and dysenteries that these drugs are astringent, although they do not share in even the least astringency. Quite the contrary: in their powers they are more rarefying and relaxing than the astringents, which draw together, compress, condense and bind tight the bodies.

beads.greek: καταφρονήσαντες γὰρ ἅπαξ τῆς αἰσθήσεως ἀνέτρεψαν ἅπαντα καὶ συνέχεαν ἃ σαφῶς ἐστιν αἰσθήσει διαγνῶναι, ταῦτα μοχθηρῷ λόγῳ πιστούμενοι.
beads.english: For having once despised sense-perception, they have overturned everything and have confounded the things that can clearly be discerned by perception, trying to establish these by faulty reasoning.

beads.greek: τὸ γοῦν αἴγειον στέαρ ἐναντιώτατόν ἐστιν τοῖς στύφουσιν ἅπασι καὶ γεύσει καὶ δυνάμει, καθάπερ καὶ τὸ τῶν πυρῶν ἄλευρον, ἄμυλόν τε καὶ ἄλλα μυρία τῶν ἐμπλασάντων τε καὶ παρηγορούντων καὶ δριμύτητας ἀμβλυνόντων καὶ ταύτῃ τοῖς δακνώδη τε καὶ δριμέα διαχωροῦσιν ἀρηγόντων.
beads.english: Goat's fat, at any rate, is most opposite to all astringents both in taste and in power, just as wheat flour is, and starch, and countless other things among those that plaster over, soothe and blunt pungencies, and in this way help those who pass biting and pungent evacuations.

greek_sentences: οὔκουν ἔτι θαυμαστὸν οὐδὲν εἰ [443] ληροῦσί τε πολλὰ καὶ παραλογίζονται σφᾶς αὐτοὺς οἱ ἄνθρωποι, μηδὲ περὶ τῶν ἐναργῶς φαινομένων ὁμολογῆσαι τἀληθὲς τολμῶντες.

Εἶτά τινες ἐξ αὐτῶν, ὥσπερ Ἡρόδοτος καὶ Διοσκουρίδης, ἐκ τοῦ φάρμακα ἄττα διαῤῥοίας τε καὶ δυσεντερίας ὠφελεῖν συλλογίζονται στύφειν αὐτὰ, καίτοι μηδ’ ἐλαχίστης μετέχοντα στύψεως, ἀλλ’ αὐτὸ τοὐναντίον ἀραιότερα τε καὶ χαλαστικὰ ταῖς δυνάμεσιν ὑπάρχοντα τῶν στυφόντων, συναγαγόντων τε καὶ πιλούντων καὶ πυκνούντων καὶ σφιγγόντων τὰ σώματα.
καταφρονήσαντες γὰρ ἅπαξ τῆς αἰσθήσεως ἀνέτρεψαν ἅπαντα καὶ συνέχεαν ἃ σαφῶς ἐστιν αἰσθήσει διαγνῶναι, ταῦτα μοχθηρῷ λόγῳ πιστούμενοι.

τὸ γοῦν αἴγειον στέαρ ἐναντιώτατόν ἐστιν τοῖς στύφουσιν ἅπασι καὶ γεύσει καὶ δυνάμει, καθάπερ καὶ τὸ τῶν πυρῶν ἄλευρον, ἄμυλόν τε καὶ ἄλλα μυρία τῶν ἐμπλασάντων τε καὶ παρηγορούντων καὶ δριμύτητας ἀμβλυνόντων καὶ ταύτῃ τοῖς δακνώδη τε καὶ δριμέα διαχωροῦσιν ἀρηγόντων.
english_sentences: It is therefore no longer at all surprising if [443] these men talk a great deal of nonsense and mislead themselves by false reasoning, since they do not dare to admit the truth even about things that are evidently apparent.

Then some of them, such as Herodotus and Dioscorides, infer from the fact that certain drugs benefit diarrhoeas and dysenteries that these drugs are astringent, although they do not share in even the least astringency.
Quite the contrary: in their powers they are more rarefying and relaxing than the astringents, which draw together, compress, condense and bind tight the bodies.
For having once despised sense-perception, they have overturned everything and have confounded the things that can clearly be discerned by perception, trying to establish these by faulty reasoning.

Goat's fat, at any rate, is most opposite to all astringents both in taste and in power, just as wheat flour is, and starch, and countless other things among those that plaster over, soothe and blunt pungencies, and in this way help those who pass biting and pungent evacuations.

beads.greek: καὶ εἰ διὰ ταῦτα στύφει, ἔστω δὴ καὶ τὸ ἔλαιον ἡμῖν τῶν στυφόντων, [444] ὅτι δὴ καὶ πολλάκις ὠφέλησεν τοὺς σφοδρῶς δακνομένους ἐνεθέν.
beads.english: And if it is astringent for these reasons, then let olive oil too be counted by us among the astringents, [444] since it too has often benefited, when injected, those suffering violent biting.

beads.greek: ἔσται δὲ καὶ κηρὸς καὶ στέαρ χοίρειον, ὀρνίθειόν τε καὶ χήνειον καὶ χόνδρου καὶ τράγου χυλός.
beads.english: And wax will be astringent too, and pig's fat, fowl's fat and goose fat, and the juice of groats and of tragos.

beads.greek: ἐνίεμεν γὰρ καὶ ταῦτα καὶ κηρωτὴν ἐνίοτε τοῖς δακνομένοις ἰσχυρῶς, ὥσπερ καὶ τὸ αἴγειον στέαρ.
beads.english: For we inject these too, and sometimes a cerate, into those suffering strong biting, just as we do goat's fat.

beads.greek: ἐναργεστέραν δὲ τὴν ὠφέλειαν τὸ αἴγειον ἐπιδείκνυται τῷ ῥᾳδίως πήγνυσθαι ἐπαλείφεσθαί τε τοῖς ἐντέροις καὶ περιμένειν ἐπὶ πλεῖστον.
beads.english: But goat's fat displays a more evident benefit, because it readily congeals, is smeared over the intestines, and remains there for a very long time.

beads.greek: εἴτε δὲ διὰ πάχος, εἴτε δι’ ἄλλην τινὰ αἰτίαν πήγνυται ταχέως, οὐδὲν δέομαι τάδε νῦν ζητεῖν ἐναργῶς φαινομένου τοῦ πράγματος.
beads.english: Whether it congeals quickly because of its thickness or for some other cause, I have no need to inquire into these things now, since the fact is plainly evident.

beads.greek: ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ ὅτι καὶ πήγνυται τάχιστα καὶ τὰς δήξεις τῶν ἐντέρων ἀμβλύνει, τῷ φαίνεσθαι πιστότερόν ἐστιν, οὕτω δὴ καὶ ὅτι μηδεμιᾶς αὐτῷ μέτεστι ψύξεως ἢ στύψεως.
beads.english: But just as the fact that it congeals very quickly and blunts the bitings of the intestines is rendered more credible by its being apparent, so too is the fact that it has no share in any cooling or astringency.

beads.greek: οὗτοι μὲν οὖν ἐξ ἀδήλων ὑπὲρ τῶν φαινομένων συλλογίζονται.
beads.english: These men, then, reason from things non-evident about things apparent; or rather, if the truth must be told, they deceive themselves by false reasoning.

beads.greek: μᾶλλον δ’, εἰ χρὴ τἀληθὲς εἰπεῖν, παραλογίζονται σφᾶς αὐτοὺς, ἡμᾶς δὲ τοσῷδε μᾶλλον ἐπὶ τὴν αἴσθησιν ἀνέρχεσθαι προσῆκεν, ἐπιμελῶς τε προσέχειν αὐτῇ διὰ παντὸς, ὅσῳ καὶ μᾶλλον οὐκ ὀλίγα καταψεύδονται πάντες αὐτῆς οἱ σοφισταί.
beads.english: We, however, ought all the more to go back to sense-perception and to attend to it carefully at all times, in proportion as all the sophists tell not a few lies against it.

greek_sentences: καὶ εἰ διὰ ταῦτα στύφει, ἔστω δὴ καὶ τὸ ἔλαιον ἡμῖν τῶν στυφόντων, [444] ὅτι δὴ καὶ πολλάκις ὠφέλησεν τοὺς σφοδρῶς δακνομένους ἐνεθέν.
ἔσται δὲ καὶ κηρὸς καὶ στέαρ χοίρειον, ὀρνίθειόν τε καὶ χήνειον καὶ χόνδρου καὶ τράγου χυλός.
ἐνίεμεν γὰρ καὶ ταῦτα καὶ κηρωτὴν ἐνίοτε τοῖς δακνομένοις ἰσχυρῶς, ὥσπερ καὶ τὸ αἴγειον στέαρ.
ἐναργεστέραν δὲ τὴν ὠφέλειαν τὸ αἴγειον ἐπιδείκνυται τῷ ῥᾳδίως πήγνυσθαι ἐπαλείφεσθαί τε τοῖς ἐντέροις καὶ περιμένειν ἐπὶ πλεῖστον.
εἴτε δὲ διὰ πάχος, εἴτε δι’ ἄλλην τινὰ αἰτίαν πήγνυται ταχέως, οὐδὲν δέομαι τάδε νῦν ζητεῖν ἐναργῶς φαινομένου τοῦ πράγματος.
ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ ὅτι καὶ πήγνυται τάχιστα καὶ τὰς δήξεις τῶν ἐντέρων ἀμβλύνει, τῷ φαίνεσθαι πιστότερόν ἐστιν, οὕτω δὴ καὶ ὅτι μηδεμιᾶς αὐτῷ μέτεστι ψύξεως ἢ στύψεως.
οὗτοι μὲν οὖν ἐξ ἀδήλων ὑπὲρ τῶν φαινομένων συλλογίζονται.

μᾶλλον δ’, εἰ χρὴ τἀληθὲς εἰπεῖν, παραλογίζονται σφᾶς αὐτοὺς, ἡμᾶς δὲ τοσῷδε μᾶλλον ἐπὶ τὴν αἴσθησιν ἀνέρχεσθαι προσῆκεν, ἐπιμελῶς τε προσέχειν αὐτῇ διὰ παντὸς, ὅσῳ καὶ μᾶλλον οὐκ ὀλίγα καταψεύδονται πάντες αὐτῆς οἱ σοφισταί.
english_sentences: And if it is astringent for these reasons, then let olive oil too be counted by us among the astringents, [444] since it too has often benefited, when injected, those suffering violent biting.
And wax will be astringent too, and pig's fat, fowl's fat and goose fat, and the juice of groats and of tragos.
For we inject these too, and sometimes a cerate, into those suffering strong biting, just as we do goat's fat.
But goat's fat displays a more evident benefit, because it readily congeals, is smeared over the intestines, and remains there for a very long time.
Whether it congeals quickly because of its thickness or for some other cause, I have no need to inquire into these things now, since the fact is plainly evident.

But just as the fact that it congeals very quickly and blunts the bitings of the intestines is rendered more credible by its being apparent, so too is the fact that it has no share in any cooling or astringency.
These men, then, reason from things non-evident about things apparent; or rather, if the truth must be told, they deceive themselves by false reasoning.
We, however, ought all the more to go back to sense-perception and to attend to it carefully at all times, in proportion as all the sophists tell not a few lies against it.

beads.greek: πάλιν οὖν ἀναμνήσαντες [445] αὐτοὺς, ὅτι ἃ τοῖς μὲν ἰδιώταις ἐστὶ δῆλα καὶ τούτοις ἦν, ὅτ’ οὔπω διὰ φιλονεικίαν ὑπερεφρόνουν τῶν αἰσθήσεων, ὕστερον δ’ ἀπώλετο διὰ περιττὴν σοφίαν, ἐπὶ τὸ συνεχὲς τοῦ λόγου μεταβήσομαι.
beads.english: Having therefore reminded [445] them once again that what is evident to laymen was evident to them too, at a time when they did not yet, out of love of contention, look down on the senses, but was afterwards lost through excessive cleverness, I shall pass on to the continuation of the argument.

beads.greek: Ἑκάστη τις φύσις τῶν αἰσθητῶν ἰδίᾳ ὑποβέβληται· θερμότης μὲν καὶ ψυχρότης καὶ σκληρότης καὶ μαλακότης ἁφῇ, λευκότης δὲ καὶ μελανότης καὶ ξανθότης, ἐρυθρότης τε καὶ συλλήβδην εἰπεῖν ἅπαν τὸ τῶν χρωμάτων γένος ὄψει, πικρότης τε καὶ γλυκύτης, αὐστηρότης τε καὶ στρυφνότης, ὀξύτης τε καὶ ἁλυκότης καὶ δριμύτης, γεύσει καὶ μαίνεσθαι δόξει σαφῶς, εἴ τις ἤ τὰς χροιὰς τῇ γεύσει κρίνειν ἐπιχειρήσειεν, ἢ τοὺς χυμοὺς τῇ ὄψει.
beads.english: Each nature among the sensibles is subject to a sense proper to it: heat and coldness and hardness and softness to touch; whiteness and blackness and yellowness, redness and, to put it summarily, the whole genus of colours to sight; bitterness and sweetness, harshness and acerbity, sourness and saltiness and pungency to taste. And anyone will plainly seem to be mad who should attempt either to judge colours by taste or flavours by sight.

beads.greek: κατὰ ταὐτὰ δὲ καὶ περὶ τῆς ἁφῆς χρὴ γινώσκειν καὶ περὶ τῶν ἄλλων αἰσθήσεων, ὡς τὰς μὲν ἁπτὰς διαφορὰς ἁφῇ κριτέον ἐστὶ, τὰς δ’ ἀκουστὰς ἀκοῇ, τὰς δ’ ἐν ἀτμοῖς ὀσφρήσει.
beads.english: In the same way one must understand concerning touch and the other senses as well, that tangible differences are to be judged by touch, audible ones by hearing, and those in vapours by smell.

beads.greek: τούτων οὖν οὕτως ἐχόντων ἀκούσωμεν εἰ βούλεσθε καὶ Πλάτωνος ὑπὲρ τῶν γευστῶν διαφορῶν ἐξηγουμένου.
beads.english: These things being so, let us hear, if you wish, Plato too, as he expounds the differences of tastes.

beads.greek: χρὴ δὲ οὐ τῇ φυσιολογίᾳ προσέχειν αὐτοῦ τὸν νοῦν.
beads.english: One must not, however, direct one's attention to his natural philosophy.

τούτων οὖν οὕτως ἐχόντων ἀκούσωμεν εἰ βούλεσθε καὶ Πλάτωνος ὑπὲρ τῶν γευστῶν διαφορῶν ἐξηγουμένου.
χρὴ δὲ οὐ τῇ φυσιολογίᾳ προσέχειν αὐτοῦ τὸν νοῦν.
english_sentences: Having therefore reminded [445] them once again that what is evident to laymen was evident to them too, at a time when they did not yet, out of love of contention, look down on the senses, but was afterwards lost through excessive cleverness, I shall pass on to the continuation of the argument.

Each nature among the sensibles is subject to a sense proper to it: heat and coldness and hardness and softness to touch; whiteness and blackness and yellowness, redness and, to put it summarily, the whole genus of colours to sight; bitterness and sweetness, harshness and acerbity, sourness and saltiness and pungency to taste.

These things being so, let us hear, if you wish, Plato too, as he expounds the differences of tastes.
One must not, however, direct one's attention to his natural philosophy.

beads.greek: οὐ γὰρ ἂν ἐν καιρῷ μοι νῦν εἴη [446] μνημονεύειν αὐτῆς, οὐδ’ εἰς τοῦτο καλῶ μάρτυρα τὸν ἄνδρα, μόνον δ’ ὑπὲρ τοῦ δεῖξαι κατὰ τίνος πράγματος ἕκαστον τῶν ὀνομάτων ἔθος ἐστὶν ἐπιφέρειν τοῖς Ἕλλησιν.
beads.english: For it would not be opportune for me now [446] to make mention of it, nor do I call the man as a witness for this, but only for the purpose of showing to what thing it is the custom among the Greeks to apply each of the names.

beads.greek: ἄκουε τοίνυν τοῦ Πλάτωνος λέγοντος· ὅσα μὲν γὰρ εἰσιόντα περὶ τὰ φλεβία, οἷόν περ δοκίμια τῆς γλώττης, τεταμένα δ’ ἐπὶ τὴν καρδίαν εἰς τὰ νοτερὰ τῆς σαρκὸς καὶ ἁπαλὰ ἐμπίπτοντα γήϊνά τινα μέρη κατατηκόμενα ξυνάγει τὰ φλεβία καὶ ἀποξηραίνει, τραχύτερα μὲν ὄντα στρυφνὰ, ἧττον δὲ τραχύνοντα αὐστηρὰ λέγεται.
beads.english: Hear, then, Plato saying: 'For whatever earthy particles, entering about the small veins, which are as it were the testers of the tongue, stretched towards the heart, and falling upon the moist and soft parts of the flesh, are melted down and contract the small veins and dry them out, these, when they are rougher, are called acerbic, and when they roughen less, harsh.

beads.greek: τὰ δὲ τούτων ῥυπτικὰ καὶ πᾶν τὸ περὶ τὴν γλῶτταν ἀποπλύνοντα πέραν μὲν τοῦ μετρίου τοῦτο δρῶντα καὶ προσεπιλαμβανόμενα, ὥστε ἀποτήκειν αὐτῆς τι τῆς φύσεως, οἷον ἡ τῶν νίτρων δύναμις, πικρὰ πάνθ’ οὕτως ὠνόμασται.
beads.english: Those of them that are cleansing and wash off everything about the tongue, if they do this beyond the moderate and lay hold of it besides, so as to melt away something of its very nature, as the power of nitres does, are all thus named bitter.

beads.greek: τὰ δὲ ὑποδεέστερα τῆς νιτρώδους ἕξεως, ἐπὶ τὸ μέτριόν τε τῇ ῥύψει χρώμενα, ἁλυκὰ ἄνευ πικρότητος τραχείας καὶ φίλα μᾶλλον ἡμῖν φαντάζεται.
beads.english: But those that fall short of the nitrous condition and employ cleansing in moderation appear to us salty, without rough bitterness, and rather more agreeable.'

english_sentences: For it would not be opportune for me now [446] to make mention of it, nor do I call the man as a witness for this, but only for the purpose of showing to what thing it is the custom among the Greeks to apply each of the names.

Hear, then, Plato saying: 'For whatever earthy particles, entering about the small veins, which are as it were the testers of the tongue, stretched towards the heart, and falling upon the moist and soft parts of the flesh, are melted down and contract the small veins and dry them out, these, when they are rougher, are called acerbic, and when they roughen less, harsh.

Those of them that are cleansing and wash off everything about the tongue, if they do this beyond the moderate and lay hold of it besides, so as to melt away something of its very nature, as the power of nitres does, are all thus named bitter.
But those that fall short of the nitrous condition and employ cleansing in moderation appear to us salty, without rough bitterness, and rather more agreeable.'

beads.greek: τὰ δὲ τῇ τοῦ στόματος θερμότητι κοινωνήσαντα καὶ λεαινόμενα ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ συνεκπυρούμενα καὶ πάλιν αὐτὰ ἀντικάοντα τὸ διαθερμῆναν, φερόμενά τε καὶ ὑπὸ κουφότητος ἄνω πρὸς τὰς τῆς κεφαλῆς [447] αἰσθήσεις, τέμνοντά τε πάνθ’ ὁπόσα ἂν προσπίπτῃ διὰ ταύτας τὰς δυνάμεις, δριμέα πάντα τὰ τοιαῦτα ἐλέχθη.
beads.english: Those, again, which share in the heat of the mouth and are smoothed by it, which are set on fire along with it and in their turn burn back that which heated them, and which are also carried upward by their lightness towards the senses of the head [447], cutting everything they fall upon: on account of these powers all such things have been called pungent. When the same things, having first been thinned by putrefaction, enter the narrow veins, and have a commensurateness with the earthy parts present there and with whatever parts of air are there, so that they set them moving about one another and cause them to be stirred up, they, being stirred up, fall around one another and, entering into one another, produce other hollows, stretching themselves around the things that enter.

beads.greek: τῶν δὲ αὐτῶν προλελεπτυσμένων μὲν ὑπὸ σηπεδόνος, εἰς δὲ τὰς στενὰς φλέβας ἐνδυομένων καὶ ἐνοῦσιν αὐτόθι μέρεσι γεώδεσιν καὶ ὅσα ἀέρος συμμετρίαν ἔχοντα, ὥστε κινήσαντα περὶ ἄλληλα ποιεῖν κυκᾶσθαι, κυκώμενα δὲ περιπίπτειν τε καὶ εἰς ἕτερα ἐνδυόμενα ἕτερα κοῖλα ἀπεργάζεσθαι περιτεινόμενα τοῖς εἰσιοῦσιν, ἃ δὴ νοτίδος περὶ ἀέρα κοίλης περιταθείσης ποτὲ μὲν γεώδους, ποτὲ δὲ καὶ καθαρᾶς, νοτερὰ ἀγγεῖα ἀέρος ὕδατα κοῖλα περιφερῆ τε γενέσθαι καὶ τὰ μὲν τῆς καθαρᾶς εἰς διαφανεῖς περιστῆναι, κληθείσας ὄνομα πομφόλυγας, τὰ δὲ τῆς γεώδους, ὁμοῦ κινουμένης τε καὶ αἰρομένης, ζέσιν τε καὶ ζύμωσιν ἐπίκλην λεχθῆναι.
beads.english: When moisture, hollow, is stretched around air, sometimes earthy moisture and sometimes also pure, these become moist vessels of air, hollow and round waters. Those of pure moisture stand around as transparent vessels, which are called by name bubbles.

beads.greek: τὸ τούτων αἴτιον τῶν παθημάτων ὀξὺ προσρηθῆναι.
beads.english: Those of earthy moisture, which is moved and raised at the same time, are called by the names boiling and fermentation. The cause of these affections is called sour.

greek_sentences: τὰ δὲ τῇ τοῦ στόματος θερμότητι κοινωνήσαντα καὶ λεαινόμενα ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ συνεκπυρούμενα καὶ πάλιν αὐτὰ ἀντικάοντα τὸ διαθερμῆναν, φερόμενά τε καὶ ὑπὸ κουφότητος ἄνω πρὸς τὰς τῆς κεφαλῆς [447] αἰσθήσεις, τέμνοντά τε πάνθ’ ὁπόσα ἂν προσπίπτῃ διὰ ταύτας τὰς δυνάμεις, δριμέα πάντα τὰ τοιαῦτα ἐλέχθη.

τῶν δὲ αὐτῶν προλελεπτυσμένων μὲν ὑπὸ σηπεδόνος, εἰς δὲ τὰς στενὰς φλέβας ἐνδυομένων καὶ ἐνοῦσιν αὐτόθι μέρεσι γεώδεσιν καὶ ὅσα ἀέρος συμμετρίαν ἔχοντα, ὥστε κινήσαντα περὶ ἄλληλα ποιεῖν κυκᾶσθαι, κυκώμενα δὲ περιπίπτειν τε καὶ εἰς ἕτερα ἐνδυόμενα ἕτερα κοῖλα ἀπεργάζεσθαι περιτεινόμενα τοῖς εἰσιοῦσιν, ἃ δὴ νοτίδος περὶ ἀέρα κοίλης περιταθείσης ποτὲ μὲν γεώδους, ποτὲ δὲ καὶ καθαρᾶς, νοτερὰ ἀγγεῖα ἀέρος ὕδατα κοῖλα περιφερῆ τε γενέσθαι καὶ τὰ μὲν τῆς καθαρᾶς εἰς διαφανεῖς περιστῆναι, κληθείσας ὄνομα πομφόλυγας, τὰ δὲ τῆς γεώδους, ὁμοῦ κινουμένης τε καὶ αἰρομένης, ζέσιν τε καὶ ζύμωσιν ἐπίκλην λεχθῆναι.
τὸ τούτων αἴτιον τῶν παθημάτων ὀξὺ προσρηθῆναι.
english_sentences: Those, again, which share in the heat of the mouth and are smoothed by it, which are set on fire along with it and in their turn burn back that which heated them, and which are also carried upward by their lightness towards the senses of the head [447], cutting everything they fall upon: on account of these powers all such things have been called pungent.

When the same things, having first been thinned by putrefaction, enter the narrow veins, and have a commensurateness with the earthy parts present there and with whatever parts of air are there, so that they set them moving about one another and cause them to be stirred up, they, being stirred up, fall around one another and, entering into one another, produce other hollows, stretching themselves around the things that enter.
When moisture, hollow, is stretched around air, sometimes earthy moisture and sometimes also pure, these become moist vessels of air, hollow and round waters.
Those of pure moisture stand around as transparent vessels, which are called by name bubbles.
Those of earthy moisture, which is moved and raised at the same time, are called by the names boiling and fermentation.
The cause of these affections is called sour.

beads.greek: ξύμπασι δὲ τοῖς περὶ ταῦτα εἰρημένοις πάθος ἐναντίον ἀπ’ ἐναντίας ἐστὶ προφάσεως, ὁπόταν ἡ τῶν εἰσιόντων ξύστασις ἐν ὑγροῖς, οἰκεία τῇ τῆς γλώττης ἕξει πεφυκυῖα, λεαίνῃ μὲν ἐπαλείφουσα τὰ τραχυνθέντα, τὰ δὲ παρὰ φύσιν συνεστῶτα ἢ κεχυμένα, τὰ μὲν [448] συνάγῃ, τὰ δὲ χαλῇ καὶ πάνθ’ ὅτι μάλιστα ἱδρύῃ κατὰ φύσιν, ἡδὺ καὶ προσφιλὲς παντὶ πᾶν τὸ τοιοῦτον ἴαμα τῶν βιαίων παθημάτων γιγνόμενον, κέκληται γλυκύ.
beads.english: To all the things that have been said about these there is an opposite affection, arising from an opposite cause, whenever the composition of what enters, in liquids, being by nature akin to the condition of the tongue, smooths by anointing the parts that have been roughened, and of the parts that are contrary to nature either compacted or diffused, the ones it [448] draws together, the others it relaxes, and settles all of them as far as possible according to nature: every such thing, becoming a remedy of the violent affections and being pleasant and agreeable to everyone, has been called sweet.

beads.greek: διὰ ταύτης ἁπάσης τῆς ῥήσεως ὁ Πλάτων ἐξηγήσατο τίνα μὲν ἔθος ἐστὶν ὀνομάζειν αὐστηρὰ, τίνα δὲ στρυφνὰ, καὶ τίνα μὲν ἁλυκὰ καὶ νιτρώδη, τίνα δὲ πικρὰ, καὶ τίνα μὲν δριμέα, τίνα δὲ ὀξέα, τίνα δὲ γλυκέα.
beads.english: Through this whole passage Plato explained which things it is customary to name harsh and which acerbic, which salty and nitrous and which bitter, and which pungent, which sour and which sweet; evidently calling 'harsh' what we call astringent, for so it was named among the ancient Greeks.

beads.greek: τὸ δὲ πρὸς ἡμῶν στῦφον αὐστηρὸν δηλονότι προσαγορεύων, οὕτω γὰρ ὠνομάζετο παρὰ τοῖς παλαιοῖς Ἕλλησιν. οὐ μὴν εἰς ταὐτόν γε συγχεῖ πάντα, καθάπερ οὗτοι, καὶ τὸ πέπερι στύφειν φάσκοντες ἐκ τῆς τῶν δριμέων φύσεως ὑπάρχον καὶ τὸ ὄξος ἐκ τῆς τῶν ὀξέων, οὐκ αἰδούμενοι δὲ καὶ τῶν γλυκυτάτων ἔνια τοῖς στύφουσι προσνέμειν.
beads.english: He does not, however, confound everything into the same thing, as these people do, who say that pepper is astringent, although it belongs to the nature of the pungent, and vinegar, although it belongs to that of the sour, and who are not ashamed to assign even some of the sweetest things to the astringents.

beads.greek: ἅτ’ οὖν ἁπάντων αὐτοῖς συγκεχυμένων, εὐθὺς κατ’ ἀρχὰς οὐδὲ δυνάμεις εὑρεθῆναι δύνανται.
beads.english: Since, then, everything is confounded by them, right at the outset not even powers can be discovered.

beads.greek: πάσης γὰρ εὑρέσεώς τε καὶ ἀποδείξεως ἀρχαὶ τὰ πρὸς αἴσθησίν τε καὶ νόησίν ἐστιν ἐναργῆ.
beads.english: For the starting-points of all discovery and demonstration are the things that are evident to perception and to understanding.

beads.greek: ταράττουσι δὲ οὗτοι ταῦτα ἀμφότερα καὶ συγχέουσιν εἰς ταὐτὸν ἅπαντα, τά τε τῶν αἰσθήσεων ἔργα τε καὶ πάθη καὶ πολὺ δὴ μᾶλλον ἔτι τὰ τῆς νοήσεως, [449] ἅτε μὴ γεγυμνασμένα κατὰ λογικὴν θεωρίαν, ὥστ’ ἔργον εἶναι φυλάξασθαι τὴν ἀδολεσχίαν αὐτῶν καὶ μὴ συναπολαῦσαί τι τῆς αὐτῶν οὕτω πολλῆς καὶ ματαίας φλυαρίας ἔργον δ’ οὐ σμικρὸν καὶ τὸ μεταδιδάξαι καὶ μεταλλάξαι τοὺς διεστραμμένους ὑπ’ αὐτῶν εἰς τοσοῦτον, ὡς καταφρονεῖν τε τῶν αἰσθήσεων, ἀγυμνάστους τε κατὰ λογικὴν εἶναι θεωρίαν, ἀνηκόους δὲ καὶ τῶν περὶ φύσεως λογισμῶν, οὓς οἱ φιλόσοφοι διασκέ πτονται.
beads.english: These men throw both of these into confusion and confound everything together, both the functions and the affections of the senses and, much more still, those of intellection, [449] inasmuch as they are not trained in logical theory. So it is a task to guard against their idle chatter and not to get some share of their so abundant and vain nonsense.

beads.greek: πάντως γὰρ ἄν που τό γε τοσοῦτον ἐπεγίνωσκον, ὧς δεδιέναι χρὴ καὶ φυλάττεσθαι τὰς ἐν αὐτοῖς ἀπορίας καὶ ταῖς αἰσθήσεσιν ἐπιτρέπειν μᾶλλον ἢ λόγοις κιβδήλοις ὑπὲρ τῆς τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων δυνάμεως.
beads.english: And it is no small task, too, to re-teach and change those who have been perverted by them to such a degree that they despise the senses, are untrained in logical theory, and have not even heard of the reasonings about nature which the philosophers investigate. For surely they would at least have recognised this much: that one must fear and guard against the difficulties (aporiai) in those reasonings, and must trust the senses rather than counterfeit arguments about the power of simple drugs.

beads.greek: Ἀλλὰ τοὺς μὲν τοιούτους οὐκ ἐγχωρεῖ μεταδιδάξαι· τῶν δ’ ἄλλων ἕνεκα τῶν ὠφεληθῆναι δυναμένων ἀναληπτέον ἐστὶν καὶ διοριστέον ἀκριβῶς τὸν περὶ τῶν ἰδίων τῆς γλώττης αἰσθητῶν λόγον.
beads.english: But it is not possible to re-teach such people. For the sake of the others, who are able to be benefited, we must take up again and define precisely the account concerning the sense-objects proper to the tongue.
