beads.greek: ὀνομάζεται μὲν οὖν ὑπὸ τῶν περὶ Θεόφραστόν τε καὶ Ἀριστοτέλην καὶ Μνησίθεον τὸν ἰατρὸν ἡ γευστὴ δύναμις χυμὸς, ἀπὸ τοῦ μ στοιχείου τῆς [450] δευτέρας συλλαβῆς ἀρχομένης. ἡ δ’ ἐξ ὑγροῦ καὶ ξηροῦ σύστασις ὑπὸ θερμότητος πεφθέντων χυλὸς, ἀπὸ τοῦ λ τῆς δευτέρας ἀρχομένης συλλαβῆς.
beads.english: Now by Theophrastus, Aristotle and Mnesitheus the physician, and those of their school, the gustatory power is named chymos, with the letter m beginning the [450] second syllable; but the consistency arising from moist and dry, when these have been concocted by heat, is named chylos, with l beginning the second syllable.

beads.greek: παρὰ μέντοι τοῖς παλαιοτέροις αὐτῶν οὐκ Ἀττικοῖς μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἴωσιν ἑκάτερα διὰ τοῦ μ γέγραπται.
beads.english: Among their older predecessors, however, not only the Attic writers but also the Ionians, both are written with m.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ καὶ παρὰ Πλάτωνι τῷ φιλοσόφῳ καὶ παρ’ Ἱπποκράτει καὶ παρὰ τοῖς παλαιοῖς κωμικοῖς οὕτως εὑρίσκεται.
beads.english: For it is found so in Plato the philosopher, in Hippocrates, and in the old comic poets.

beads.greek: ἰστέον οὖν ὡς οἱ μὲν καθ’ ἕκαστον φυτόν τε καὶ ζῶον, ἤδη δὲ καὶ οἱ κατὰ τὴν γῆν εὑρισκόμενοι χυμοὶ πάμπολλοί τινές εἰσι καὶ οὐκ εὐαρίθμητοι ταῖς ἰδέαις.
beads.english: It must be understood, then, that the chymoi found in each plant and animal, and indeed also those found in the earth, are very numerous and not easily counted in their kinds (ἰδέαις).

beads.greek: αἱ δ’ ἐν αὐτοῖς γευσταὶ διαφοραὶ τοῖς μὲν ὀκτὼ τὸν ἀριθμὸν ἔδοξαν εἶναι, τοῖς δὲ ἑπτὰ, τοῖς δὲ καὶ τούτων ἐλάττους.

beads.greek: ὁ μὲν οὖν Πλάτων ἐν Τιμαίῳ διὰ τῆς προγεγραμμένης ῥήσεως πρῶτον μὲν δυοῖν μέμνηται χυμῶν ὁμοειδῶν μὲν, ἀλλὰ τῷ μᾶλλόν τε καὶ ἧττον [451] διαφερόντων.
beads.english: Plato, then, in the Timaeus, in the passage quoted above, first mentions two flavours that are of the same kind but differ by more and less [451].

beads.greek: ὀνομάζει δ’ αὐτῶν τὸν μὲν αὐστηρὸν, τὸν δὲ στρυφνόν.
beads.english: He calls one of them harsh, the other acerbic.

beads.greek: εἴη δ’ ἂν ὁ μὲν αὐστηρὸς κατὰ τὸν ὑφ’ ἡμῶν στύφοντα προσαγορευόμενος, ὁ δὲ στρυφνὸς ἐπιτάσει τούτου γιγνόμενος, ὥσπερ οὖν καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Πλάτων ἐδήλωσεν.
beads.english: The harsh would correspond to the one we call astringent, while the acerbic arises from an intensification of it, just as Plato himself also made clear.

beads.greek: τούτους μὲν οὖν ὡς ἓν εἶδος ἀριθμητέον· ἕτερον δὲ τὸ τῶν ἀντικειμένων αὐτοῖς τῶν νιτρωδῶν τε καὶ ἁλυκῶν καὶ πικρῶν.
beads.english: These, then, must be counted as a single kind. Another kind is that of their opposites, the nitrous, the salty and the bitter.

beads.greek: ἔστι δὲ κᾀν τούτοις ὁ μὲν πικρὸς ἐξ ἐπιτάσεως τοῦ νιτρώδους γενόμενος, ὁ δὲ ἁλυκὸς ἤτοι τοῦ νιτρώδους ἀσθενέστερος, ἢ καὶ στύψεώς τι προσλαμβάνων.
beads.english: Among these too, the bitter arises from an intensification of the nitrous, while the salty is either weaker than the nitrous or else also takes on something of astringency.

beads.greek: ἑξῆς δὲ ὑπὸ Πλάτωνος μὲν ὁ δριμὺς εἴρηται καὶ μετ’ αὐτὸν ὁ ὀξὺς καὶ τελευταῖος ὁ γλυκύς.
beads.english: Next, Plato names the pungent, after it the sour, and last the sweet. Theophrastus also adds the oily.

beads.greek: ὑπὸ Θεοφράστου δὲ καὶ ὁ λιπαρὸς πρόσκειται, παραλελειμμένος μὲν ὑπὸ τοῦ Πλάτωνος ἐν τῷ περὶ τῶν τῆς γλώττης ἰδίων αἰσθητῶν λόγῳ, γεγραμμένος δ’ ἐν τοῖς τῶν φυτῶν χυλοῖς ἔμπροσθεν εὐθὺς, ἐν οἷς διῃρεῖτο τὸν οἰνώδη τοῦ ἐλαιώδους τε καὶ μελιτώδους.
beads.english: Plato omitted it in his account of the sensibles proper to the tongue, but had written of it shortly before, among the juices of plants, where he distinguished the wine-like from the oil-like and the honey-like.

beads.greek: ἀλλ’ ἐν ἐκείνῳ μὲν τῷ λόγῳ πρὸς τοῖς τρισὶν οἷς εἴρηκα νῦν τέταρτον ἐτίθει γένος χυμοῦ περιλαμβάνων ἑνὶ προσρήματι καὶ καλῶν ὀπόν.
beads.english: In that account, besides the three I have just named, he posited a fourth genus of juice, comprehending it under a single appellation and calling it 'sap' (opos).

beads.greek: ἐν οἷς δὲ ἐπὶ τὰ τῇ γεύσει αἰσθητὰ μετέβη, τοῦ μὲν γλυκέος εὐθὺς ἐν αὐτοῖς ἐμνημόνευσεν.
beads.english: But where he passed on to the things perceptible to taste, he at once mentioned the sweet among them.

greek_sentences: ὁ μὲν οὖν Πλάτων ἐν Τιμαίῳ διὰ τῆς προγεγραμμένης ῥήσεως πρῶτον μὲν δυοῖν μέμνηται χυμῶν ὁμοειδῶν μὲν, ἀλλὰ τῷ μᾶλλόν τε καὶ ἧττον [451] διαφερόντων.
ὀνομάζει δ’ αὐτῶν τὸν μὲν αὐστηρὸν, τὸν δὲ στρυφνόν.
εἴη δ’ ἂν ὁ μὲν αὐστηρὸς κατὰ τὸν ὑφ’ ἡμῶν στύφοντα προσαγορευόμενος, ὁ δὲ στρυφνὸς ἐπιτάσει τούτου γιγνόμενος, ὥσπερ οὖν καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Πλάτων ἐδήλωσεν.
τούτους μὲν οὖν ὡς ἓν εἶδος ἀριθμητέον· ἕτερον δὲ τὸ τῶν ἀντικειμένων αὐτοῖς τῶν νιτρωδῶν τε καὶ ἁλυκῶν καὶ πικρῶν.
ἔστι δὲ κᾀν τούτοις ὁ μὲν πικρὸς ἐξ ἐπιτάσεως τοῦ νιτρώδους γενόμενος, ὁ δὲ ἁλυκὸς ἤτοι τοῦ νιτρώδους ἀσθενέστερος, ἢ καὶ στύψεώς τι προσλαμβάνων.
ἑξῆς δὲ ὑπὸ Πλάτωνος μὲν ὁ δριμὺς εἴρηται καὶ μετ’ αὐτὸν ὁ ὀξὺς καὶ τελευταῖος ὁ γλυκύς.

ὑπὸ Θεοφράστου δὲ καὶ ὁ λιπαρὸς πρόσκειται, παραλελειμμένος μὲν ὑπὸ τοῦ Πλάτωνος ἐν τῷ περὶ τῶν τῆς γλώττης ἰδίων αἰσθητῶν λόγῳ, γεγραμμένος δ’ ἐν τοῖς τῶν φυτῶν χυλοῖς ἔμπροσθεν εὐθὺς, ἐν οἷς διῃρεῖτο τὸν οἰνώδη τοῦ ἐλαιώδους τε καὶ μελιτώδους.
ἀλλ’ ἐν ἐκείνῳ μὲν τῷ λόγῳ πρὸς τοῖς τρισὶν οἷς εἴρηκα νῦν τέταρτον ἐτίθει γένος χυμοῦ περιλαμβάνων ἑνὶ προσρήματι καὶ καλῶν ὀπόν.
ἐν οἷς δὲ ἐπὶ τὰ τῇ γεύσει αἰσθητὰ μετέβη, τοῦ μὲν γλυκέος εὐθὺς ἐν αὐτοῖς ἐμνημόνευσεν.
english_sentences: Plato, then, in the Timaeus, in the passage quoted above, first mentions two flavours that are of the same kind but differ by more and less [451].
He calls one of them harsh, the other acerbic.
The harsh would correspond to the one we call astringent, while the acerbic arises from an intensification of it, just as Plato himself also made clear.
These, then, must be counted as a single kind.
Another kind is that of their opposites, the nitrous, the salty and the bitter.
Among these too, the bitter arises from an intensification of the nitrous, while the salty is either weaker than the nitrous or else also takes on something of astringency.
Next, Plato names the pungent, after it the sour, and last the sweet.
Theophrastus also adds the oily.

Plato omitted it in his account of the sensibles proper to the tongue, but had written of it shortly before, among the juices of plants, where he distinguished the wine-like from the oil-like and the honey-like.
In that account, besides the three I have just named, he posited a fourth genus of juice, comprehending it under a single appellation and calling it 'sap' (opos).
But where he passed on to the things perceptible to taste, he at once mentioned the sweet among them.

beads.greek: οὐδὲν γὰρ διαφέρει δήπου γλυκὺ ἢ [452] μελιτῶδες φάναι, καθάπερ οὐδὲ λιπαρὸν ἢ ἐλαιῶδες.
beads.english: For it surely makes no difference whether one says 'sweet' or [452] 'honey-like', just as it makes none whether one says 'oily' or 'olive-oil-like'.

beads.greek: παραλέλοιπε δὲ τὸν λιπαρὸν ὡς οὐδὲν προσήκοντα τῇ γεύσει.
beads.english: But he has left out the oily as having nothing to do with taste.

beads.greek: Ἐρμηνεῦσαι μὲν ἀκριβῶς οὐχ οἷόν τε, διότι μηδ’ ἄλλο τι τῶν αἰσθητῶν παθῶν, ἀναμνῆσαι μέντοι τὸν τῆς αὐτῆς αἰσθήσεως κεκοινωνηκότα δυνατόν.
beads.english: To express it precisely is not possible, since neither can any other of the perceptible affections be so expressed; but it is possible to remind someone who has shared in the same sensation.

beads.greek: εἰ δέ τις ἐγεύσατό ποτε κυδωνίων, ἢ μήλων, ἢ μύρτων, ἢ μεσπίλων, οἶδε μὲν σαφῶς ἑτέραν μὲν τὴν ἀπὸ τούτων αἴσθησιν ἡμῖν ἐν τῇ γλώττῃ γιγνομένην, ἑτέραν δὲ τὴν ἀπὸ τῶν στυφόντων σωμάτων.
beads.english: If anyone has ever tasted quinces, or apples, or myrtle-berries, or medlars, he knows clearly that the sensation arising in us on the tongue from these is one thing, and that from astringent bodies another.

beads.greek: τὰ μὲν γὰρ στύφοντα ἢ ψύχοντα συνωθεῖν ἔσω φαίνεται τὸ ψαῦον ἡμῶν μόριον ἐκ παντὸς μέρους ὁμαλῶς, οἷον ὠθοῦντά τε καὶ πιλοῦντα καὶ συνάγοντα· τὰ δ’ αὐστηρὰ κατὰ βάθους τε διαδύεσθαι δοκεῖ καί τινα τραχεῖάν τε καὶ ἀνώμαλον αἴσθησιν ἐπάγειν, ὡς ἀναξηραίνοντα καὶ πᾶσαν ἐκβοσκόμενα τὴν ἰκμάδα τῶν αἰσθητικῶν σωμάτων, ὥσθ’ ἑτέραν εἶναι τὴν τῶν παθῶν ἰδιότητα, μηδὲ ῥηθῆναι σαφῶς δυναμένην, ἀπό τε τῶν στυφόντων ἡμᾶς σωμάτων καὶ τῶν αὐστηρῶν χυμῶν.
beads.english: For astringent or cooling things appear to press the part of us that touches them inward evenly from every side, as if pushing, compressing and drawing it together; whereas harsh things seem both to penetrate into the depth and to bring on a rough and uneven sensation, as if drying up and grazing away all the moisture of the sensing bodies. So the particular character of the affections produced in us by astringent bodies and by harsh flavours is different, and it cannot even be stated clearly.

greek_sentences: οὐδὲν γὰρ διαφέρει δήπου γλυκὺ ἢ [452] μελιτῶδες φάναι, καθάπερ οὐδὲ λιπαρὸν ἢ ἐλαιῶδες.
παραλέλοιπε δὲ τὸν λιπαρὸν ὡς οὐδὲν προσήκοντα τῇ γεύσει.

τὰ μὲν γὰρ στύφοντα ἢ ψύχοντα συνωθεῖν ἔσω φαίνεται τὸ ψαῦον ἡμῶν μόριον ἐκ παντὸς μέρους ὁμαλῶς, οἷον ὠθοῦντά τε καὶ πιλοῦντα καὶ συνάγοντα· τὰ δ’ αὐστηρὰ κατὰ βάθους τε διαδύεσθαι δοκεῖ καί τινα τραχεῖάν τε καὶ ἀνώμαλον αἴσθησιν ἐπάγειν, ὡς ἀναξηραίνοντα καὶ πᾶσαν ἐκβοσκόμενα τὴν ἰκμάδα τῶν αἰσθητικῶν σωμάτων, ὥσθ’ ἑτέραν εἶναι τὴν τῶν παθῶν ἰδιότητα, μηδὲ ῥηθῆναι σαφῶς δυναμένην, ἀπό τε τῶν στυφόντων ἡμᾶς σωμάτων καὶ τῶν αὐστηρῶν χυμῶν.

But he has left out the oily as having nothing to do with taste.
To express it precisely is not possible, since neither can any other of the perceptible affections be so expressed; but it is possible to remind someone who has shared in the same sensation.

If anyone has ever tasted quinces, or apples, or myrtle-berries, or medlars, he knows clearly that the sensation arising in us on the tongue from these is one thing, and that from astringent bodies another.

For astringent or cooling things appear to press the part of us that touches them inward evenly from every side, as if pushing, compressing and drawing it together; whereas harsh things seem both to penetrate into the depth and to bring on a rough and uneven sensation, as if drying up and grazing away all the moisture of the sensing bodies.
So the particular character of the affections produced in us by astringent bodies and by harsh flavours is different, and it cannot even be stated clearly.

beads.greek: ἀλλ’ ὅστις γε ἄνθρωπος νοῦν ἔχει οἶδεν [453] ὃ λέγω.
beads.english: But any man who has sense knows [453] what I mean.

beads.greek: ὅταν δὲ τὸ πλησιάζον τῇ γλώττῃ σῶμα σφοδρῶς ξηραίνῃ καὶ ξυνάγῃ καὶ τραχύνῃ μέχρι βάθους πλέονος αὐτὴν, ὥσπερ ἀχράδες ἄωροι καὶ κράνες στυφνὸν ἅπαν τὸ τοιοῦτον ὀνομάζεται, τῶν αὐστηρῶν ἐπιτάσει διαφέρον.
beads.english: When the body that comes into contact with the tongue dries it vehemently, draws it together and roughens it to a greater depth, as unripe wild pears and cornels do, everything of this kind is called acerbic, differing from the harsh by intensity.

beads.greek: ὃ δὲ καλοῦμεν ἡμεῖς στῦφον, οὐ πάνυ μέντοι πρὸς τῶν περὶ τὸν Θεόφραστον εὑρεῖν ἔστιν εἰρημένον.
beads.english: What we call astringent, however, is scarcely to be found mentioned by Theophrastus and his school.

beads.greek: ἔοικε δή τι ταὐτὸν δηλοῦν τῷ αὐστηρῷ, ἢ κοινὸν εἶναί τι γένος τούτου τε καὶ στρυφνοῦ.
beads.english: It seems either to signify the same thing as the harsh, or to be a genus common to this and to the acerbic.

beads.greek: ὅσα δ’ ἐν τῷ ψαύειν τῆς γλώττης οὐ συνάγει μὲν αὐτὴν, οὐδὲ σφίγγει καθάπερ τὰ στύφοντα, τὸ δ’ ἐναντίον ἅπαν φαίνεται ποιοῦντα, ῥύπτοντα καὶ ἀποπλύνοντα, κᾂν εἴ τι τῶν στυφόντων παρακέοιτο, ταῦτα σύμπαντα προσαγορεύομεν ἁλυκά.
beads.english: Those things which, in touching the tongue, do not draw it together, nor constrict it as astringents do, but appear to do entirely the opposite, cleansing and washing away even whatever of the astringents may be lying upon it, all these we call salty.

beads.greek: τὰ δ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον τούτων ῥύπτοντα, μέχρι τοῦ καὶ τραχύνειν ἀνιαρῶς, πικρὰ προσαγορεύεται.
beads.english: Those that cleanse still more than these, to the point of roughening it painfully, are called bitter.

beads.greek: τὰ δέ γε δάκνοντά τε καὶ διαβιβρώσκοντα μετὰ θερμότητος ἰσχυρᾶς δριμέα.
beads.english: Those that are biting and corroding with strong heat are called pungent.

beads.greek: τὰ δ’ ἄνευ αὐτῆς δάκνοντα καλεῖται μὲν ὀξέα, πρόσεστι δὲ αὐτοῖς καὶ τὸ ζυμοῦν.
beads.english: Those that are biting without it are called sour, and to these belongs also the property of leavening.

greek_sentences: ἀλλ’ ὅστις γε ἄνθρωπος νοῦν ἔχει οἶδεν [453] ὃ λέγω.

ὅταν δὲ τὸ πλησιάζον τῇ γλώττῃ σῶμα σφοδρῶς ξηραίνῃ καὶ ξυνάγῃ καὶ τραχύνῃ μέχρι βάθους πλέονος αὐτὴν, ὥσπερ ἀχράδες ἄωροι καὶ κράνες στυφνὸν ἅπαν τὸ τοιοῦτον ὀνομάζεται, τῶν αὐστηρῶν ἐπιτάσει διαφέρον.
ὃ δὲ καλοῦμεν ἡμεῖς στῦφον, οὐ πάνυ μέντοι πρὸς τῶν περὶ τὸν Θεόφραστον εὑρεῖν ἔστιν εἰρημένον.
ἔοικε δή τι ταὐτὸν δηλοῦν τῷ αὐστηρῷ, ἢ κοινὸν εἶναί τι γένος τούτου τε καὶ στρυφνοῦ.

ὅσα δ’ ἐν τῷ ψαύειν τῆς γλώττης οὐ συνάγει μὲν αὐτὴν, οὐδὲ σφίγγει καθάπερ τὰ στύφοντα, τὸ δ’ ἐναντίον ἅπαν φαίνεται ποιοῦντα, ῥύπτοντα καὶ ἀποπλύνοντα, κᾂν εἴ τι τῶν στυφόντων παρακέοιτο, ταῦτα σύμπαντα προσαγορεύομεν ἁλυκά.
τὰ δ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον τούτων ῥύπτοντα, μέχρι τοῦ καὶ τραχύνειν ἀνιαρῶς, πικρὰ προσαγορεύεται.
τὰ δέ γε δάκνοντά τε καὶ διαβιβρώσκοντα μετὰ θερμότητος ἰσχυρᾶς δριμέα.
τὰ δ’ ἄνευ αὐτῆς δάκνοντα καλεῖται μὲν ὀξέα, πρόσεστι δὲ αὐτοῖς καὶ τὸ ζυμοῦν.
english_sentences: But any man who has sense knows [453] what I mean.

When the body that comes into contact with the tongue dries it vehemently, draws it together and roughens it to a greater depth, as unripe wild pears and cornels do, everything of this kind is called acerbic, differing from the harsh by intensity.
What we call astringent, however, is scarcely to be found mentioned by Theophrastus and his school.
It seems either to signify the same thing as the harsh, or to be a genus common to this and to the acerbic.

Those things which, in touching the tongue, do not draw it together, nor constrict it as astringents do, but appear to do entirely the opposite, cleansing and washing away even whatever of the astringents may be lying upon it, all these we call salty.
Those that cleanse still more than these, to the point of roughening it painfully, are called bitter.
Those that are biting and corroding with strong heat are called pungent.
Those that are biting without it are called sour, and to these belongs also the property of leavening.

beads.greek: ὅσα δ’ οἷον ἐπαλείφει τε καὶ ἀναπληροῖ καὶ καθίστησι τὰ τετραχυμένα τε καὶ οἷον διαβεβρωμένα τῆς [454] γλώττης μόρια, ταῦτα μετὰ μὲν ἡδονῆς ἐναργοῦς ψαύοντα γλυκέα, χωρὶς δὲ ταύτης λιπαρὰ προσαγορεύεται.
beads.english: Those things which, as it were, smear over, fill up and restore the roughened and, as it were, eaten-through parts of the [454] tongue are called sweet when they touch it with manifest pleasure, and oily when they do so without it.

beads.greek: ἐγὼ μὲν οὖν, ὡς οἷόν τέ μοι μάλιστα λόγῳ διελθεῖν ἐπεχείρησα δυσερμήνευτα πράγματα.
beads.english: I, then, have attempted to set out in words, as far as I possibly could, matters that are hard to express.

beads.greek: θαυμάζω δὲ τῶν ἑτοίμως ἅπαντα στύφοντα προσαγορευόντων, καὶ τὰ δριμέα καὶ τὰ πικρὰ καὶ τὰ γλυκέα καὶ τὰ λιπαρὰ καὶ τὰ ὀξέα.
beads.english: But I am astonished at those who readily call everything astringent: the pungent, the bitter, the sweet, the oily and the sour.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ ὀνόματα διαφέροντα κεῖται τοῖς πράγμασιν εὐθὺς ἐκ παλαιοῦ καὶ τῶν αἰσθητῶν παθῶν. οὐ σμικρά τις ἡμῖν ἐστιν ἡ διαφορά.
beads.english: For different names have been assigned to these things from ancient times, and the difference among the perceptible affections is no small one for us.

beads.greek: βέλτιον δ’ ἦν ἴσως, εἶπερ ἐβούλοντο φυσιολογεῖν, οὐκ ἀνατρέπειν τὰ φαινόμενα καὶ συγχεῖν τὰς προσηγορίας, ἀλλὰ ζητῆσαι τίνος μὲν κράσεως ἢ διαθέσεως, ἢ κατασκευῆς σώματος, ἢ ὅπως ὀνομάζειν ἐθέλωσιν, ἔγγονος γίνεται στύψις, τίνος δ’ ἁλυκότης καὶ πικρότης ὀξύτης τε καὶ δριμύτης καὶ γλυκύτης καὶ λιπαρότης, ἅπερ οἱ περὶ Πλάτωνά τε καὶ Ἀριστοτέλην καὶ Θεόφραστον ἐπειράθησαν διορίσασθαι.
beads.english: It would perhaps have been better, if they wished to study nature, not to overturn the phenomena and confound the appellations, but to seek of what mixture or condition or constitution of body (or however they may wish to name it) astringency is the offspring, and of what saltiness and bitterness, sourness and pungency, sweetness and oiliness are the offspring. These are the very things that Plato, Aristotle and Theophrastus attempted to define.

greek_sentences: ὅσα δ’ οἷον ἐπαλείφει τε καὶ ἀναπληροῖ καὶ καθίστησι τὰ τετραχυμένα τε καὶ οἷον διαβεβρωμένα τῆς [454] γλώττης μόρια, ταῦτα μετὰ μὲν ἡδονῆς ἐναργοῦς ψαύοντα γλυκέα, χωρὶς δὲ ταύτης λιπαρὰ προσαγορεύεται.
ἐγὼ μὲν οὖν, ὡς οἷόν τέ μοι μάλιστα λόγῳ διελθεῖν ἐπεχείρησα δυσερμήνευτα πράγματα.
θαυμάζω δὲ τῶν ἑτοίμως ἅπαντα στύφοντα προσαγορευόντων, καὶ τὰ δριμέα καὶ τὰ πικρὰ καὶ τὰ γλυκέα καὶ τὰ λιπαρὰ καὶ τὰ ὀξέα.
καὶ γὰρ ὀνόματα διαφέροντα κεῖται τοῖς πράγμασιν εὐθὺς ἐκ παλαιοῦ καὶ τῶν αἰσθητῶν παθῶν.
οὐ σμικρά τις ἡμῖν ἐστιν ἡ διαφορά.

βέλτιον δ’ ἦν ἴσως, εἶπερ ἐβούλοντο φυσιολογεῖν, οὐκ ἀνατρέπειν τὰ φαινόμενα καὶ συγχεῖν τὰς προσηγορίας, ἀλλὰ ζητῆσαι τίνος μὲν κράσεως ἢ διαθέσεως, ἢ κατασκευῆς σώματος, ἢ ὅπως ὀνομάζειν ἐθέλωσιν, ἔγγονος γίνεται στύψις, τίνος δ’ ἁλυκότης καὶ πικρότης ὀξύτης τε καὶ δριμύτης καὶ γλυκύτης καὶ λιπαρότης, ἅπερ οἱ περὶ Πλάτωνά τε καὶ Ἀριστοτέλην καὶ Θεόφραστον ἐπειράθησαν διορίσασθαι.
english_sentences: Those things which, as it were, smear over, fill up and restore the roughened and, as it were, eaten-through parts of the [454] tongue are called sweet when they touch it with manifest pleasure, and oily when they do so without it.
I, then, have attempted to set out in words, as far as I possibly could, matters that are hard to express.
But I am astonished at those who readily call everything astringent: the pungent, the bitter, the sweet, the oily and the sour.
For different names have been assigned to these things from ancient times, and the difference among the perceptible affections is no small one for us.

It would perhaps have been better, if they wished to study nature, not to overturn the phenomena and confound the appellations, but to seek of what mixture or condition or constitution of body (or however they may wish to name it) astringency is the offspring, and of what saltiness and bitterness, sourness and pungency, sweetness and oiliness are the offspring.
These are the very things that Plato, Aristotle and Theophrastus attempted to define.

beads.greek: δῆλον γὰρ ὡς εἴπερ ἐκ θερμοῦ καὶ ψυχροῦ καὶ ξηροῦ καὶ ὑγροῦ συνιόντων κέκραται πάντα, καὶ τῶν εἰρημένων ἑκάστη ποιότης ἐκ τῆς τούτων κράσεώς [455] ἐστιν.
beads.english: For it is clear that, if all things have been mixed from hot, cold, dry and moist coming together, each of the qualities mentioned also arises from the mixture [455] of these.

beads.greek: εἰ μὲν οὖν ὅπως τῶν εἰρημένων ἕκαστος γίνηται χυμῶν ἐπιχειροῖεν ἐξηγεῖσθαι, κᾂν ἡδέως ἐπακούσαιμι καὶ χάριν γνοίην αὐτοῖς οὐ μικράν.
beads.english: If, then, they were to attempt to explain how each of the flavours mentioned comes about, I would gladly listen to them and would feel no small gratitude towards them.

beads.greek: εἰ δὲ οὐδὲ τοῦτο ποιοῦσιν, ἔτι τε συγχέουσιν εἰς ταὐτὸν ἁπάσας τὰς αἰσθητὰς διαφορὰς, ὡς κινδυνεύειν ἅπαντα τὰ σώματα στύφοντα προσαγορεύειν, οὔτ’ ἂν αὐτοὺς ἐπακούειν ἐθέλοιμι, κᾀκείνους ἂν εὐξαίμην παύσασθαι ματαίου φιλονεικίας.
beads.english: But if they do not even do this, and moreover confound all the perceptible differences into one and the same thing, so that they run the risk of calling all bodies astringent, I would not wish to listen to them, and I would pray that they too might cease from their vain contentiousness.

beads.greek: Ἀλλ’ ἡμεῖς μὲν ἐν τοῖς μετὰ ταῦτα πειρασόμεθα δεῖξαι τίνος ἕκαστος τῶν χυμῶν ἐστι κράσεως ἔγγονος.
beads.english: But we, in what follows, shall try to show of what mixture each of the flavours is the offspring.

beads.greek: ἐν δὲ τῷ παρόντι τὸ χρήσιμον εἰς τὴν τέχνην αὐτὸ μόνον ἐθίσαι βούλομαι, πρότερον ἐκλέγειν τοὺς μανθάνοντας ἐπὶ τὴν πεῖραν ἐρχομένους, ἐπειδὰν κρῖναι βουληθῶσιν ὅπως ἡμᾶς ἕκαστον τῶν φαρμάκων διατίθησιν.
beads.english: For the present I wish only to accustom the learners, as they come to the test of experience, first to pick out just that which is useful for the art, whenever they wish to judge how each of the drugs disposes us.

beads.greek: οὐ γὰρ δὴ καθ’ αὑτό γε καὶ πρὸς τὴν ὅλην φύσιν ὁποῖόν ἐστιν ἐπισκεπτόμεθα.
beads.english: For we are certainly not examining what sort of thing it is in itself and in relation to nature as a whole.

beads.greek: δῆλον γὰρ ὡς οὕτω μὲν οὔτ’ ἂν ὄξος οὔτε θάλαττα λέγοιτο ξηραῖνον ἡμᾶς, ἢ ξηρὸν εἶναι τὴν δύναμιν.
beads.english: For it is clear that in this way neither vinegar nor sea-water could be said to dry us, or to be dry in power.

greek_sentences: δῆλον γὰρ ὡς εἴπερ ἐκ θερμοῦ καὶ ψυχροῦ καὶ ξηροῦ καὶ ὑγροῦ συνιόντων κέκραται πάντα, καὶ τῶν εἰρημένων ἑκάστη ποιότης ἐκ τῆς τούτων κράσεώς [455] ἐστιν.
εἰ μὲν οὖν ὅπως τῶν εἰρημένων ἕκαστος γίνηται χυμῶν ἐπιχειροῖεν ἐξηγεῖσθαι, κᾂν ἡδέως ἐπακούσαιμι καὶ χάριν γνοίην αὐτοῖς οὐ μικράν.

εἰ δὲ οὐδὲ τοῦτο ποιοῦσιν, ἔτι τε συγχέουσιν εἰς ταὐτὸν ἁπάσας τὰς αἰσθητὰς διαφορὰς, ὡς κινδυνεύειν ἅπαντα τὰ σώματα στύφοντα προσαγορεύειν, οὔτ’ ἂν αὐτοὺς ἐπακούειν ἐθέλοιμι, κᾀκείνους ἂν εὐξαίμην παύσασθαι ματαίου φιλονεικίας.
Ἀλλ’ ἡμεῖς μὲν ἐν τοῖς μετὰ ταῦτα πειρασόμεθα δεῖξαι τίνος ἕκαστος τῶν χυμῶν ἐστι κράσεως ἔγγονος.

ἐν δὲ τῷ παρόντι τὸ χρήσιμον εἰς τὴν τέχνην αὐτὸ μόνον ἐθίσαι βούλομαι, πρότερον ἐκλέγειν τοὺς μανθάνοντας ἐπὶ τὴν πεῖραν ἐρχομένους, ἐπειδὰν κρῖναι βουληθῶσιν ὅπως ἡμᾶς ἕκαστον τῶν φαρμάκων διατίθησιν.
οὐ γὰρ δὴ καθ’ αὑτό γε καὶ πρὸς τὴν ὅλην φύσιν ὁποῖόν ἐστιν ἐπισκεπτόμεθα.
δῆλον γὰρ ὡς οὕτω μὲν οὔτ’ ἂν ὄξος οὔτε θάλαττα λέγοιτο ξηραῖνον ἡμᾶς, ἢ ξηρὸν εἶναι τὴν δύναμιν.
english_sentences: For it is clear that, if all things have been mixed from hot, cold, dry and moist coming together, each of the qualities mentioned also arises from the mixture [455] of these.
If, then, they were to attempt to explain how each of the flavours mentioned comes about, I would gladly listen to them and would feel no small gratitude towards them.

But if they do not even do this, and moreover confound all the perceptible differences into one and the same thing, so that they run the risk of calling all bodies astringent, I would not wish to listen to them, and I would pray that they too might cease from their vain contentiousness.
But we, in what follows, shall try to show of what mixture each of the flavours is the offspring.

For the present I wish only to accustom the learners, as they come to the test of experience, first to pick out just that which is useful for the art, whenever they wish to judge how each of the drugs disposes us.
For we are certainly not examining what sort of thing it is in itself and in relation to nature as a whole.
For it is clear that in this way neither vinegar nor sea-water could be said to dry us, or to be dry in power.

beads.greek: ἐνεργείᾳ γάρ ἐστιν ἑκάτερον αὐτῶν ὑγρὸν, ἀλλ’ ἐὰν ξηραίνειν ἡμᾶς [456] φαίνηται, ξηρὰ λεχθήσεται πρὸς ἡμᾶς δηλονότι καὶ τὴν ἡμετέραν φύσιν, ἐν ἴσῳ τῷ ξηραντικά.
beads.english: For each of them is moist in actuality; but if it appears to dry us, [456] it will be called dry, evidently in relation to us and to our nature, equivalent to 'drying'.

beads.greek: καὶ δὴ καὶ θερμὰ καὶ ψυχρὰ καὶ ὑγρὰ κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον, ὅταν ἡμᾶς θερμαίνῃ καὶ ψύχῃ καὶ ὑγραίνῃ, λεχθήσεται πρὸς ἡμᾶς, οὐ πρὸς τὴν ὅλην οὐσίαν, οὐδὲ καθ’ ἑαυτά.
beads.english: And indeed, in the same way, things will be called hot, cold and moist when they heat, cool and moisten us: in relation to us, not in relation to the whole of substance, nor in themselves.

beads.greek: καὶ μὴν εἴπερ τούτου μόνου μνημονεύοιμεν, ἡ πεῖρα μόνη κριτήριον ἁπάντων ἔσται βεβαιότατον, ὥσθ’ ὅσαι ταύτην καταλιπόντες ἑτέρωθεν ἐπιχειροῦσιν οὐ ψεύδονται μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ χρήσιμον ἀνατρέπουσι τῆς πραγματείας.
beads.english: And indeed, if we keep this alone in mind, experience alone will be the most secure criterion of all, so that those who abandon it and argue from elsewhere not only speak falsely but also overturn what is useful in the inquiry.

beads.greek: ἡμῖν γὰρ οὐχ οἷόν τι κατὰ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ φύσιν ἕκαστον τῶν φαρμάκων ἐστὶ πρόκειται ζητεῖν, ἀλλ’ οἷόν τι δρᾷν πέφυκεν εἰς ἡμᾶς.
beads.english: For our task is not to investigate what each of the drugs is in its own nature, but what it is naturally disposed to do to us.

beads.greek: ὁ μὲν δὴ πρῶτός μοι λόγος ἐνταυθοῖ τελευτάτω.
beads.english: So let my first book end here.

beads.greek: κατὰ δὲ τὸν ἐφεξῆς ἔτι τὸν δεύτερον, ἔλαιόν τε καὶ ῥόδινον ἐν παραδείγματι τῷ λόγῳ προχειρισάμενος ἐπιδείξω κᾀνταῦθα τὰς μοχθηρὰς ὁδοὺς τῶν ἐπιχειρημάτων, αἷς οἱ πολλοὶ τῶν ἰατρῶν χρώμενοι παραλογίζονται σφᾶς μὲν αὑτοὺς πρῶτον, σὺν ἑαυτοῖς δ’ ἤδη καὶ ἄλλους πολλούς.
beads.english: In the next, the second, taking oil and rose oil as an example for the discussion, I shall show here too the faulty paths of argument. Most physicians use these paths and so mislead first themselves, and then, along with themselves, many others as well.

greek_sentences: ἐνεργείᾳ γάρ ἐστιν ἑκάτερον αὐτῶν ὑγρὸν, ἀλλ’ ἐὰν ξηραίνειν ἡμᾶς [456] φαίνηται, ξηρὰ λεχθήσεται πρὸς ἡμᾶς δηλονότι καὶ τὴν ἡμετέραν φύσιν, ἐν ἴσῳ τῷ ξηραντικά.
καὶ δὴ καὶ θερμὰ καὶ ψυχρὰ καὶ ὑγρὰ κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον, ὅταν ἡμᾶς θερμαίνῃ καὶ ψύχῃ καὶ ὑγραίνῃ, λεχθήσεται πρὸς ἡμᾶς, οὐ πρὸς τὴν ὅλην οὐσίαν, οὐδὲ καθ’ ἑαυτά.

καὶ μὴν εἴπερ τούτου μόνου μνημονεύοιμεν, ἡ πεῖρα μόνη κριτήριον ἁπάντων ἔσται βεβαιότατον, ὥσθ’ ὅσαι ταύτην καταλιπόντες ἑτέρωθεν ἐπιχειροῦσιν οὐ ψεύδονται μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ χρήσιμον ἀνατρέπουσι τῆς πραγματείας.
ἡμῖν γὰρ οὐχ οἷόν τι κατὰ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ φύσιν ἕκαστον τῶν φαρμάκων ἐστὶ πρόκειται ζητεῖν, ἀλλ’ οἷόν τι δρᾷν πέφυκεν εἰς ἡμᾶς.
ὁ μὲν δὴ πρῶτός μοι λόγος ἐνταυθοῖ τελευτάτω.

κατὰ δὲ τὸν ἐφεξῆς ἔτι τὸν δεύτερον, ἔλαιόν τε καὶ ῥόδινον ἐν παραδείγματι τῷ λόγῳ προχειρισάμενος ἐπιδείξω κᾀνταῦθα τὰς μοχθηρὰς ὁδοὺς τῶν ἐπιχειρημάτων, αἷς οἱ πολλοὶ τῶν ἰατρῶν χρώμενοι παραλογίζονται σφᾶς μὲν αὑτοὺς πρῶτον, σὺν ἑαυτοῖς δ’ ἤδη καὶ ἄλλους πολλούς.
english_sentences: For each of them is moist in actuality; but if it appears to dry us, [456] it will be called dry, evidently in relation to us and to our nature, equivalent to 'drying'.
And indeed, in the same way, things will be called hot, cold and moist when they heat, cool and moisten us: in relation to us, not in relation to the whole of substance, nor in themselves.

And indeed, if we keep this alone in mind, experience alone will be the most secure criterion of all, so that those who abandon it and argue from elsewhere not only speak falsely but also overturn what is useful in the inquiry.
For our task is not to investigate what each of the drugs is in its own nature, but what it is naturally disposed to do to us.
So let my first book end here.
In the next, the second, taking oil and rose oil as an example for the discussion, I shall show here too the faulty paths of argument.
Most physicians use these paths and so mislead first themselves, and then, along with themselves, many others as well.

beads.greek: ἐπειδὰν δὲ τοῦτο περανθῇ, μεταβὰς ἐπὶ τὸ τρίτον τῶνδε τῶν ὑπομνημάτων, ὅσα λογικὰ [457] ζητήματα προηγεῖται τῆς περὶ τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων ἁπάσης διεξόδου, ταῦτα πειράσομαι διελθεῖν, ὥστε κατὰ τὸ τέταρτον αὐτὰς ἤδη τὰς δυνάμεις ἁπάντων διορίζειν, ὧν εὐθὺς ἂν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἡψάμην, εἰ μὴ μεστὰ παραλογισμῶν ἦν σχεδὸν ἅπαντα τὰ τῶν νεωτέρων ἰατρῶν βιβλία.
beads.english: And when this has been brought to completion, I shall pass on to the third of these commentaries and try to go through all the logical questions [457] that precede the whole exposition concerning simple drugs, so that in the fourth I may at last define the powers themselves of all of them. I would have taken these up straight from the beginning, had not almost all the books of the more recent physicians been full of paralogisms.

beads.greek: τούτους οὖν ἐκκαθᾶραί τε καὶ ἀποσκευάσασθαι χρὴ πρῶτον ἐκ τῆς τοῦ μανθάνοντος ψυχῆς, ὅπως μηδὲν ἐμποδίζοιεν τοῖς ἀληθέσιν.
beads.english: These, then, must first be cleansed out and cleared away from the soul of the learner, so that they may in no way obstruct the truths.

beads.greek: ὡς γὰρ Ἱπποκράτης φησὶν, οὕτω καὶ Πλάτων ἔλεγεν· οὐ μόνον τὰ μὴ καθαρὰ σώματα, ὁπόσῳ ἂν θρέψῃς μᾶλλον βλάψεις, ἀλλὰ καὶ ταῖς ἀκαθάρτοις ψυχαῖς, εἰ τροφίμους προσφέρεις λόγους, οὐ μόνον οὐδὲν ὠφελήσῃς ἂν, ἀλλὰ καὶ βλάψεις οὐ σμικρά.
beads.english: For as Hippocrates says, so Plato too used to say: not only with bodies that are not pure, the more you nourish them, the more you will harm them; but also to impure souls, if you offer nourishing discourses, not only would you benefit them in nothing, but you will also harm them in no small degree.

greek_sentences: ἐπειδὰν δὲ τοῦτο περανθῇ, μεταβὰς ἐπὶ τὸ τρίτον τῶνδε τῶν ὑπομνημάτων, ὅσα λογικὰ [457] ζητήματα προηγεῖται τῆς περὶ τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων ἁπάσης διεξόδου, ταῦτα πειράσομαι διελθεῖν, ὥστε κατὰ τὸ τέταρτον αὐτὰς ἤδη τὰς δυνάμεις ἁπάντων διορίζειν, ὧν εὐθὺς ἂν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἡψάμην, εἰ μὴ μεστὰ παραλογισμῶν ἦν σχεδὸν ἅπαντα τὰ τῶν νεωτέρων ἰατρῶν βιβλία.
τούτους οὖν ἐκκαθᾶραί τε καὶ ἀποσκευάσασθαι χρὴ πρῶτον ἐκ τῆς τοῦ μανθάνοντος ψυχῆς, ὅπως μηδὲν ἐμποδίζοιεν τοῖς ἀληθέσιν.

ὡς γὰρ Ἱπποκράτης φησὶν, οὕτω καὶ Πλάτων ἔλεγεν· οὐ μόνον τὰ μὴ καθαρὰ σώματα, ὁπόσῳ ἂν θρέψῃς μᾶλλον βλάψεις, ἀλλὰ καὶ ταῖς ἀκαθάρτοις ψυχαῖς, εἰ τροφίμους προσφέρεις λόγους, οὐ μόνον οὐδὲν ὠφελήσῃς ἂν, ἀλλὰ καὶ βλάψεις οὐ σμικρά.
english_sentences: And when this has been brought to completion, I shall pass on to the third of these commentaries and try to go through all the logical questions [457] that precede the whole exposition concerning simple drugs, so that in the fourth I may at last define the powers themselves of all of them.
I would have taken these up straight from the beginning, had not almost all the books of the more recent physicians been full of paralogisms.
These, then, must first be cleansed out and cleared away from the soul of the learner, so that they may in no way obstruct the truths.

For as Hippocrates says, so Plato too used to say: not only with bodies that are not pure, the more you nourish them, the more you will harm them; but also to impure souls, if you offer nourishing discourses, not only would you benefit them in nothing, but you will also harm them in no small degree.

beads.greek: διὰ ταῦτα μὲν οὖν αὐτὰ καὶ ὅτι πολλοὶ τῶν ἑταίρων ἐξελεγχθῆναι τοὺς παραλογισμοὺς τῶν νεωτέρων ἰατρῶν ἠβουλήθησαν, οὐκ ἐν ταῖς συνουσίαις μόνον ἃς ἑκάστοτε ποιούμεθα συνδιατρίβοντες αὐτοῖς, ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ τῶνδε τῶν ὑπομνημάτων, ἀνάγκην ἔσχον ἐπιπλέον ἐγχρονίσαι τοῖς πρώτοις δύο βιβλίοις, ἵνα ἐν τῷ τρίτῳ καθαρὸν ἤδη τῇ ψυχῇ τὸν ἀκροατὴν ἔχων καὶ δυνάμενον ἕπεσθαι τοῖς ἀληθέσι λόγοις, ὅσα τε χρὴ περὶ τῶν ἀρχῶν τῆς προκειμένης ἡμῖν [458] θεωρίας ἐγνωκέναι διέλθω, μετὰ ταῦτά τε τῶν φαρμάκων ἑκάστου πάσας ἐπέλθω τὰς δυνάμεις.
beads.english: For these very reasons, then, and because many of my companions wished the paralogisms of the more recent physicians to be refuted not only in the meetings which we hold on each occasion when spending time with them, but also through these commentaries, I was compelled to linger at greater length over the first two books. My purpose was that in the third, having by then a hearer pure in soul and able to follow true arguments, I might go through everything that one must know about the principles of the theory set before us [458], and after that might go over all the powers of each of the drugs.

beads.greek: ἔσται δὲ τοῦτο διὰ βιβλίων, ὡς οἶμαι, τῶν πάντων ἕνδεκα τηλικούτων μάλιστα τὸ μέγεθος ἡλίκον καὶ τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ πάντων πρῶτον.
beads.english: This will be done, as I think, in eleven books in all, each of very much the same size as this one also is, the first of them all.

beads.greek: ᾧ μέτρον ἤδη τὸ δέον ἔχοντι τελευτὴν ἐπιτίθημι ταύτην αὐτῷ τὴν ῥῆσιν.
beads.english: And since this book already has its due measure, I place this very statement upon it as its ending.

greek_sentences: διὰ ταῦτα μὲν οὖν αὐτὰ καὶ ὅτι πολλοὶ τῶν ἑταίρων ἐξελεγχθῆναι τοὺς παραλογισμοὺς τῶν νεωτέρων ἰατρῶν ἠβουλήθησαν, οὐκ ἐν ταῖς συνουσίαις μόνον ἃς ἑκάστοτε ποιούμεθα συνδιατρίβοντες αὐτοῖς, ἀλλὰ καὶ διὰ τῶνδε τῶν ὑπομνημάτων, ἀνάγκην ἔσχον ἐπιπλέον ἐγχρονίσαι τοῖς πρώτοις δύο βιβλίοις, ἵνα ἐν τῷ τρίτῳ καθαρὸν ἤδη τῇ ψυχῇ τὸν ἀκροατὴν ἔχων καὶ δυνάμενον ἕπεσθαι τοῖς ἀληθέσι λόγοις, ὅσα τε χρὴ περὶ τῶν ἀρχῶν τῆς προκειμένης ἡμῖν [458] θεωρίας ἐγνωκέναι διέλθω, μετὰ ταῦτά τε τῶν φαρμάκων ἑκάστου πάσας ἐπέλθω τὰς δυνάμεις.
ἔσται δὲ τοῦτο διὰ βιβλίων, ὡς οἶμαι, τῶν πάντων ἕνδεκα τηλικούτων μάλιστα τὸ μέγεθος ἡλίκον καὶ τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ πάντων πρῶτον.
ᾧ μέτρον ἤδη τὸ δέον ἔχοντι τελευτὴν ἐπιτίθημι ταύτην αὐτῷ τὴν ῥῆσιν.
english_sentences: For these very reasons, then, and because many of my companions wished the paralogisms of the more recent physicians to be refuted not only in the meetings which we hold on each occasion when spending time with them, but also through these commentaries, I was compelled to linger at greater length over the first two books.

My purpose was that in the third, having by then a hearer pure in soul and able to follow true arguments, I might go through everything that one must know about the principles of the theory set before us [458], and after that might go over all the powers of each of the drugs.
This will be done, as I think, in eleven books in all, each of very much the same size as this one also is, the first of them all.
And since this book already has its due measure, I place this very statement upon it as its ending.

beads.greek: [459] ΓΑΛΗΝΟΥ ΠΕΡΙ ΚΡΑΣΕΩς ΚΑΙ ΛΥΝΑΜΕΩς ΤΩΝ ΑΠΛΩΝ ΦΑΡΜΑΚΩΝ ΒΙΒΛΙΟΝ Β.
beads.english: [459] GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK II.

beads.greek: Οἱ τοὺς οἰκείους ὅρους ὑπερβαίνοντες σοφισταὶ μακρὸν ἡμῖν ποιοῦσιν τὸν περὶ τῆς τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων δυνάμεως λόγον.
beads.english: The sophists who overstep their proper bounds make our account of the power of simple drugs a long one.

beads.greek: πόῤῥωθεν γὰρ ἀρχόμενοι καὶ τὴν αἴσθησιν ἀτιμάζοντες, ἐμβάλλοντές τε σφᾶς αὑτοὺς εἰς τὰ καὶ ἐν τοῖς φιλοσόφοις ἠπορημένα, προσαπολλύουσιν οἷς ἀγνοοῦσιν καὶ τὰ σαφῶς γινωσκόμενα.
beads.english: For by beginning from far back and slighting sense-perception, and by throwing themselves into questions that remain unresolved even among the philosophers, they ruin, along with the things they do not know, the things that are clearly known as well.

greek_sentences: [459] ΓΑΛΗΝΟΥ ΠΕΡΙ ΚΡΑΣΕΩς ΚΑΙ ΛΥΝΑΜΕΩς ΤΩΝ ΑΠΛΩΝ ΦΑΡΜΑΚΩΝ ΒΙΒΛΙΟΝ Β.
Οἱ τοὺς οἰκείους ὅρους ὑπερβαίνοντες σοφισταὶ μακρὸν ἡμῖν ποιοῦσιν τὸν περὶ τῆς τῶν ἁπλῶν φαρμάκων δυνάμεως λόγον.
πόῤῥωθεν γὰρ ἀρχόμενοι καὶ τὴν αἴσθησιν ἀτιμάζοντες, ἐμβάλλοντές τε σφᾶς αὑτοὺς εἰς τὰ καὶ ἐν τοῖς φιλοσόφοις ἠπορημένα, προσαπολλύουσιν οἷς ἀγνοοῦσιν καὶ τὰ σαφῶς γινωσκόμενα.
english_sentences: [459] GALEN, ON THE MIXTURE AND POWER OF SIMPLE DRUGS, BOOK II.
The sophists who overstep their proper bounds make our account of the power of simple drugs a long one.

For by beginning from far back and slighting sense-perception, and by throwing themselves into questions that remain unresolved even among the philosophers, they ruin, along with the things they do not know, the things that are clearly known as well.

beads.greek: καὶ ταῦτα ποιοῦσιν οἱ πλείους αὐτῶν ἀμαθεῖς ὑπάρχοντες οὐ τῆς φυσικῆς θεωρίας [460] μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν λογικῶν μεθόδων, αἷς ἀναγκαῖον ἐστιν χρῆσθαι τὸν ὁτιοῦν ἀποδείξαντα, ὥστε μήθ’ ὅσα καλῶς εὕρηται τοῖς φυσικοῖς ἀνδράσιν μήθ’ ὑπὲρ ὧν αὐτῶν εὐλόγως ἠπόρηται γινώσκοντες, ἑκατέροις πολλάκις ἀποφαίνεσθαι τολμῶσι τἀναντία.
beads.english: And most of them do this while being ignorant not only of natural theory [460] but also of the logical methods which anyone who demonstrates anything whatsoever must necessarily use; so that, knowing neither what has been rightly discovered by the natural philosophers nor the very points about which these men have reasonably been in doubt, they often dare to declare the opposite in both cases. Come now, by the gods: suppose I now began to speak in some such way as this: that, there being four elements, air and earth and water and fire, the white and bright colour is innate in nothing else except light and fire.

beads.greek: φέρε δὲ ὦ πρὸς θεῶν, εἴπερ ἐγὼ νῦν ἀρξάμενος ὧδέ πως λέγειν, ὡς τεττάρων ὄντων στοιχείων ἀέρος καὶ γῆς ὕδατός τε καὶ πυρὸς, ὡς οὐδενὸς ἄλλου ξύμφυτόν ἐστι τὸ λευκὸν καὶ λαμπρὸν χρῶμα, πλὴν αὐγῆς καὶ πυρὸς, εἶτα καὶ τὸν Ἐμπεδοκλέα καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους τινας τῶν φυσικῶν ἐπὶ τῷ λόγῳ καλέσας μάρτυρας, ἅπαντα τὰ λαμπρὰ σώματα πυρὸς πλείστου μετέχειν ἀποφηναίην ἀμελήσας ἐμβλέψαι χιόνι καὶ ψιμυθίῳ καὶ κρυστάλλῳ ἑτέροις τε μυρίοις τῶν λαμπροτάτων τε ἅμα καὶ ψυχροτάτων, εἶτά τινος αὐτὰ προχειριζομένου, τὸν ἀπὸ τῆς αἰσθήσεως ἔλεγχον ἀποδιδράσκων ἀξιοίην ἐπὶ τὸν λόγον ἰέναι καὶ τούτῳ σκοπεῖσθαι περὶ φύσεως πραγμάτων, οὐκ αἰσθήσεσιν ἀλόγοις ἐπιτρέπειν τὸ πᾶν, ἆρ’ οὐκ ἂν τοῖς νοῦν ἔχουσιν μαίνεσθαι δόξαιμι, μηδ’ ἀφ’ ὧν ἄρχομαι τοῦ λόγου γινώσκων;
beads.english: Suppose that I then called Empedocles and certain others of the natural philosophers as witnesses to the argument, and declared that all bright bodies partake of fire in the greatest measure, having neglected to look at snow and white lead and ice and countless other things that are at once brightest and coldest. Suppose further that, when someone put these forward, I ran away from the refutation that comes from sensation and demanded that we proceed to reason, and by it examine the nature of things, rather than entrust everything to the irrational senses.
Would I not seem to those who have sense to be mad, not knowing even the things from which I begin my argument?

greek_sentences: καὶ ταῦτα ποιοῦσιν οἱ πλείους αὐτῶν ἀμαθεῖς ὑπάρχοντες οὐ τῆς φυσικῆς θεωρίας [460] μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν λογικῶν μεθόδων, αἷς ἀναγκαῖον ἐστιν χρῆσθαι τὸν ὁτιοῦν ἀποδείξαντα, ὥστε μήθ’ ὅσα καλῶς εὕρηται τοῖς φυσικοῖς ἀνδράσιν μήθ’ ὑπὲρ ὧν αὐτῶν εὐλόγως ἠπόρηται γινώσκοντες, ἑκατέροις πολλάκις ἀποφαίνεσθαι τολμῶσι τἀναντία.

φέρε δὲ ὦ πρὸς θεῶν, εἴπερ ἐγὼ νῦν ἀρξάμενος ὧδέ πως λέγειν, ὡς τεττάρων ὄντων στοιχείων ἀέρος καὶ γῆς ὕδατός τε καὶ πυρὸς, ὡς οὐδενὸς ἄλλου ξύμφυτόν ἐστι τὸ λευκὸν καὶ λαμπρὸν χρῶμα, πλὴν αὐγῆς καὶ πυρὸς, εἶτα καὶ τὸν Ἐμπεδοκλέα καὶ τοὺς ἄλλους τινας τῶν φυσικῶν ἐπὶ τῷ λόγῳ καλέσας μάρτυρας, ἅπαντα τὰ λαμπρὰ σώματα πυρὸς πλείστου μετέχειν ἀποφηναίην ἀμελήσας ἐμβλέψαι χιόνι καὶ ψιμυθίῳ καὶ κρυστάλλῳ ἑτέροις τε μυρίοις τῶν λαμπροτάτων τε ἅμα καὶ ψυχροτάτων, εἶτά τινος αὐτὰ προχειριζομένου, τὸν ἀπὸ τῆς αἰσθήσεως ἔλεγχον ἀποδιδράσκων ἀξιοίην ἐπὶ τὸν λόγον ἰέναι καὶ τούτῳ σκοπεῖσθαι περὶ φύσεως πραγμάτων, οὐκ αἰσθήσεσιν ἀλόγοις ἐπιτρέπειν τὸ πᾶν, ἆρ’ οὐκ ἂν τοῖς νοῦν ἔχουσιν μαίνεσθαι δόξαιμι, μηδ’ ἀφ’ ὧν ἄρχομαι τοῦ λόγου γινώσκων;
english_sentences: And most of them do this while being ignorant not only of natural theory [460] but also of the logical methods which anyone who demonstrates anything whatsoever must necessarily use; so that, knowing neither what has been rightly discovered by the natural philosophers nor the very points about which these men have reasonably been in doubt, they often dare to declare the opposite in both cases.

Come now, by the gods: suppose I now began to speak in some such way as this: that, there being four elements, air and earth and water and fire, the white and bright colour is innate in nothing else except light and fire.

Suppose that I then called Empedocles and certain others of the natural philosophers as witnesses to the argument, and declared that all bright bodies partake of fire in the greatest measure, having neglected to look at snow and white lead and ice and countless other things that are at once brightest and coldest.

Suppose further that, when someone put these forward, I ran away from the refutation that comes from sensation and demanded that we proceed to reason, and by it examine the nature of things, rather than entrust everything to the irrational senses.
Would I not seem to those who have sense to be mad, not knowing even the things from which I begin my argument?

beads.greek: ἐξ αἰσθήσεως [461] γὰρ, οἶμαι, καὶ δι’ αἰσθήσεως ἅπαντα τὰ τοιαῦτα τῶν ἀξιωμάτων ἐμάθομεν, ὡς ὁ μὲν ἥλιος λαμπρὸς ἐστιν, αἱ δὲ φλόγες ὑπόξανθοι, τῶν δ’ ἀνθράκων οἱ πλεῖστοι ξανθοί.
beads.english: For it is from sensation [461], I think, and through sensation that we have learned all such axioms as these: that the sun is bright, that flames are yellowish, and that most live coals are yellow.

beads.greek: εἰ μὲν οὖν ἀποστητέον ἐστὶ ταῖς αἰσθήσεσιν, οὐδεμίαν ἕξομεν ἀπόδειξιν οὔθ’ ἡμεῖς ὧν νῦν εἰρήκαμεν οὔτε Ἐμπεδοκλῆς ὡδὶ γράφων, Ἠέλιον μὲν θερμὸν ὁρᾷν καὶ λαμπρὸν ἁπάντη. εἰ δέ ἐστιν ἀληθῆ ταῦτα, δῆλον ὡς πολὺ πρότερον αὐτῶν τὴν αἴσθησιν εἶναι χρὴ πιστήν.
beads.english: If, then, we must abandon the senses, we shall have no demonstration, neither we of the things we have just stated, nor Empedocles when he writes thus: 'Behold the sun, hot and bright everywhere.' But if these things are true, it is clear that sensation must be trustworthy long before them.

beads.greek: ἀλλ’ ἄρχεσθαι μέν φασιν ἀπὸ τῶν αἰσθήσεων ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστιν ἀνθρώπους γε ὄντας, οὐ μὴν ἐπ’ αὐτήν γε προσήκει καταμένειν διὰ παντὸς, ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ τὸ θειότερον ἰέναι τὸν λόγον.
beads.english: 'But,' they say, 'it is necessary for us, being human, to begin from the senses; yet it is not fitting to remain with sensation forever, but rather to proceed to what is more divine, reason.

beads.greek: αἰσθήσεως μὲν γὰρ καὶ τοῖς ἀλόγοις ζώοις μετεῖναι, λόγου δὲ μόνον τοῖς θεοῖς. κᾀντεῦθεν ἀρξάμενοι, δολιχὸν ἀποτείνουσι τὸν λόγον.
beads.english: For we share sensation even with irrational animals, but reason only with the gods.' And beginning from this point they draw the argument out to great length.

beads.greek: καί τινες ἐξ αὐτῶν καὶ τὸν Ἀναξαγόραν ἐπικαλοῦνται μάρτυρα, περὶ τῆς χιόνος ἀποφηνάμενον, ὡς οὐκ εἴη λευκή.
beads.english: And some of them even call upon Anaxagoras as a witness, since he declared of snow that it was not white.

greek_sentences: ἐξ αἰσθήσεως [461] γὰρ, οἶμαι, καὶ δι’ αἰσθήσεως ἅπαντα τὰ τοιαῦτα τῶν ἀξιωμάτων ἐμάθομεν, ὡς ὁ μὲν ἥλιος λαμπρὸς ἐστιν, αἱ δὲ φλόγες ὑπόξανθοι, τῶν δ’ ἀνθράκων οἱ πλεῖστοι ξανθοί.

εἰ δέ ἐστιν ἀληθῆ ταῦτα, δῆλον ὡς πολὺ πρότερον αὐτῶν τὴν αἴσθησιν εἶναι χρὴ πιστήν.

αἰσθήσεως μὲν γὰρ καὶ τοῖς ἀλόγοις ζώοις μετεῖναι, λόγου δὲ μόνον τοῖς θεοῖς.
κᾀντεῦθεν ἀρξάμενοι, δολιχὸν ἀποτείνουσι τὸν λόγον.
καί τινες ἐξ αὐτῶν καὶ τὸν Ἀναξαγόραν ἐπικαλοῦνται μάρτυρα, περὶ τῆς χιόνος ἀποφηνάμενον, ὡς οὐκ εἴη λευκή.
english_sentences: For it is from sensation [461], I think, and through sensation that we have learned all such axioms as these: that the sun is bright, that flames are yellowish, and that most live coals are yellow.

If, then, we must abandon the senses, we shall have no demonstration, neither we of the things we have just stated, nor Empedocles when he writes thus: 'Behold the sun, hot and bright everywhere.' But if these things are true, it is clear that sensation must be trustworthy long before them.
'But,' they say, 'it is necessary for us, being human, to begin from the senses; yet it is not fitting to remain with sensation forever, but rather to proceed to what is more divine, reason.
For we share sensation even with irrational animals, but reason only with the gods.' And beginning from this point they draw the argument out to great length.
And some of them even call upon Anaxagoras as a witness, since he declared of snow that it was not white.

beads.greek: οὗτος ἄρα, φασί, φυσικὸς ἀνὴρ ὑπὲρ τὴν αἴσθησίν ἐστιν καὶ καταφρονεῖ [462] μὲν τῶν ταύτης φαντασμάτων, ἐπὶ δὲ τὸν λόγον ἀνέρχεται, καὶ τούτῳ τὴν τῶν ὄντων θηρᾶται φύσιν.
beads.english: This man, then, they say, being a natural philosopher, is above the senses and despises [462] their appearances; he ascends instead to reason, and by it hunts down the nature of the things that are.

beads.greek: ἐμὲ δ’ εἰ χρὴ τὸ παριστάμενον εἰπεῖν, ὡς ἐλευθέριόν τε καὶ παρ’ ὅλον τὸν βίον ἀλήθειαν σπουδάσαντα, μελαγχολίας ἐπέκεινα προεληλυθέναι νομίζω τοὺς τὰ τοιαῦτα ληροῦντας.
beads.english: But if I must say what occurs to me, as one of free and liberal spirit who has pursued truth throughout his whole life, I consider that those who talk such nonsense have gone beyond melancholy.

beads.greek: εἰ μὲν γὰρ ἀνατρέψουσι τὰ διὰ τῶν αἰσθήσεων ἐναργῶς φαινόμενα, πόθεν ἄρξονται τῶν ἀποδείξεων οὐχ ἕξουσιν.
beads.english: For if they overturn what appears clearly through the senses, they will have no point from which to begin their demonstrations.

beads.greek: εἰ δ’ ὡς ἀπὸ πιστῶν ἄρξονται, πῶς ὕστερον εὐλόγως ἀπιστήσουσιν;
beads.english: But if they begin from these as from things worthy of trust, how will they afterwards reasonably withdraw their trust?

beads.greek: αἱ γὰρ τῶν ἀποδείξεων ἀρχαὶ πιστότεραι τῶν ἀποδεικνυμένων, ἃ τῆς ἐξ ἑτέρων δεῖται πίστεως.
beads.english: For the starting-points of demonstrations are more trustworthy than the things demonstrated, which need to be made credible from other things.

beads.greek: αἱ δ’ ἀρχαὶ τῶν ἀποδείξεων οὔ μόνον αὐταὶ καθ’ ἑαυτὰς, ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς τὴν τῶν ζητουμένων εὕρεσιν ὑπάρχουσι πισταί.
beads.english: And the starting-points of demonstrations are trustworthy not only in and by themselves, but also for the discovery of the things sought.

beads.greek: Καὶ ἔγωγ’ ἂν εὐξαίμην ἅπαντα τὰ πράγματα ταῖς αἰσθήσεσιν ἡμῶν ἐναργῶς ὑποπίπτειν καὶ μηδὲν εἶναι τὸ διαφεῦγον αὐτὰς, ὡς οὕτως ἂν οὔτ’ ἄπορον οὔτ’ ἀμφισβητούμενον ἦν οὐδέν.
beads.english: For my part, I would pray that all things fell clearly under our senses and that nothing escaped them, since in this way nothing would be either insoluble or disputed.

greek_sentences: οὗτος ἄρα, φασί, φυσικὸς ἀνὴρ ὑπὲρ τὴν αἴσθησίν ἐστιν καὶ καταφρονεῖ [462] μὲν τῶν ταύτης φαντασμάτων, ἐπὶ δὲ τὸν λόγον ἀνέρχεται, καὶ τούτῳ τὴν τῶν ὄντων θηρᾶται φύσιν.
ἐμὲ δ’ εἰ χρὴ τὸ παριστάμενον εἰπεῖν, ὡς ἐλευθέριόν τε καὶ παρ’ ὅλον τὸν βίον ἀλήθειαν σπουδάσαντα, μελαγχολίας ἐπέκεινα προεληλυθέναι νομίζω τοὺς τὰ τοιαῦτα ληροῦντας.

english_sentences: This man, then, they say, being a natural philosopher, is above the senses and despises [462] their appearances; he ascends instead to reason, and by it hunts down the nature of the things that are.

But if they begin from these as from things worthy of trust, how will they afterwards reasonably withdraw their trust?
For the starting-points of demonstrations are more trustworthy than the things demonstrated, which need to be made credible from other things.
And the starting-points of demonstrations are trustworthy not only in and by themselves, but also for the discovery of the things sought.
For my part, I would pray that all things fell clearly under our senses and that nothing escaped them, since in this way nothing would be either insoluble or disputed.

beads.greek: ἐπεὶ δ’ ἐκφεύγει τινὰ, πειρατέον ἐπάγειν αὐτοῖς τὸν λόγον, ἀλλ’ οὔτε πόῤῥωθεν, ὡς ἐκεῖνοι ποιοῦσιν, οὔτ’ ἀπέραντα συλλογιζομένους, ἀλλὰ πρῶτον μὲν [463] τὰ σημαινόμενα τῶν ὀνομάτων ἀκριβῶς διαιρουμένους, ἵνα μή τις παρὰ τὴν ὁμωνυμίαν ἐν τοῖς μετὰ ταῦτα ἀπάτη γίγνηται. δεύτερον δὲ τὸ καθ’ αὑτό τι δρῶν, τοῦ κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς ἀφορίζοντας.
beads.english: But since some things do escape them, one must try to bring reason to bear on them, though neither from afar, as those people do, nor by drawing inconclusive syllogisms, but first [463] by precisely distinguishing the meanings of the names, so that no deception arises in what follows through homonymy; and second, by separating off that which acts in some way per se from that which acts per accidens.

beads.greek: εἴρηται δ’ ἐν τοῖς ἔμπροσθεν ὑπὲρ ἀμφοῖν ἀκριβῶς, καὶ τὰ σημαινόμενα τῶν δυνάμει θερμῶν, ἢ ψυχρῶν, ἢ ξηρῶν, ἢ ὑγρῶν, ἢ ὁτιοῦν ἄλλο λεγομένων εἶναι διῄρηται.

beads.greek: τί γὰρ ἔδει τὴν χρόαν ἐλαίου σκοπεῖν, ἢ ῥόδων, ἔχοντάς γε αὐτοῖς χρῆσθαι τοῖς πράγμασιν πολυειδῶς, οὐκ ἐπὶ τῶν ὑγιαινόντων μόνον; ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν νοσούντων σωμάτων;
beads.english: For why should one examine the colour of oil, or of roses, when one is able to use the things themselves in many ways, not only on healthy bodies but also on diseased ones?

ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν νοσούντων σωμάτων;
english_sentences: But since some things do escape them, one must try to bring reason to bear on them, though neither from afar, as those people do, nor by drawing inconclusive syllogisms, but first [463] by precisely distinguishing the meanings of the names, so that no deception arises in what follows through homonymy; and second, by separating off that which acts in some way per se from that which acts per accidens.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ αὐτὰ καθ’ ἑαυτὰ ῥόδα καὶ τὸν χυλὸν αὐτῶν ἔνεστι λαμβάνοντας ἐπιτιθέναι ﻿ [464] τῷ σώματι καὶ ὑγιαίνοντι καὶ νοσοῦντι νόσον ἁπλῆν, ὡς ἔμπροσθεν, εἴρηται καὶ μιγνύντας ἐλαίῳ γλυκεῖ, κατά τε τῶν ἰσχυρῶς ἐψυγμένων ἢ τεθερ μασμένων σωμάτων ἐπιφέρειν, ἀνατρίβοντάς τε καὶ κατατλοῦντας καὶ καταβρέχοντας, εἴσω τε τοῦ σώματος λαμβάνειν ἢ ἄνωθεν διὰ τοῦ στόματος, ἢ κάτωθεν διὰ τῆς ἕδρας, εἶθ’ ὁρᾷν τὸ γιγνόμενον ἐφ’ ἑκάστῃ χρήσει.
beads.english: For it is possible to take roses themselves, on their own, and their juice, and apply them [464] to the body, both when it is healthy and when it is suffering from a simple disease, as was said earlier; and also, mixing them with sweet oil, to apply them to bodies that have been strongly chilled or heated, rubbing them in, pouring them over (?) and soaking the parts; and to take them into the inside of the body, either from above through the mouth or from below through the anus; and then to observe what happens with each use.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ δὴ καὶ τούτου χάριν ἐπισκεπτόμεθα τὴν δύναμιν πάντων τῶν φαρμάκων, ἵνα ἔχωμεν οἷς δεῖ χρῆσθαι, διακαιομένων ὑποχονδρίων καὶ κεφαλῆς, ἢ κατεψυγμένων, ἢ ἡλκωμένων, ἢ φλεγμαινόντων, ἤ τι τοιοῦτον ἕτερον πασχόντων, αὐτῶν τε τούτων καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων μελῶν τοῦ σώματος.
beads.english: Indeed, it is for this reason too that we investigate the power of all drugs: so that we may have the ones we must use when the hypochondria and the head are burning, or have been chilled, or are ulcerated, or are inflamed, or suffer some other such affection, both these parts themselves and all the other members of the body.

beads.greek: εἶθ’ οὕτως ἐναργῆ τε ἅμα καὶ σύντομον ὁδὸν ἔχοντες ἐφ’ ἃ ζητοῦμεν, ἔτι χρόας ἐξετάσομεν, ἢ ὀσμὰς, ἢ συστάσεις, ἢ ψόφους ἑκάστου τῶν φαρμάκων ὅμοιόν τι δρῶντες, τοῖς ἐξ εἰκόνος ἤτοι πλαστῆς, ἢ γραπτῆς ἄνθρωπόν τινα διαγνῶναι βουλομένοις ἐνὸν, αὐτὸν θεάσασθαι τὸν γνωρισθησόμενον.
beads.english: Then, when we thus have a road to what we are seeking that is at once evident and short, shall we still examine the colours, or smells, or consistencies, or sounds of each of the drugs? In doing so we would be acting much like those who wish to recognise some man from an image, whether sculpted or painted, when it is possible to look at the very man who is to be recognised.

english_sentences: For it is possible to take roses themselves, on their own, and their juice, and apply them [464] to the body, both when it is healthy and when it is suffering from a simple disease, as was said earlier; and also, mixing them with sweet oil, to apply them to bodies that have been strongly chilled or heated, rubbing them in, pouring them over (?) and soaking the parts; and to take them into the inside of the body, either from above through the mouth or from below through the anus; and then to observe what happens with each use.

Indeed, it is for this reason too that we investigate the power of all drugs: so that we may have the ones we must use when the hypochondria and the head are burning, or have been chilled, or are ulcerated, or are inflamed, or suffer some other such affection, both these parts themselves and all the other members of the body.
Then, when we thus have a road to what we are seeking that is at once evident and short, shall we still examine the colours, or smells, or consistencies, or sounds of each of the drugs?
In doing so we would be acting much like those who wish to recognise some man from an image, whether sculpted or painted, when it is possible to look at the very man who is to be recognised.

beads.greek: [465] Ταύτῃ τοίνυν ἁμαρτάνειν μοι δοκοῦσιν οὐ σμικρὰ, καὶ τούτων ἔτι μᾶλλον ἐν οἷς ἀπέραντα καὶ ἀναπόδεικτα φλυαροῦσιν, ἀμαθεῖς ὑπάρχοντες ἀποδεικτικῆς μεθόδου.
beads.english: [465] In this respect, then, they seem to me to err in no small way, and still more in those matters in which they babble inconclusive and undemonstrated things, being ignorant of demonstrative method.

beads.greek: ὑποκείσθω γὰρ τὸ πῦρ, εἴτε ξανθὸν εἴτε ἐρυθρὸν, ἢ ὡς ἂν ἐθέλωσιν, οὐ γὰρ μοι διαφέρει.
beads.english: For let fire be supposed to be either yellow or red, or however they wish, for it makes no difference to me.

beads.greek: τί οὖν τοῦτο πρὸς τὸ πᾶν ἐρυθρὸν θερμὸν· εἶναι;
beads.english: What, then, has this to do with everything red being hot?

beads.greek: πᾶν μὲν γὰρ πῦρ, εἰ οὕτως ἔτυχεν, ἐρυθρὸν εἶναι λεκτέον ἐστίν.
beads.english: For every fire, if it should so happen, must be said to be red.

beads.greek: πᾶν δὲ τὸ ἐρυθρὸν πῦρ εἶναι φάναι καταγέλαστον, ἔτι δὲ μᾶλλον εἰ πᾶν τὸ ἐρυθρὸν θερμὸν εἶναι λέγοι τις.
beads.english: But to say that everything red is fire is ridiculous, and still more so if one were to say that everything red is hot.

beads.greek: εἰ μὲν ἐξ ἀρχῆς εἴληπτο κατὰ τὸν λόγον, ὡς πᾶν τὸ θερμὸν ἐρυθρὸν ἐστιν, ἦν ἴσως διαστρέψαντα τὸ ἀξίωμα τὸ ἐρυθρὸν ἅπαν ἀποφῆναι θερμὸν ἁμαρτάνοντα μὲν κᾀν τούτῳ προφανῶς.
beads.english: If it had been assumed from the beginning in the argument that everything hot is red, it would perhaps have been possible, by twisting the proposition round, to declare everything red hot, though erring plainly even in this.

beads.greek: οἱ γὰρ ἀντιστρέφοντες, οὐχ οἱ ἀναστρέφοντες ἀλλήλοις λόγοι συναληθεύονται, ἀλλ’ ὅμως ἦν ἂν, οἶμαι, πλησίον ὁ παραλογισμός.
beads.english: For it is propositions that convert (antistrephontes) with one another, not those that are reversed (anastrephontes), that are true together; but nevertheless the paralogism would, I think, have been a near one.

beads.greek: ἐπεὶ δὲ οὐδ’ αὐτὸ τοῦτο κατ’ ἀρχὰς εἴληπται, λέγω δὴ τὸ πᾶν εἶναι τὸ θερμὸν ἐρυθρὸν, οὐδ’ ἀναστρέψαντα δυνατὸν εἰπεῖν ἅπαν εἶναι τὸ ἐρυθρὸν θερμόν.
beads.english: But since not even this itself has been assumed at the outset, I mean that everything hot is red, it is not possible, even by reversing it, to say that everything red is hot.

For let fire be supposed to be either yellow or red, or however they wish, for it makes no difference to me.
What, then, has this to do with everything red being hot?
For every fire, if it should so happen, must be said to be red.
But to say that everything red is fire is ridiculous, and still more so if one were to say that everything red is hot.

If it had been assumed from the beginning in the argument that everything hot is red, it would perhaps have been possible, by twisting the proposition round, to declare everything red hot, though erring plainly even in this.

For it is propositions that convert (antistrephontes) with one another, not those that are reversed (anastrephontes), that are true together; but nevertheless the paralogism would, I think, have been a near one.
But since not even this itself has been assumed at the outset, I mean that everything hot is red, it is not possible, even by reversing it, to say that everything red is hot.

beads.greek: τριχῶς οὖν ἁμαρτάνουσι κατὰ τὸν λόγον οἱ φάσκοντες τὰ ῥόδα θερμὰ τὴν κρᾶσιν ὑπάρχειν, [466] ὅτι καὶ ἐρυθρά.
beads.english: Those who assert that roses are hot in their mixture, [466] because they are also red, therefore err in three ways in their argument.

beads.greek: πρῶτον μὲν ὅτι μὴ δείξαντες ὅτι πᾶν πῦρ ἐρυθρὸν ἀντιστρέφειν αὐτῷ, ὅτι πᾶν ἐρυθρὸν πῦρ πειρῶνται λόγον ἕτερον, ὡς ἀληθῆ· δεύτερον δ’ ὅτι μὴ γινώσκουσι τοὺς ἀντιστρέφοντας, οὐ τοὺς ἀναστρέφοντας τοῖς ἀληθέσι λόγοις ἀληθεῖς εἶναι καὶ αὐτούς.

beads.greek: ὅτι δ’ οὐ μόνον ἄχρηστον εἰς τὰ παρόντα τὸ τοιοῦτον, ἀλλὰ καὶ προφανῶς ψεῦδός ἐστιν, δῆλον παντί.
beads.english: That such a proposition is not only useless for the present purposes but also manifestly false is clear to everyone.

beads.greek: δεόμεθα γὰρ οὐκ εἰ τὸ ἐρυθρὸν ἅπαν πῦρ ἐστιν, ἀλλ’ ὅτι θερμὸν ἀποδειχθῆναι.
beads.english: For what we need to have demonstrated is not whether everything red is fire, but that it is hot.

beads.greek: ὡς εἴ γε πῦρ ἐστι πᾶν τὸ ἐρυθρὸν, ἔσται δηλονότι καὶ τὸ ῥόδον ἡμῖν πῦρ.
beads.english: Indeed, if everything red is fire, then evidently the rose too will be fire for us.

beads.greek: ἀλλ’ οἱ μὴ γινώσκοντες, οἶμαι, τὰς λογικὰς μεθόδους ἰατροὶ, πρῶτον μὲν ἐπ’ αὐτῷ τούτῳ μέγιστα σφάλλονται, τῷ τοὺς οἰκείους ὅρους ὑπερβαίνειν.
beads.english: But physicians who do not know the logical methods, I think, go most gravely wrong first of all in this very thing: in overstepping their own proper boundaries.

beads.english: For experience together with brief inferences is sufficient to discover the powers of drugs; and then they also err in their arguments, like boys newly instructed [467] in logical theory.

beads.greek: τῆς δ’ αὐτῆς πλημμελείας ἔχονται καὶ ὅσοι ταῖς ὀδμαῖς τεκμαίρονταί τι περὶ δυνάμεως φαρμάκων.
beads.english: The same fault is committed by all who infer something about the power of drugs from their odours.

beads.greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ ἅπαν εὐῶδες θερμὸν, ὡς λέγουσί τίνες, ἀγνοοῦντες ὅπως ἀκούειν χρὴ τῶν ὑπ’ Ἀριστοτέλους καὶ Θεοφράστου περὶ τούτων εἰρημένων, ἃ κατὰ τὸ τέταρτον τῶνδε τῶν ὑπομνημάτων ἡμεῖς διοριοῦμεν, οὔθ’ ἅπαν θερμὸν εὐῶδες, οὐ μὴν οὐδὲ δυσῶδες ἅπαν θερμὸν, οὐδ’ εἴ τι θερμὸν ὑπάρχει, δυσῶδες.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ καὶ τῶν θερμῶν μυρία τὰ μὲν εὐώδη, τὰ δὲ δυσώδη, τὰ δ’ οὐδέτερα καὶ τῶν ψυχρῶν ὡσαύτως.

beads.greek: καίτοι τί λέγω ψυχρὰ καὶ θερμὰ, δέον θερμαίνοντα καὶ ψύχοντα λέγειν ἡμᾶς, ἅπερ καὶ ζητοῦμεν.

beads.greek: οὐ γὰρ δὴ τό γε ἁπλῶς θερμὸν ἢ τὸ πρὸς τοῦτο ἐξεταζόμενον ἐπισκέπτεσθαι πρόκειται νῦν, ἀλλὰ τὸ θερμαῖνον ἀνθρώπειον σῶμα.
beads.english: For what is now proposed for examination is not what is hot simply, or what is assessed in relation to this, but what heats the human body.

beads.greek: καὶ δὴ καὶ ψυχρὸν οὐχ ἁπλῶς, ἀλλ’ ὅ τι περ ἂν ἄνθρωπον ψύχῃ.
beads.english: And likewise not cold simply, but whatever cools a human being.

For what is now proposed for examination is not what is hot simply, or what is assessed in relation to this, but what heats the human body.

beads.greek: πάλιν οὖν ἐνταῦθα μὴ διελόμενοι τὰ σημαινόμενα τῶν ὀνομάτων [468] σφάλλονται παρὰ τὴν ὁμωνυμίαν, ὥσπερ εἰ καὶ περὶ χερσαίου τις κυνὸς διαλεγόμενος ἐπὶ τὸν θαλάττιον μεταβαίνοι τῷ λόγῳ, νομίζων ὥσπερ τοὔνομα τῶν ζώων ἀμφοτέρων ἕν ἐστιν, οὕτω καὶ τὴν φύσιν αὐτῶν μίαν ὑπάρχειν.
beads.english: Here again, then, by not distinguishing the things signified by the names, [468] they are misled through the homonymy, just as if someone discoursing about the land dog were to pass over in his argument to the sea dog, supposing that, as the name of both animals is one, so too their nature is one.

beads.greek: ἀλλ’ ἡμῖν δέδεικται σαφῶς ἐν τοῖς περὶ κράσεως ὑπομνήμασιν, ἃ καὶ κατ’ ἀρχὰς εὐθὺς ἡγεῖσθαι τῆσδε τῆς πραγματείας ἔφαμεν, ἄλλο μὲν εἶναι τὸ δυνάμει θερμὸν, ἄλλο δὲ τὸ ἐνεργείᾳ.
beads.english: But it has been shown clearly by us in the commentaries On Mixtures, which we said right at the beginning should precede this treatise, that what is hot in potentiality is one thing, and what is hot in actuality another.

beads.greek: καὶ τούτου τοῦ ἐνεργείᾳ θερμοῦ τὸ μὲν ἁπλῶς λέγεσθαι θερμὸν, τὸ δὲ κατ’ ἐπικράτησιν, τὸ δὲ πρὸς τὸ σύμμετρον ὁμογενὲς, τὸ δὲ πρὸς ὁτιοῦν τὸ ἐπιτυχόν.
beads.english: And of this hot in actuality, one is called hot simply, another by predominance, another in relation to the well-proportioned thing of the same kind, and another in relation to any chance thing whatever.

beads.greek: καὶ δὴ καὶ τὸν ἄνθρωπον οὐχ ἀπλῶς θερμὸν, ὥσπερ τὸ πῦρ, ἀλλ’ ἐπικρατήσει θερμὸν ὑπάρχειν ἐλέγομεν.
beads.english: And indeed we said that man is hot not simply, as fire is, but hot by predominance; for there is in him a greater portion of the hot than of the cold.

beads.greek: εἶναι γὰρ ἐν αὐτῷ πλείονα τοῦ θερμοῦ μοῖραν ἢ τοῦ ψυχροῦ. καὶ τοίνυν καὶ ὅσα πρὸς τούτων λέγεται θερμὰ δυνάμει, τῷ τοῦτον θερμαίνειν λεχθήσεται.
beads.english: And so whatever things are said in relation to these [πρὸς τούτων; perhaps to be read πρὸς τοῦτον, 'in relation to him'] to be hot in potentiality will be so called by virtue of heating him.

beads.greek: καὶ ἡ κρίσις αὐτῶν ῥᾴστη τέ ἐστι καὶ διὰ τῆς ἐμπειρίας ἐξετασθήσεται, βραχέων, ὡς εἴρηται, καὶ πρόσθεν ἐπιλογισμῶν δεομένη.

beads.greek: τούτους οὖν ὑπερβαίνοντες οἱ σοφισταὶ, τόν τε χρόνον ﻿ [469] ἀναλίσκουσι τῶν μειρακίων καὶ σοφίσμασι παράγοντες ἀνθρώπους ἀγυμνάστους. λύσεως σοφισμάτων ἀναπιμπλᾶσι ψευδῶν δογμάτων.
beads.english: Passing over these, then, the sophists both waste the time [469] of the young men and, leading astray with sophisms people untrained in the solution of sophisms, fill them up with false doctrines.

beads.greek: ἐχρῆν γὰρ μήτε χρόας μνημονεύειν αὐτοὺς μήτ’ ὀδμῆς, ἀλλὰ μηδὲ συστάσεως, ἢ λειότητος, ἢ τραχύτητος, ἤ τινος ἑτέρου τοιούτου.
beads.english: For they ought to have mentioned neither colour nor smell, nor indeed consistency, or smoothness, or roughness, or any other such thing.

beads.greek: τί γὰρ ὅτι γλίσχρον τοὔλαιον, ἢ ὅτι λεῖον, ἢ ὅτι στίλβον, ἢ ὑγρὸν, ἢ ὠχρὸν, ἢ λιπαρὸν, ἢ ὀλισθηρὸν, ἢ δυσξήραντον ἐπαλειφόμενον τοῖς σώμασιν;
beads.english: For what does it matter that oil is viscous, or that it is smooth, or that it glistens, or is liquid, or pale yellow, or oily, or slippery, or slow to dry when smeared on bodies?

beads.greek: οὔτε γὰρ εἰ θερμὸν, οὔτε εἰ ψυχρὸν, οὔτ’ εἰ ξηρὸν, οὔτ’ εἰ ὑγρόν ἐστιν τὴν δύναμιν, ἐξ οὐδενὸς ἔνεστι τῶν τοιούτων συλλογίσασθαι.
beads.english: For from none of such things is it possible to infer whether it is hot, or cold, or dry, or moist in power.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ τῶν γλίσχρων καὶ τῶν λείων καὶ τῶν στιλβόντων τὰ μὲν θερμαίνει φανερῶς ἡμᾶς, τὰ δὲ ψύχει, καὶ τὰ μὲν ξηραίνει, τὰ δὲ ὑγραίνει.
beads.english: For of viscous and smooth and glistening things, some evidently heat us, others cool us, and some dry, others moisten.

beads.greek: καὶ καθ’ ἕκαστον τῶν συμβεβηκότων οὐκ ἐλαίῳ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἅπασιν οὐδέν ἐστιν εὑρεῖν πάγιον οὐδὲ διηνεκὲς, ὡς ἐπ’ αὐτῷ συστήσασθαί τινα καθόλου πρότασιν.
beads.english: And with respect to each of the accidents, not in oil alone but in all other things as well, it is impossible to find anything fixed or constant, so as to establish on it some universal premise.

beads.greek: Ἐῶ γὰρ λέγειν ὅτι οὐδὲ ἐπιστημονικοῖς ἐν ἅπασι τοῖς τοιούτοις λόγοις οἱ σοφισταὶ χρῶνται [470] πρὸς τὴν τῶν λημμάτων εὕρεσιν, ἀλλ’ ἐξ ἐπαγωγῆς, καὶ τὸ χεῖρον ἁπάντων, ὅτι μηδ’ ἐπισκεψάμενοί ποτε περὶ φύσεως ἐπαγωγῆς, μηδ’ ἄν τις αὐτοὺς εἰς τοῦτο προκαλῆται, τολμῶντες ἀκολουθεῖν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς ὑπὲρ ἀποδείξεώς τι πραγματευομένοις ἐπιτιμῶντες.
beads.english: For I pass over the fact that in all such matters the sophists do not even use scientific arguments [470] for finding the lemmas, but argue from induction. Worst of all, they have never once examined the nature of induction, and they do not dare to follow even if someone challenges them to it; they even censure those who devote some labour to demonstration.

beads.greek: ἔτι δὲ χεῖρον ὅτι μηδ’ ἐξ ἐπαγωγῆς μόνον, ἀλλ’ ἐκ παραδειγμάτων ἐνίοτε συλλογίζονται, καθάπερ οἱ ῥήτορες.
beads.english: Still worse, they draw their conclusions not from induction alone but sometimes from examples, as the rhetors do. For the man who says that oil is cold because it is viscous, as phlegm also is, reasons through an example.

beads.greek: ὅ τε γὰρ φάσκων ψυχρὸν εἶναι τοὔλαιον, ὅτι καὶ γλίσχρον, ὥσπερ καὶ τὸ φλέγμα, διὰ παραδείγματος συλλογίζεται, τὴν ἴσην ἰσχὺν τῆς ἀποδείξεως παρέχων ὁμοίως τῷ λέγοντι θερμὸν ὑπάρχειν αὐτὸ, διότι γλίσχρον ἐστὶν, ὡς ὁ ἰξός· ὅ τε φάσκων θερμὸν εἶναι, ὅτι ῥᾳδίως ἐκφλογοῦται καθάπερ ἄσφαλτος, τῷ λέγοντι ψυχρὸν εἶναι, διότι ῥᾳδίως πήγνυται, καθάπερ ὕδωρ.
beads.english: He offers a demonstration of equal force with that of the man who says it is hot because it is viscous, like birdlime. Likewise, the man who says it is hot because it easily bursts into flame, like bitumen, offers a demonstration of equal force with that of the man who says it is cold because it easily congeals, like water.

beads.greek: συνεκπυροῦσθαί τε γὰρ, φησὶ, καὶ ἐπικαίειν τὸ ἔλαιον ὑπὸ τῆς τρίψεως θερμαινόμενον [472] ἐνόμιζεν καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο ἐξικμάζειν καὶ ξηραίνειν ἱκανῶς, ὥσπερ τῶν ὀπτωμένων τὰ χριόμενα.
beads.english: For he thought, he says, that the oil, being heated by the rubbing, becomes fiery along with [the body] and scorches, [472] and in this way draws out the moisture and dries considerably, just as, among things being roasted, those that are anointed do.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ καὶ ταῦτα σκληρύνεσθαι μᾶλλον ἢ εἰ χωρὶς ἐλαίου τις ὀπτήσειεν.
beads.english: For these too become harder than if one were to roast them without oil.

beads.greek: αὐτὴν δὲ ἴσως ἄμεινον ὅλην παραγράψαι τοῦ Διοκλέους τὴν ῥῆσιν.
beads.english: But perhaps it is better to copy out the whole statement of Diocles itself.

beads.greek: ἔχει δὲ ᾧδε· τὸ δὲ μετ’ ἐλαίου τρίβειν οὐχ ὁμοίως ἐδοκίμαζε.
beads.english: It runs thus: 'Rubbing with oil he did not approve of in the same way.

beads.greek: πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ ἀνώμαλον ᾤετο γίνεσθαι τὴν τοιαύτην τρίψιν παρὰ τὸ τὰς χεῖρας ὀλισθαίνειν καὶ μὴ δύνασθαι τῆς σαρκὸς ὁμοίως ἀντιλαμβάνεσθαι διὰ τὸ λίπος.
beads.english: For in the first place he thought that such rubbing turns out uneven, because the hands slip and cannot take hold of the flesh evenly on account of the fat.

beads.greek: ἔτι δὲ καὶ σκληρύνεσθαι καὶ ἐπικαίεσθαι τὸ δέρμα τοῖς οὕτω τριβομένοις ἔφη μᾶλλον ἢ τοῖς ξηροῖς.
beads.english: Further, he said that the skin is also hardened and scorched in those rubbed in this way more than in those rubbed dry.

beads.greek: συνεκπυροῦσθαι γὰρ καὶ ἐπικαίειν τὸ ἔλαιον θερμαινόμενον ὑπὸ τῆς τρίψεως, καθάπερ τῶν ὀπτωμένων τὰ χριόμενα τῶν μὴ χριομένων, ἐκπυρουμένου τοῦ ἐλαίου θερμαινόμενα καὶ ἐξικμαζόμενα λίαν σκληρύνεσθαι μᾶλλον.
beads.english: For the oil, heated by the rubbing, becomes fiery along with it and scorches, just as, among things being roasted, those that are anointed, being heated as the oil becomes fiery and having their moisture drawn out excessively, become harder than those not anointed.

beads.greek: ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ τὰ ἐν τῷ ἐλαίῳ ἑψόμενα κραῦρα καὶ καπυρὰ γίνεσθαι διὰ τὴν αὐτὴν αἰτίαν.
beads.english: Likewise things boiled in oil also become brittle and crisp for the same cause.

beads.greek: πρὸς δὲ τούτοις, ὥσπερ τὰ ξύλα καὶ τὰ δέρματα καὶ τὰ ἄλλα τὰ μετ’ ἐλαίου τριβόμενα συνδιαδίδωσιν εἴσω τὸ ἔλαιον, οὕτως ᾤετο καὶ τὰ σώματα.
beads.english: In addition to these, just as wood and hides and the other things rubbed with oil let the oil pass through inwards along with them, so, he thought, do bodies also.'
